records.text: 5 North America Economic Research 21 August 2026 J P M O R G A N Global Data Watch: Not friendly, but fair • Expansion on track, rates up across the curve for fundamental reasons • Jackson Hole unlikely to deliver clues; BoJ to hike earlier and more • China weakens in July; upsides to rest of EM Asia • Next week: US Jul real PCE (0.0), Core (0.3); BoK +25, NBH -25 Since the COVID inflation shock, a “high-for-long” interest rate view has been a key tenet of our macroeconomic narrative. Expectations for inflation to remain at uncomfortably sticky levels has been a central feature of a view that central bank policy rates would not return to pre-COVID levels before the next global recession. But our narrative also incorporated a shift upward in both short and longer rates for reasons beyond sticky inflation. Understanding these forces is important for gauging the trajectory of financial conditions and the expansion. At the short end, we argued for a resilient expansion in the face of the synchronized global hiking cycle in 2022-2024, as neutral real rates were higher than many had expected in response to strong cyclical fundamentals. Relative to the post-GFC expansion, healthy balance sheets and supportive credit conditions pointed to stronger and more resilient private sector demand. records.text: US Rates Weekly 21 August 2026 Citi Research 24 Canada showed that Canadians were net sellers of US Treasuries in June. So, this is likely some other country buying with Canada as a custodial center. We would not attach much significance to a single data point from Canada, unless we see a string of monthly sales or purchases. The large increase in Canda holdings was offset by sales from the Cayman Islands and the UK. The Cayman Islands had a decrease of $32.1bn in long-term holdings (z-score of - 3.03). We think this was private investors rotating into some T-bills, as Cayman T-bill holdings increased around $15bn in June. It could also hedge funds domiciled in Cayman Islands moving out of cash-futures basis trades as basis opportunities decreased significantly in recent months. The United Kingdom decreased their long-term holdings by $9.2bn in June (z-score of -0.81). In the first five months of the year private investors in the UK bought around $80bn of USTs, so it would make sense that investors exited some of their positions that they entered when volatility picked up in June. We also saw holdings in Germany, Spain, and Belgium increase by $19.5bn collectively. We think this increase is likely being driven by China moving their long- term Treasuries into these European custodial centers. records.text: M Global Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 Valuations: Watch Out for Curve Balls Historically, yields beyond 4.5%-5% start to pose a challenge for multiples In a past report, we've noted that while the level of nominal bond yields is not a huge challenge for equity multiples, we caveated with how it's only true when rates are within a certain range. Historical data show that in the US, nominal yields past 4-5% are typically associated with lower P/E ratios, and this phenomenon holds when looking across the UST curve. That said, history shows that large spikes in yields also have repricing implications. Typically, multiples start to decline rapidly when 10Y yields move by 100bp or more within 6 months. We assume that the increased buybacks will be funded entirely with greater bill issuance. The increased front-end supply should have a muted impact on funding markets and front-end swap spreads. Funding conditions have been benign, and while front-end uncertainty has likely contributed to more bill volatility, we would not expect the incremental supply to have a notable impact on absorption. At the long end, standard rules of thumb for the impact of duration removal on long-end yields imply modest impact from the increase in buyback size—our estimate of QE was that 1% of GDP worth of UST purchases pushes 10y yields down by about 4bp, though about half the effect is attributable to the guidance channel (i.e. duration removal alone is worth closer to 2bp per 1% of GDP). Most deployments remain in copilot or supervised modes where humans execute decisions or approve consequential actions despite agents being technically capable of greater autonomy. Delegated and fully autonomous workflows concentrate legal, operational and financial risk with the enterprise. General counsel, risk functions, insurers and auditors may therefore influence adoption as much as the teams selecting the underlying model. Enterprise deployment should accelerate as agent reliability becomes independently measurable and liability becomes assignable, transferable and insurable. Bounded, checkable and reversible workflows will reach production first. The strongest initial agentic use cases involve constrained decisions, observable outcomes, reversible actions and clear thresholds for escalation. Invoice processing provides one example, with AI extracting structured fields, applying automated checks, routing low-confidence cases for review and posting transactions into a reversible ERP workflow. records.text: Takeaways from Private Companies Daloopa Company Introduction Daloopa is an AI-powered financial data and research platform that automates the extraction, standardization and validation of financial statement line items, KPIs and company guidance from regulatory filings, earnings materials and other corporate disclosures. The platform is designed for equity analysts, investors and financial institutions, providing source-linked and audit-ready financial data that can be integrated directly into research workflows and valuation models. It supports model maintenance, earnings analysis, financial forecasting and investment research workflows. The platform is used by hedge funds, asset managers and investment banks seeking to improve productivity, data quality and workflow efficiency. As a result, federal loan allocations alone contributed significantly, accounting for roughly EUR 10 bn of the year-over-year increase in core budget investments (see Figure 10 and Figure 16; for a more detailed discussion see also here). When these (core budget) loan disbursements and other financial transactions – such as participations or guarantee drawdowns – are excluded, and fully adjusted total investment figures are examined, YTD investment spending was almost EUR 13 bn lower than the headline figure suggests (see Figure 11 and Figure 12). Notably, YTD adjusted core budget investment spending reached only about EUR 15 bn in July. This is significantly lower than at the same point in previous years, falling well over EUR 3 bn – roughly 18% – below the prior-year level. This shortfall is primarily driven by the sluggish disbursement of allocations and grants, alongside slow progress in building and construction investments (see Figure 14). records.text: July price. Asia’s LNG premium has come down: June-to-date has seen a trend of a narrowing JKM premium over the European LNG benchmark. This summer JKM priced on average about USD2.3/MMBtu over DES NWE. By August 18 it had eroded to USD0.5/MMBtu before rising to about USD1.45/MMBtu today (August 24). This narrowing is driven by Asian LNG procurement ha ving slowed down after aggressive buying earlier this summer (for example, Japanese and South Korea inventories look adequate). Cheaper freight adds to this. A lower Asian bid has helped ease the premium over Europe but hasn’t narrowed enough to provide a sustained incentive to diverge cargoes into Europe . Figure 1 shows the premium for JKM LNG prices over those in northwestern Europe, corrected for the cost of shipping LNG from the USGC to both locations. It shows that Asian prices are more attractive for LNG shipped through the Panama Canal. I f the LNG need s to traverse t he Cape of Good Hope or the Suez Canal (the latter isn’t particularly relevant now given the disruptions in the Middle East), however, diverting t o Europe becomes more attractive. In short, Warsh may wish to counter one market narrative that any Fed policy actions could be delayed until the task forces have completed their work. records.text: US Economics 21 August 2026 Citi Research 2 Data – The preliminary August manufacturing PMI index fell modestly to 53.2 from 53.9 in July, softer than consensus expectations for it to remain unchanged on the month and contrary to our expectations for another modest increase. The output component to 51.9, the lowest level in just over a year, while new orders moved largely sideways at 54.2. Employment rose modestly to 51.4. Manufacturing input prices moved largely sideways at 66.2, while output prices fell to 58.9. The services PMI index (business activity) rose notably in August to 56.8, stronger than consensus expectations at 54.0 and our 54.5 forecast. New business activity rose to 55.3 while employment rose substantially to 53.2. Services input prices fell to 59.3 while output prices fell to 55.4. Citi’s view – Overall strong PMI survey data will continue the narrative of US resilience, especially with the service PMI index back at recent highs of the last few years. But while activity overall likely continues to grow at a solid pace, supported both by consumption and AI investment, we would note that recently strengthening survey data, especially in services, is a bit at odds with hard data that have if anything been softening. The manufacturing PMI index, while still solidly in expansion, has been moderating in recent months. records.text: US long-term rates and developments around Iran will remain in the spotlight in the week ahead, while Jackson Hole also attracts attention. Regarding Iran, US President Trump declared an “economic war” against the nation on the 19th, and Treasury Secretary Bessent has said specific measures will be announced at a press conference on the 24th (eg, Bloomberg), so geopolitical headlines will be closely watched at the start of the week. In terms of monetary policy, the Jackson Hole Economic Symposium will be held on 27-29 August. The theme for 2026 is “Financial Innovation: Implications for Payments and Policy, ” suggesting policy responses to new payment methods may be discussed. The detailed schedule will be released the day before the symposium, but at this stage, a speech by Fed Chair Warsh on the evening of the 28th has already been announced. As Jackson Hole runs from Friday through Sunday, any important remarks over the weekend are likely to become a factor for the following week. In addition, BoJ Deputy Governor Himino is scheduled to speak on the 27th, and we will watch for comments suggesting a September rate hike. On the data front, releases include August US consumer confidence on the 25th, July Australian CPI, July US PCE deflator and Q2 US GDP growth on the 26th and August Tokyo CPI on the 28th. Over the last year, although KTB yields have increased, the carry and the upward movement in FX implied yields have resulted in a net profit for the trade. The free cash flow for Korean exporters has risen rapidly over the past few months, leading to an increase in USD liquidity onshore, which in turn has driven the cross-currency basis and FX implied yields higher in recent weeks (Figure 1). As the positive carry has diminished at current levels due to the move in FX implied yields (Figure 2), we prefer to close the position. We exited the bond at 3.43% and now unwind the remaining FX implied position at 3.34%, capturing a total profit of USD165.4k on the trade idea, including carry and rolldown. records.text: 21 August 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 12 Fed and repo outlook A string of soft economic data over the past week has reduced market pricing for Fed hikes this year to just under one hike by December. The odds of a September hike have also fallen to around 35%. The scale of the move feels slightly stretched for two reasons. First, the data details were more mixed than the headlines suggested. Payrolls were significantly weaker, but the unemployment rate also fell to its lowest level in 18 months. Retail sales were weak as well, but that followed several months of strength and may have been distorted by the timing shift associated with Prime Day. Second, there is still a meaningful amount of data before the next FOMC meeting, whose outcome will likely depend on new developments around labor market conditions, the Middle East, a nd energy prices. Our economists maintain their base case for a 25bp hike in September, though conviction is arguably lower. In terms of market pricing, Fed funds OIS for the Z6 carry period is near the top of the estimated range implied by plausible FOMC outcomes over the next three to four months. This reflects the view that the Fed is still likely to hike at least once this year, which we think is broadly justified. For the SOFR-FF basis, nearly $500bn of net bill issuance during July and August, or about $450bn after Fed purchases, has been absorbed well, with little spillover into repo. On the prime auto side, most issuers do not issue down to the high yield ratings and instead choose to retain the bottom equity tranche and issue only investment grade notes, if not only AAA rated. CRVNA is the only regular issuer of high yield notes on the prime side as it holds 5% vertical risk retention. CRVNA 2026-P3 totalled $1.6bn in size, with BB notes $0.02bn while AAA tranches totaled $1.3bn. The other notable issuance in prime auto ABS was Santander Bank’s SBAT shelf in its 2025-SF1 transaction last year as it issued down to a single B rating. Instead of ABS, the CLN structure is where the banks usually issue BB and B tranches referencing prime auto loan performance, with YTD high yield CLN supply and outstanding at $606.5mn and $1088.2mn, respectively, across various issuers. Aside from auto ABS, MPL unsecured consumer ABS programs such as PAID and UPST are other active issuers of high yield ABS, with current outstandings of $1,503mn and $745mn, respectively, followed by BNPL and branch issuers AFRMT and OPTN at $313mn and $248mn, respectively. The gap is especially pronounced in central Tokyo area, where the difference in growth is now nearly 2 percentage points. In reality, this gap may be smaller than it seems when accounting for changes in building quality. Current CPI rent statistics do not adjust for quality deterioration caused by aging. Even if the nominal rent remains the same, a decline in building quality would imply a higher real (quality-adjusted) rent. Since wooden houses normally deteriorate faster than non-wooden ones, we believe a quality adjustment would result in a higher growth rate for wooden home rents than presently reported, thereby narrowing the gap with non-wooden rents. Data users have long called for the introduction of quality adjustments in rent statistics, but the measure was rejected even in the recently revision in the CPI to a 2025 base year. Consequently, we expect the gap in growth between wooden and non-wooden house rents to persist for the foreseeable future. This structural difference is one factor keeping imputed rents (over 16% of CPI) lower than actual market trends. records.text: Japan Viewpoint | 24 August 2026 5 Concerned about undermining the BoJ's rate hike cycle? As a result, some market participants argue that intervention is ultimately ineffective, or that the Japanese government's commitment to correcting yen weakness is limited. (Interestingly, however, market participants who experienced the coordinated US-Japan interventions of the 1990s remain alert to the possibility of further intervention and yen appreciation.) Our view is that the US and Japanese authorities may be deliberately refraining from further intervention. Coordinated intervention carries not only the credibility of Japan's Ministry of Finance but also that of the US Treasury. Having embarked on such a policy, it seems unlikely that authorities would allow it to end inconclusively or that their commitment to addressing yen weakness is inherently weak. One possible explanation for passing up an ideal intervention opportunity is concern that excessive FX market moves could interfere with the BoJ's rate hike path. A break below 155 could alter market behavior, turning USD/JPY into a sell-on-rallies market and raising the possibility of a move below 150. If market volatility were to become excessive, the likelihood of the BoJ delaying rate hikes could increase. There have been reports that the Takaichi administration supports early rate hikes to reinforce the effectiveness of intervention. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 15 Preliminary estimate of the benchmark revision to payrolls. The BLS will release its preliminary estimate of the benchmark revision to payrolls. The estimate is based on administrative data from the unemployment insurance system that provide a direct count of payrolls and a benchmark for the level of payrolls as of March 2026. This is just a preliminary estimate. The full and final revision will be pulled into the monthly payroll estimates next February. We expect little revision, for several reasons. First, through December 2025, the 12-month changes for QCEW and for payroll survey estimates of private payrolls are very similar; the slowing between March 2025 and December 2025, too, are very similar. Second, the BLS last year adopted new methods for estimating the effects of business 'births' and deaths', which should have (marginally) improved the accuracy of the initial, pre- benchmark estimates. That said, this estimate of the benchmark revision will incorporate QCEW data for 1Q that are not yet published; and the 1Q data could make a difference. Payrolls are currently shown as accelerating sharply.

records.text: M Idea 2 Headline Further Up, Core Stable Our EA August inflation forecasts | Headline up to 3.3%Y and core stable at 2.5%Y: August could bring another uptick of headline (3.3%Y) and stable core (2.5%Y) inflation, primarily due to higher energy inflation. We expect energy inflation to move up sharply (14.5%Y from 10.3%Y), as fuel prices are elevated across countries – with a notable push in Germany potentially linked to low Rhine water levels affecting supply – while the uptick in wholesale natural gas prices increasingly feeds through to retail gas and electricity tariffs. Food inflation should edge down slightly (1.1%Y from 1.2%Y), as base effects from last year's sharp increases continue to dominate in the absence of near-term pipeline pressures. We expect services inflation to hold stable at 3.3%Y, with potentially some strengthening in tourism-related items but steady non-tourism services inflation. We forecast goods inflation up further (1.1%Y from 0.9%Y), as ongoing IT-related ("chipflation") price pressures continue to build, with no correction expected from the German medicine-price jump observed in July. Together, this would keep core inflation unchanged at a firm 2.5%Y. The nitrogen issue is real but should not be major. Some of the fastest-growing parts of the Midland Basin have elevated nitrogen concentrations, up to 5 to 8% in some parts of the basin. For LNG plants, nitrogen, which is inert, occupies liquefaction capacity and lowers LNG energy density. Nitrogen can create operating inefficiencies in liquefaction trains and LNG carrier fuel systems. LNG buyers generally demand much tighter nitrogen specifications than domestic pipeline customers. Several LNG operators and developers have publicly identified rising Permian nitrogen concentrations as a growing operational challenge. In practice, LNG plants often want feedgas nitrogen levels at around 1% or less, while some LNG-bound pipelines impose limits around 2.0-2.6 mol%. Nonetheless, nitrogen can be removed, such as using Nitrogen Rejection Units (NRUs), blending with better-quality gas, or upstream treating and processing. Thus, nitrogen is an economic issue and raises processing, compression and blending costs. If delivered Permian gas is much cheaper than Haynesville gas, then these costs and additional process can be incorporated. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

Figure 5 reinforces this view, showing that media sentiment around Fed credibility remains intact and that the recent rise in inflation expectations has not elicited an outsized response. The shaded periods denote episodes when the FOMC adopted a very dovish stance, typically occurring alongside falling , rather than rising , inflation expectations, suggesting that perceptions of Fed tone tend to follow shifts in inflation expectations. records.text: sizes unchanged for the next several quarters, the increase in long-end buybacks will effectively be funded with T-bills. Shifting from bonds into T-bills shortens Treasury’s WAM at the margin, but we estimate that it takes roughly $100bn of 30-year buybacks financed with bill issuance to reduce Treasury’s WAM by one month, so long-end buybacks barely move the needle on this. In terms of direct market impact, QE rules of thumb suggest the removal of $64bn in long-end securities per year should also have fairly modest effects, with Fed research suggesting QE equivalent to 1% of GDP, or about $300bn in today’s terms, would lower 10y term premia and yields by 10bps. The bigger story may be what the surprise announcement reveals about Treasury’s reaction function and approach to debt management going forward. First, Treasury is acting on its commitment to keep long-end yields contained while also signaling that it is perhaps more attuned to market conditions than many thought. On this, the use of tactical communications is now officially part of Treasury’s toolkit. The buyback announcement also comes on the heels of Treasury’s recent suggestion that Japan should make greater use of the Fed’s FIMA repo facility to finance its FX interventions. The combination of tactical signaling and a willingness to operate outside established precedent raises the bar to market participants being short rates and could help to limit long-end yield increases in the near term. Liquidity-saving mechanisms and netting can remain valuable even in technologically advanced payment systems. Fintech Credit and Monetary Transmission Cornelli, De Fiore, Gambacorta, and Manea (2024) find that fintech credit responds less strongly to monetary-policy shocks than bank lending. As nonbank lending expands, borrowers may therefore substitute toward fintech credit following monetary tightening. Policy implication: financial innovation may strengthen transmission through bank liabilities by increasing deposit betas while weakening it through bank assets as lending migrates outside banks. The aggregate effect of innovation on monetary transmission is therefore theoretically ambiguous and likely to evolve with the size of nonbank credit. A Unifying Perspective: More Substitutable Money Financial innovation creates near-money substitutes and raises the elasticity of substitution among monetary assets. Lower transaction and switching costs make it easier to move between deposits, money market funds, stablecoins, CBDC, and, in some cases, domestic and foreign currency. PPI and import price inflation (JPY basis) declined slightly from June to July, but remained elevated at +7.2% y/y and +29.1% y/y, respectively (see July PPI: Focus shifts to CPI pass-through, 13 August). International benchmark crude prices reversed at the start of July and are currently in an upward trend. With the overlapping impact of JPY depreciation, import-led inflationary pressure is likely to persist. records.text: M Idea 2 Treasury Buybacks in the Context of Our "Run It Hot" Thesis Over 6 years ago, at the depths of the COVID recession, we made a call that investors should get ready for a return of inflation. At the time, the world was mired in deflation, with stocks down sharply from their recent highs, the 10-year US Treasury yield below 1% and gold near $1500/oz. Our core recommendation at the time for equities was to position aggressively in lower-quality, early-cycle stocks that would benefit the most from a reversal in the changing inflationary trend. Over the following year, low-quality cyclical stocks outperformed significantly until the rate of change on money supply growth peaked in late March 2021, a time when we pivoted on our recommendations and moved to a large cap high-quality bias. Over the last 12 months, we have made a similar call, recommending a preference for lower-quality cyclicals near the trough of the Liberation / "Capitulation" Day lows of the rolling recession and then pivoting back in July of this year to a large cap quality preference. This all aligns with our Hotter but Shorter Cycle thesis we laid out in 2021 that can be summarized as follows: In a world of returning inflation, it is likely that economic cycles will no longer be able to persist for the extended 8-10 year periods like we experienced during the ~40-year disinflationary boom between 1982 and 2020. records.text: Changing Architecture of Monetary Policy The topic of the 2026 Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium is "Financial Innovation: Implications for Payments and Policy," which we think could include stablecoins, tokenized deposits, central bank digital currencies, instant payments, blockchain and distributed ledgers, open banking, and fintech lending. From the perspective of a central bank, recent financial innovation raises the following questions: Who creates money-like liabilities? What assets back those liabilities? How readily can households and firms substitute among them? Who bears liquidity and credit risk? And what happens to the transmission of monetary policy? Put simply, it is our view that the symposium will focus on how – or whether – financial innovation changes the architecture in which monetary and financial markets operate. A useful organizing principle is that recent innovations are making different forms of money more substitutable. Moving funds from a bank deposit to a stablecoin, money market fund, digital bank, or potentially a central bank digital currency is becoming progressively cheaper and faster. At the same time, new technologies are separating functions that historically came bundled together inside banks: payments, deposit taking, information production, and credit provision. records.text: Takeaways from Venture Capital Visits Models and Infrastructure Capability gains continue. AI capabilities are improving through better data curation, training techniques, model architectures, inference methods and infrastructure efficiency. AI is also helping researchers write code, optimize kernels and develop subsequent model generations, creating a recursive improvement cycle. These advances allow leading labs to generate substantially more intelligence from the same compute. Frontier intelligence retains value. Complex and economically valuable workloads continue to favor frontier models given their higher accuracy, reliability and task-completion rates. Model economics should therefore be measured by the cost of successfully completing a task, including token consumption and success rates, not nominal token prices. The frontier market could support several large providers with differentiated positions, resembling hyperscale cloud computing. Open models serve distinct workloads. Open models offer attractive economics for constrained, localized and cost-sensitive workloads, while frontier models retain an advantage where reliability justifies higher costs. Applications can route work across frontier, open and internally tuned models, although optimization generally becomes a priority only after reaching meaningful scale. Raw data reported by the Treasury shows the market value of foreign holdings of US issuer corporate bonds saw a $31.3bn increase on a month-to-month basis in June (Figure 7), but this value change reflects multiple drivers: actual net purchases or sales by foreign investors, changes in interest rates that affect bond prices, and exchange rate movements that alter the dollar value of "reverse Yankee" (non-dollar) bonds of U.S. companies. T o isolate the true flow of capital (that is, the net purchases by foreigners), we must strip out the valuation effects from interest rate and currency movements. First, we add back the $12.9bn loss in market value from rising US corporate interest rates. Dollar-denominated bonds, representing 83.12% of total holdings, declined 0.34% in value as higher rates pushed bond prices lower. Second, we add back the $10.4bn loss in market value from exchange rate and foreign interest rate effects on non-dollar holdings, which consist primarily of euro-denominated reverse Yankees. After adjusting for these valuation effects — which netted to a $23.3bn reduction in the value of reported holdings — the unexplained portion of the increase represents estimated net inflows of $54.5bn in foreign purchases during June. Japan lacks a probability-distribution survey comparable to that of the New York Fed, so we use the implied breakeven rate as a proxy for the inflation risk premium . This premium—which represents the market's price for upside skew in the inflation distribution—is computed from the forward spread between inflation-linked JGBs. The 5y5y window sits beyond the direct impact of the food tax cut, which takes effect in April 2027, leaving the measure largely immune to the temporary drag on headline CPI. Furthermore, b ecause the liquidity premium in linkers tends to depress breakevens , the resulting level can be seen as a conservative lower bound. The 5y5y BEI currently stands at 1.72% and has tracked the 5y5y nominal forward rate closely. On the policy front, the BoJ revised its FY26 inflation forecast down to 2.5% at the July meeting, while simultaneously adding the exchange rate to the list of factors that could prompt a policy adjustment. A gap is emerging between measured CPI, which is slowing into the 1% range, and underlying inflation, which remains in the upper-2% range. This gap, soon to be mechanically widened by the food tax cut, creates a risk that soft headline prints could be used to justify delaying policy normalization, allowing inflation expectations to drift higher. records.text: US Rates Weekly 21 August 2026 Citi Research 7 What does Treasury Secretary Bessent do next? We believe the discussion around the possible loss of confidence in the long-end of the curve, on the back of increased buybacks, is a media overreaction. Treasury is merely reacting to a poor decision from 2019-2020—the introduction of the 20y bond, which has consistently weighed down the long-end of the curve. Bessent is unlikely to be fazed by the media, and we would be surprised if the market did not reward him for fixing this mistake of too much long-end issuance. Here are Bessent’s options as we see it today: nBuybacks can be increased further. Bessent indicated that there was no limit for potential buybacks increases. If Treasury is able to lean on T-bills for the near future, they may continue to shift outstanding debt into the front-end, especially given the calmness in funding markets recently. In our view, there is scope for such an increase. See Alejandra’s section for more on how the front- end market will function in the coming years. nSignal there are no coupon increases to come. It is growing more likely that the Treasury will lean on T-bills to finance the deficit for the remainder of the Trump administration. Private T-bill share is currently only around 21%, so they have a couple years before T-bill share explodes without coupon increases (Figure 12). The planned consolidation rests on favourable assumptions, including a 6.0% real GDP growth target, lower subsidy spending and a relatively benign oil/rates backdrop. Implementation could prove challenging if growth undershoots expectations, oil prices stay elevated, or subsidy savings are harder to realise, particularly given the government’s broader growth and wel- fare objectives. The subsidy reduction is a key swing factor, especially with the govern- ment’s tendency to limit pass-through of energy prices to domestic inflation. Revenue assumptions also look demanding, with the budget relying on still-strong revenue growth despite a declining revenue-to-GDP ratio and a real GDP growth target above consensus. Our economists therefore maintain a 2027 deficit forecast of 2.7% of GDP, narrowing from 3.0% in 2026, but still above the official target. For now, we take a wait-and-see approach: the policy direction is encouraging, but execution risks remain meaningful. These capabilities connect decisions that traditionally sit across separate engineering teams, suppliers and production systems. Divergent illustrates how vertical AI can create value by integrating an industry’s complete design-to-production workflow. Proprietary production data improves design and manufacturing over time. Divergent controls its software, Model One printers, manufacturing processes and factory operations, providing access to process data that competitors without a similarly integrated platform may struggle to reproduce. Historical production data helps predict how parts will deform during printing, while computational methods compensate for that distortion through changes to the manufacturing process. The resulting manufacturing insights also feed back into design, allowing engineers to evaluate whether a part can be produced reliably before it reaches the factory. Continued production creates additional information that can improve future design and manufacturing decisions. Divergent demonstrates how proprietary domain data can strengthen vertically integrated AI applications. A modular architecture balances innovation with reliability. In addition, Warsh’s comments during the July presser raised questions about the Committee’s willingness to raise rates in response to persistent inflationary pressures, triggering a rise in longer-term inflation expectations and bond yields. We discuss the possible features of either approach to this speech. “Big-picture speech” topics During his short chairmanship so far, Warsh has focused on big picture topics. As such, this approach would be less likely to break new ground on topics that are market relevant over the coming months. One bigger-picture topic that likely requires some additional elucidation is the Fed's task forces. At this point, our understanding of the task forces is limited to the leaders (see here) and a general description of the topics of focus and timeline for reporting back. However, uncertainty remains about many of the specifics of the task forces: the scope within each topic, how the task forces interact with the FOMC and Fed staff, when specifically they will report their findings / recommendations, and how those conclusions may ultimately be translated into framework or operational changes for the Fed. Though Warsh noted that he would be “checking with” the task forces between the July meeting and Jackson Hole, it is likely too early for indications about progress being made. For our part, we have written summaries of each of the task forces and recorded podcasts discussing communications and the balance sheet with outside experts.

Federal states’ budget pressure intensifies, but “credit quality resilient” Already in July, S&P published a report highlighting that pressure on budgets of German federal states had intensified. According to S&P, German federal states' budgets are under more pressure than it anticipated at the end of last year. The key fiscal headwind is the negative impact of the war in the Middle East on economic growth, and hence on states’ tax revenue. States' rising staff costs and municipalities' deteriorating fiscal positions are also important factors. S&P now anticipate s moderately weaker budgetary performance for German states than it foresaw at the end of 2025. S&P calculates that the municipal sector’s aggregate deficit after capital accounts reached a new record high in 2025. It exceeded EUR 28bn, which is equivalent to more than 8% of the sector's total revenue. The municipal deficit significantly exceeded the state deficit of about EUR 10bn in 2025, or 2% of total revenue, although state budgets are significantly larger overall. Federal states are constitutionally obligated to provide sufficient funds to municipalities to ensure that they can govern themselves effectively, but there are no specific goals that they need to meet. Figure 2 Data slow down bolsters doves Source: State Street Markets, Bloomberg, MKT MediaStats Historically, Jackson Hole has provided an opportunity for Fed Chairs to shape expectations for the remainder of the year and reset market narratives when necessary. Typically, that kind of steering is not needed, with the most extreme reaction over the la st ten years being in 2025 when the market increased odds of easing by 8bps in the week following Chair Powell’s speech (Figure 3). Even so, 8bps is more akin to a nudge than a full push. 2026 could be a similar case, with market pricing for September in flux . Current pricing at 8bps signal about a 35% change of a hike but given the Tier 1 data that sit between now and the next meeting, it’s understandable if the market waits for data to fully solidify its view. records.text: M Idea 10 Special focus: Update on demand reports This week we got data on balance of payments data for the month of June and some Dutch National Bank data on Dutch portfolios in 2Q26. The ECB’s June BoP data showed a record ~€200bn of foreign purchases of euro-area debt securities, almost twice as much as the previous recent high (Exhibit 16 ), pointing to exceptionally strong non-resident demand for euro-area fixed income. Looking at the geographical breakdown, France (~€63bn), Italy (~€54bn) and Germany (~€27bn) all recorded sizeable inflows, while data for Spain will be released later. The strength was also evident in government debt securities alone (Exhibit 17 ), although less impressive. Should we fear the data is wrong and will be revised? We do not think so. Regressing the sum of country-level net inflows excluding Spain on the corresponding euro-area series (which need not match exactly, given differences in the definition of the “rest of the world”) confirms that June was an exceptional month. The absolute level was a clear historical record, although it remained broadly consistent with the historical relationship between country-level and aggregate euro-area flows. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 Jackson Hole: If you want to say less, say less Don't expect answers from the Fed If we think the Treasury buyback announcement raises more questions than answers, it would be useful if we expected the Fed to provide some clarity on its thinking at the upcoming Kansas City Fed's Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium, August 27-29. However, we believe Fed Chair Kevin Warsh is sincere in his desire to communicate less and we do not expect him to provide anything that would clarify his thinking on the near- term outlook for the economy and monetary policy. While we believe that market movements and the evolution of the data will ultimately push the Chairman into providing more substantive comments than he has so far during his tenure, we do not believe we are at that point yet. We do not believe Chairman Warsh will reverse his policy of talking less following the critical feedback he received after the July FOMC meeting. Instead, we think he reads the criticism as a sign that financial markets and analysts (like us) need to be weaned off of excessive dependence on Fed guidance. Hence, we expect him to stay the course, say less, and diminish the importance of events like Jackson Hole in the Fed's communication apparatus. records.text: ab 24 August 2026 Global Research US Economic Perspectives US-Canada trade talks break down Trade talks fail to secure a deal, new 50% tariffs for Canada come into effect Trade talks between the US and Canada broke down over the weekend with reporting suggesting a number of potential drivers, see here. As a result, an additional 50% tariff on certain imports from Canada came into effect on Saturday. With roughly $20 billion of 2024 imports covered by the new tariff we estimate that this has lifted the US weighted average tariff rate (WATR) by 0.3pp to 11.4%. This is still below the 12.9% tariff that was in place under the IEEPA tariff regime, but is incrementally creeping higher from the relative low seen under the temporary section 122 tariffs between February and July. See the chart below. The tariffs were imposed under a never used trade law provision, section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which grants the President the authority to impose tariffs, up to a maximum of 50%, where they "find as a fact" that a foreign country discriminates against US industry. This provision does not appear to require an investigation, nor have a time limit the tariffs. However, little judicial precedent exists. There is disagreement over whether there are further finding requirements, how to interpret “discrimination” and whether other statutes like Section 301 have superseded the provision. All of which could lead to legal challenges of the new tariffs. Canada announces retaliatory tariffs

Securitization issuance Stabilized data center assets today, GPUs tomorrow? Since the first 144A data center securitization was issued in 2018, the outstanding market has grown quickly, to $66bn as of July 31, 2026. We believe the market could reach $180bn by year- end 2028, although investors are likely to demand changes to structure and/or wider spreads to digest the supply, in our view. Importantly, current ABS/CMBS exposure is primarily to stabilized real estate assets and contracted lease cash flows rather than direct exposure to AI compute or hardware. In general, data center operators (ie, the transaction sponsors) provide data center space, power and cooling, and connectivity to tenants. Tenants are responsible for the IT equipment housed within the securitized data center's real estate. In addition, a return to full-fledged duration investment would likely require several conditions to be met, including a need to rebuild JGB portfolios in response to a deterioration in earnings conditions, a pause in the JPY depreciation trend, and greater clarity regarding the terminal rate, easing fiscal concerns, reduced attractiveness of other risk assets, and a shift in investment behavior among the major banks. records.text: 24 August 2026 Focus Germany Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG A look at the MoF's August 2026 Monthly Report In this update, we take a look at the August 2026 Monthly Report from the Federal Ministry of Finance (MoF), which contains the financial statistics data on federal budget developments for the first seven months of the year. The analysis builds on our previous work regarding Germany's fiscal policy shift (see also here and here). It considers the latest dynamics of a) the federal government's core budget as well as b) the two major off-budgetary funds SV BW (Federal Armed Forces Fund) and SV IK (Infrastructure & Climate Protection Fund) for which the government provides monthly credit stock/flow data.1 The MoF's July 2026 budget print Monthly budgetary developments in a nutshell As Figure 1 illustrates, the total federal financing deficit (comprising the core budget, SV BW, and SV IK) widened to EUR 159 bn in July on a 12-month smoothed basis (approx. 3.5% of 2026F GDP; full-year target: 4%), up from about EUR 150 bn in June. Consequently, the total deficit, based on the trailing twelve-month sum, has expanded by nearly EUR 100 bn since the 2025 federal budget effectively took effect in October last year. records.text: US Focus 1H26 trading volume recap: A broad-based increase in activity Volumes were mostly higher across US credit products in the first half of 2026, with large percentage gains in CLOs, HY TRS, CDX.IG, IG ETFs, and portfolio trades. Single-name CDS activity rebounded amid heavy interest in banks and AI credits, while cash volumes reached record highs. Macro credit volumes in the US were mostly higher in 1H26, led by large gains in CDX.IG and investment grade ETFs (both +34% y/y), with both products at a new record. HY CDX and ETF gains were more modest, at 13% and 6%, respectively, as elevated dispersion likely drove more focus toward single-name selection. Single-name CDS activity rebounded amid heavy activity in banks and AI-related credits, with US and European corporate CDS volumes rising 14% and 18%, respectively, to the highest levels in at least a decade. Investment grade cash index volumes increased 14% y/y, with turnover increasing across ratings buckets. AA turnover increased materially, driven by hyperscalers, which saw trading volumes increase 74% compared with 2H25 and 246% compared with 1H25. High yield cash index volumes also increased, with TRACE volumes up close to 7% y/y. While the index grew modestly y/y, trading volumes expanded more rapidly, leading turnover to increase across the index. BB TRACE volumes increased the most, rising 15% versus 1H25. World models address this challenge by compressing observations into the features most relevant to predicting future outcomes. In one example, six hours of unstructured drone flight data produced a model that predicted movement through a room while preserving walls, windows and doors and excluding less relevant detail. This compression can reduce data and compute requirements, although discarding too much information can lower fidelity while retaining too much can impair generalization. Effective deployment will therefore require matching model capacity and representation detail to the specific task. World models provide a native signal for uncertainty and potential failure. Probabilistic world models generate a distribution of possible outcomes, allowing the system to detect when predictions become uncertain or move beyond conditions represented in training data. A robotic system can use this signal to pause, escalate or request additional information before completing an incorrect action. In one example, uncertainty increased immediately before a robot failed to connect a cable, creating an opportunity for human intervention. The signal does not create a complete safety system by itself because thresholds, fallback processes and escalation authority must still be defined. Getting long the 20y bond with the Treasury put On Wednesday we got long the 20y bond after Treasury announced that its long- end buybacks (10y-20y and 20y-30y sectors) would be increased from $2bn to “at least” $4bn per operation (Figure 4; 5.24% as of 4pm 8/20/26 see US Rates Strategy - Getting long 20y after today’s buyback announcement). Previously we recommended that duration longs focus on the front-end, given the uncertainty around term premium and the long-run fiscal picture (see US Rates Strategy - FOMC takeaways). Our view that inflation would slow and labor markets remain weak in the summer months has played out, placing a light ceiling on 2y yields (see US Rates Weekly - FOMC premiums and Treasury refunding preview). However, long-end levels are now too attractive to ignore, and we believe the risk-reward looks best at the 20y point (or 10y10y forwards) rather than at the front-end. In our view, the Treasury Secretary acted as 30y yields approached 5.3% to limit term premium expansion. Indeed, price action into August 19th was very unique. Two-year yields were lower, while 30y yields increased, from the yield peak on July 23rd, steepening 5s30s by a little over 20bp. A major factor will be the preferred minimum range of reserves (PMRR) and when reserves reach it, as this can indicate when the BoE ends active QT (recent BoE estimates put the PMRR at GBP365–515bn). Also key will be the scale of active QT beyond September. We think the pick-up in repo operations will be telling – if/when it fully offsets the APF unwind, this may signal reserves have reached the PMRR. BoE Governor Andrew Bailey has stressed he wants to transfer interest-rate risk to the market from the BoE balance sheet. Because of the pickup in repo operations, we do not expect total reserves to go below the PMRR upper bound in the next QT period (October 2026–September 2027) and therefore see the BoE continuing active QT. Including GBP31bn of BoE redemptions due over that time, we forecast GBP50bn of total QT rundown (where BoE keeps its active sales the same as in the current period of October 2025-Septemner 2026), which would be a GBP20bn decrease from the current GBP70bn rundown. While 2025 saw healthy Japanese buying of overseas long -term debt totaling Y13.75tr, in the first half of 2026 Japanese investors were net sellers of overseas bonds to the tune of Y8.5tr. This leaves Japan's net balance in long -term debt portfolio transactions at a surplus of Y17.8tr so far in 2026. That is already the strongest inflow in any calendar year since the data started in 1996, and we are only halfway through (Figure 4). This does not eliminate the influence of the very large existing stock of foreign assets, but it does challenge the claim that continuing purchases of overseas bonds are the main source of current Yen weakness. Figure 4 Bond money returning to Japan Source: State Street Markets, Japan Ministry of Finance Direct talk The evidence therefore challenges the idea that recent Yen weakness has been caused by a broad, persistent migration of portfolio capital out of Japan. In four of the last six years Japan has recorded a portfolio balance surplus . The regime will go from ‘abundant’ to ‘ample’ in 2027, by our estimates, with excess liquidity seen at EUR2trn at the end of this year, and at EUR1.6trn at end-2027 (10.1% of nominal GDP). The ECB is moving toward a demand-driven floor system, whereby the ‘optimal’ amount of liquidity is revealed endogenously as banks shift towards ECB refinancing operations. While the ECB avoids anchoring to a single number, staff scenarios suggest a wide range of potential demand (EUR600bn–2.2trn). Currently, the main drivers of reserve rundown are the passive roll-off of the APP and PEPP portfolios. When forecasting the path of liquidity, the main unknowns are 1) the precise ‘Liquidity Coverage Ratio-driven’ reserve floor, 2) autonomous factors and 3) the timing of the introduction of new ECB structural operations. To make these metrics comparable, each is re-scaled using a 100-day moving min-max normalization. This approach helps reduce noise from high-frequency movements and better reflects whether sentiment is improving or deteriorating over the medium term. Normalization Formula: Normalized Value = (Latest Value−Min (Last 100 Days)) / (Max (Last 100 Days)−Min (Last 100 Days)) Each normalized series is expressed on a 0-100 scale, where higher values indicate stronger or more active sentiment conditions. The 12 metrics included are: 1. ChiNext Turnover: Daily trading turnover on ChiNext, normalized using the 100-day moving min-max method (available daily; weekly closing values used for analysis). 2. A-share Turnover: Daily turnover of all A-shares, normalized using the 100-day moving min-max method (available daily; weekly closing values used for analysis). 3. records.text: Data center bond issuance The US data center bond market has continued to see a robust pipeline in 2026, as developers continue looking at alternative sources of funding beyond typical construction/project finance loans. Since our previous update, there have been two IG issues (TXEDCI and QTSODY) totaling $16.5bn and five HY issues (STNGRY, ELNFOR, YNDRDC, GALAXY, and ZENARC) totaling $8.9bn. Year to date in 2026, about $76.2bn of data center bonds have been issued, including $33.6bn HY and $42.6bn IG (representing 15% and 3% of total year-to-date USD issuance in each asset class, respectively, from $35.9bn in 2025, including $8.6bn HY and $27.3bn in IG). The market has "standardized" around certain structures, with differences emerging between high yield (~5NC2; partial amortizing) and investment grade features (construction risk mitigation, fully amortizing). We recently initiated on the HY data centers, as well as the new IG TXEDCI deal, and more information on the entire sector can be found in our latest Data Center Bond Comp Sheet. The cadence of issuance in the first half of the year slowed somewhat this summer, but has begun to pick back up recently as developer pipelines continue to grow. In Figure 15, we show our updated T-bill supply forecasts for the rest of the year, note that these figures also account for the recent pause in RMPs. As a reminder, last week, the Fed announced that they would continue to roll off expiring MBS holdings into T-bills, however, they will not conduct RMPs for the upcoming month. Prior to Warsh’s speech, we will receive important information on inflation that could influence the outcome of the September FOMC meeting. Recall that the July FOMC meeting minutes revealed that “many” participants anticipated a need to tighten policy if inflation fails to quickly decline. Given this backdrop, market participants will heavily scrutinize Wednesday’s core PCE print. Based on the recent CPI and PPI reports, we are tracking 0.18% month -over-month for July core PCE, which would correspond to a 3.22% year-over-year growth rate for the Fed’s preferred inflation metric. If our forecast is correct – and there appears to be greater disagreement /uncertainty around this translation than normal – it would lower the probability of a rate hike in September, which remains our baseline expectation. Beyond the PCE inflation readings, Wednesday and Thursday’s data releases should collectively sharpen expectations for Q3 growth by providing a more complete read on consumer demand, business investment, and trade flows at the start of the quarter. We forecast personal income and consumption to rise by 0.1% and 0.2% in July, respectively. Meanwhile, durable goods orders should post strong gains, growing by 0.7% in July (versus +0.5% previously), with both ex - transportation orders

The UK is exhibiting more resilience than fragility Big picture, UK GDP continues to show more resilience than many expected. Summer survey data have already outshot our own expectations, with the latest PMI data pointing to a firming in activity (the August flash composite index jumped to 52.5 from 52.2). And we now see more upside to our H2 -26 growth projections, particularly in Q3 -26. A strong carry -over effect, plus sustained momentum could see GDP push a tenth higher to 0.2% q -o-q (our current projection has GDP growth projected at 0.1% q-o-q in Q3 and Q4) (Figure 4). Why the slowdown? The energy shock will see a second wave hit across households and businesses in the summer (and beyond). Pump prices are already on the rise. And dual fuel bills have jumped 13% in July, with potentially more increases in the pipeline. Budget uncertainty will also start to creep in later this year, we think, impacting investment. All in all, while we see GDP growth tracking at 1.1% this year, there’s some upside risk brewing. Risks are skewed to yet another upward revision in the coming months (Figure 5). Using the JPMorgan US Treasury Total Return Index as our measure of ex-post performance, we look at 3M, 6M, and 12M ex-post returns against ex ante yield levels, both nominal (10Y UST) and real (10Y TIPS), across a sample spanning January 1997 to present. World models could nevertheless combine autonomous decision-making with continuous monitoring in mission-critical physical systems. Physical AI will likely remain application specific in the near term. Broad world models spanning all physical environments remain difficult to build because each application requires observations, actions and outcomes that represent its unique dynamics. Narrow models can already learn useful behaviors from modest datasets, including several hours of drone flight or recordings of industrial workflows. Near-term commercial opportunities are likely to emerge in contained environments where tasks are repetitive, labor is scarce and human safety risks are high, including mines, refineries, factories and warehouses. Companies with domain expertise and access to relevant operating environments should be well positioned, although limited data requirements may also enable specialized entrants. Transfer across unrelated applications and the development of broadly reusable base world models remain open research questions. Enterprise agent adoption is constrained by accountability, not capability. records.text: Lee Ferridge 24 August 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Classification: Complimentary Material What ’ s really driving the Yen? Since the start of 2024 there have been four separate rounds of official Yen support, the first three by Japan alone and, on July 30th this year, the first joint U.S. -Japan intervention since 2011. Yet despite repeated official support and a record current-account surplus, the Yen has struggled to strengthen on a sustained basis. By most valuation measures it remains extraordinarily cheap. Our own PriceStats PPP model suggests the Yen is around 52% undervalued against the U.S. Dollar. If Japan is running its largest current -account surplus on record and foreign investors are buying Japanese assets in size, why does the Yen remain so weak? To answer that question, we take a detailed look at the current-account, portfolio and direct -investment flows behind USDJPY and assess whether the conventional explanation for Yen weakness still stands up to the data. Current account still supportive Japan has run consistent current account surpluses for much of the last 50 years. As a percentage of GDP 2025 saw Japan record its largest ever surplus at 4.84%, helped by the aforementioned Yen weakness. In JPY terms, the surplus in 2025 was Y32.2tr (just over $200bn at the current exchange rate (Figure 1). Expectations have historically been formed in a largely adaptive manner, with past inflation outcomes exerting a strong influence on future expectations. As a result, a sharp decline in inflation expectations in the near term appears unlikely. Figure 18 and Figure 19 apply a framework inspired by Kaihatsu and Shiraki (2016), in which firms' 5y-ahead inflation expectations are explained by their own lagged values and changes in USDJPY, among other factors. Our results are broadly consistent with their findings. While JPY depreciation exerts upward pressure on inflation expectations and remains a driver, most of the variation in long-term inflation expectations is explained by their own past behavior. This suggests that adaptive expectation formation remains the dominant mechanism shaping inflation expectations even during the current BoJ tightening cycle. The results are also consistent with Ito, Kaihatsu, Haba, and Hirano (2026), who argue that adaptive expectation formation remains a defining characteristic of inflation expectations in Japan. Similar conclusions emerge from our analysis of upside inflation risks. Indeed, we see evidence that similar actions from other DMOs globally have all had temporary effects on the term structure and not a lasting impact. Indeed, we think we can look to the UK as a guide, which has cut the long end share of net issuance from a projected 28.4% in April 2022, to 9.1% today. The UK DMO has reduced the long end share of its issuance in 12 instances over the last 4 years, and historically, the gilt curve has flattened around these events, on average by 2bp in the 5 days after the event. Policy action is building as community pushback to data centers intensifies. Texas is auditing every data center advancing through ERCOT's interconnection process against more than 474 GW of pending requests, ~90% data center-related, with major developers indicating they will comply. Virginia's July 31 Rider T1 order moves Dominion toward "cost causer pays" for direct-connect transmission. Ohio's debate has become electoral through Vivek Ramaswamy's "Ohioans-First" proposal, which is not current law and is better read as a sentiment indicator than a change to project economics. Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro issued an executive order ending the state’s fast-track permitting program and mandating that data center projects must first be approved by local officials. It also prevents NDAs from being used, introduces new environmental standards, and requirements to bring their own capacity. We expect this conversation to spread as it gains relevance with voters ahead of the midterms - the majority of community pushback is concentrated around 3 issues: (1) Affordability and the concern that data center power consumption will raise consumer power bills, (2) Environmental issues especially water use and air pollution, and (3) Quality of life concerns including noise, dust, and traffic. Together, the two levels account for over half of the universe, indicating a clear bimodal distribution. Among the 324 firms for which assumptions are comparable with those at the time of FY2025 full-year results, 247 left their assumptions unchanged and 77 revised them toward a weaker yen. records.text: 21 August 2026 Thrills & Chills Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 Samsonite to Acquire BÉIS. Samsonite has agreed to acquire an 85% stake in BÉIS for ~$178.5 million, implying an enterprise value of $210 million, with the transaction funded through existing cash and available revolving credit facility capacity. Founded in 2018, BÉIS is a fast -growing, profitable, digitally native lifestyle and travel brand that generated ~$210 million of net sales in 2025 and has built a strong following among younger, predominantly female consumers through its direct-to-consumer model and highly engaged social media presence. Strategically, the acquisition would broaden Samsonite's exposure to faster - growing lifestyle bag categories, strengthen its digital and e -commerce capabilities, and enhance its growth profile in North America. Management expects BÉIS to continue operating as a standalone brand under its existing leadership team, while benefiting from Samsonite's global distribution, sourcing and logistics platform, creating potential revenue and operating synergies over time. From a credit perspective, the transaction appears modest relative to Samsonite's scale and is broadly leverage -neutral, supported by the company’s solid liquidity profile, cash generation and expectation of maintaining adjusted leverage in the low-to-mid 2x range despite a softer travel demand environment and weaker consumer spending backdrop. The upcoming Chair Warsh speech at Jackson Hole poses binary risks to gold prices. Citi Economics Research expects a relatively benign core PCE and sees risks as balanced dovish for Jackson Hole. A hawkish Warsh speech will likely bring the ongoing gold rally to a halt. As the rally has been more paper/spec-driven rather than physical demand-driven, it’s likely more susceptible to spec profit taking. Still, we would look to buy dips in the low-4k range in this scenario. In contrast, a dovish surprise at Jackson Hole will be ultra-bullish for gold, as the market will not only continue to price out Fed rate hikes but also refocus on the debasement trade amid renewed concerns on Fed independence and US debt sustainability issues. Strong momentum will also lead to more investors returning to the market, e.g. China retail. records.text: Foreign Flows in U.S. Fixed Income 24 August 2026 Citi Research 2 US Credit: June foreign demand stays strong Foreign demand for U.S.-issuer corporate bonds stayed strong in June, adding a third consecutive month of over $50bn in inflow. This also continues a 19-month streak of strong overseas demand for credit. According to our value-adjusted framework, we estimate that overseas investors increased holdings of U.S. issuer corporate bonds by $54.5bn in June (Figure 1). Higher-frequency indications of demand lead us to expect that foreign investor net buying will remain strong but taper in July compared to June stemming from Tech supply indigestion. With roughly 49% of the estimated $569bn in net supply (up until June) absorbed by overseas investors (Figure 2), foreigners’ take-down of U.S. corporate debt has stayed on pace. This is roughly in line compared to prior January-July periods, where overseas investors absorbed 63% of net supply in 2025, 43% in 2024 and above the longer-run average of about 44%. Heftier foreign-currency funding of US hyperscalers may tend to overstate demand for the USD credit market. TIC estimates for foreign holdings do include reverse-yankee issuance from US based firms, which has increased from $23.7bn per month in H1 2025 to $29bn per month in H1 2026 due to increased hyperscaler funding needs. In addition, fiscal concerns associated with the FY27 budget formation process, which will begin later this year, could emerge as another source of upward pressure. That said, supply-demand dynamics, particularly in the superlong sector, are likely to continue offsetting part of these upward pressures on term premia. As discussed in Supply- demand factors: Support for the superlong sector , ongoing BoJ quantitative tightening creates headwinds around the 10y sector, where increased JGB issuance coincides with declining BoJ holdings. By contrast, net supply in the superlong sector remains contained. Looking ahead, potential changes in pension fund asset allocations and increased issuance of retail JGBs could exert additional downward pressure on term premia. These factors could more than offset fiscal deterioration concerns in the superlong sector at least in the near term, while also providing some support to the 10y sector. On balance, we expect 10y term premia to remain broadly unchanged, while term premia in the superlong sector retain some room to decline. However, at EUR440bn per year on average, it is the largest decline across G4, and the regime will soon shift from "abundant" to "ample“ in 2027, with excess liquidity projected to reach EUR2trn at the end of the year, and EUR1.6trn at end-2027 (10.1% of nominal GDP). The ECB is moving toward a demand-driven floor system. This means that rather than the ECB prescribing a specific reserve level, the "optimal" amount of liquidity will be revealed endogenously as banks shift their behavior towards ECB refinancing operations. While the ECB avoids anchoring to a single number, staff scenarios suggest a wide range of potential demand (EUR600bn–EUR2.2trn). Currently, the main drivers of reserve rundown are the passive roll-off of the APP and PEPP portfolios. Rather than one hike every six months, we now expect hikes every three to four months. Hedging their bets So how does all of this square with the continued weakness of the Yen? Outside of speculative JPY selling (of which there has been plenty) the likely explanation lies in hedging activity. All of the numbers outlined above are pure flow measures, they do not account for investor hedging. Our Hedge Ratio Indicator shows that real money investors who buy Japanese Fixed Income hedge around 60% of their Yen exposure. Those into equities barely hedge, meanwhile, with our indicator showing a level of just around 5% (Figure 8). Figure 8 Hedging increasing Source: State Street Markets, Japan Ministry of Finance As Figure 8 illustrates, we have seen a relatively sharp increase in the Fixed Income hedge ratio i n recent weeks. Why wouldn’t you hedge if you are buying JGBs? A US investor who buys 10-yr JGBs and hedges for 3m (and rolls that hedge over the course of the year) can actually earn around 1% more than they can in 10-yr US Treasuries. Applying a 60% fixed -income hedge ratio and a 5% equity hedge ratio to the relevant portfolio inflows reduces Japan's estimated FX-relevant basic balance surplus in 2025 from Y22tr to about Y8tr. records.text: 21 August 2026 Euro Weekly Digest Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG Week in review August flash PMIs The August PMIs sent a broadly resilient signal for the euro area. The composite PMI rose to 52.1, beating expectations of 51.7, even though Germany and France both underperformed. That implies the rest of the euro area did better, with services outside the two largest economies strengthening enough to offset weakness in France and Germany. At the country level, France was mixed, with a healthier manufacturing print but softer services, consistent with only weak Q3 growth of around 0–0.1%. Germany’s composite was slightly weaker, as a stronger manufacturing sector was offset by services slipping back into contraction. Manufacturing was the main support. In Germany, manufacturing output and orders rose to their highest levels in four to five years, with export orders also improving and only a slight lengthening in delivery times, suggesting that river transport constraints were not yet a material drag. French manufacturing also improved, with output back above 50 and employment at its highest for a year. Services were the softer part of the report: activity weakened in both France and Germany, with the weakness potentially reflecting temporary weather effects from the heatwaves, and possibly some drag from higher energy costs given services’ more domestic orientation. records.text: Australia and New Zealand Foreign developments keep AUD yields sticky; NZD curve to still steepen. n Despite the softer labor market report, which saw the unemployment rate edge up, and our economists’ expectations for a softer July inflation print, AUD rates broadly drifted sideways this week. We think foreign spillovers, especially from higher US yields, have been an important factor in restraining AUD yields from a more substantial decline over the last few months. We expect the benign data outlook and cheap valuations to ultimately support AUD duration, however, and we maintain our receive 10y AUD recommendation. Across the Tasman, hike premium has continued to fade, with markets now pricing 80bp to year-end, vs a peak of 140bp in July, albeit still above our economists’ baseline of two further hikes. We thus continue to prefer 2s10s steepeners to position for a more constrained tightening path than priced on account of sufficient labor market slack; we extend target and raise the stop on our recommendation. We closed our pay 5y5y JPY vs EUR OIS 5y5y for a potential flat return as it hit our revised stop. records.text: The US Treasury’s decision to increase long-end buybacks does not address what we see as the main sources of recent long-end volatility. Fundamental factors and macro risks—rather than a supply-demand imbalance—are the primary drivers of the selloff, while global spillovers are keeping a higher floor under long-end yields across markets. As long as the underlying drivers including cyclical resilience, inflation risk, and policy uncertainty remain unresolved, attempting to suppress long-end rates volatility via supply adjustments will simply push the pressure elsewhere—i.e. cheaper belly rates and/or a weaker currency. The experience in the Gilt and JGB markets in recent years underscores the limited capacity of long-end supply reductions to compress risk premia without more favorable macro dynamics materializing. Clarity around the Fed’s reaction function could bring relief, but in the near-term we see multiple routes to US belly underperformance with our preference still for cross market steepening versus Europe. While fiscal risks are not the cause of the recent rise in Gilt term premium, we think the anticipation of the Autumn budget should keep the recent reset sticky. By March, the energy shock looked set to hit GDP meaningfully. Fears of uncertainty impacting consumption and investment were rife. Nonetheless, they appear to capture a meaningful portion of inflation risk premia. Indeed, the upside tail of the inflation-expectation distribution is closely correlated with movements in OIS term premia ( Figure 16). Specifically, the larger the share of respondents expecting inflation to exceed the 2% target by more than 100bp, the higher the OIS term premium tends to be. This suggests that rising inflation risk premia have been an important contributor to the recent surge in yields. The evidence is also broadly consistent with Grishchenko and Wilcox (2024), who show that increases in the probability mass in the right tail of future inflation distributions contributed to higher inflation risk premia in both the US and the euro area. The gap between observed OIS term premia and fair value implied by upside deviation in inflation expectations may correspond to a premium associated with fiscal concerns. Persistent JPY depreciation driven by "Takaichi policy risk premium, " reflecting fiscal concerns etc, appears to have gradually influenced firms' inflation expectations. While the proportion of dividend increases appears lower than the previous year's actual result of 72%, companies tend to provide conservative dividend guidance at the beginning of the fiscal year and subsequently revise it upward as earnings trends become clearer. The simplest way to see this change is via the quality factor, which has started to outperform again after 12 months of underperformance—typical of post-recession periods and coincident with the peak rate of change in revisions breadth. This all makes perfect sense to us in the context of our investing framework and we expect it to continue. Such transitions typically happen in a down tape, which is exactly what happened in June and July, with many stocks down 30%+. This helps to explain the record momentum unwind as well, and why it's unlikely for the new leadership to be like the old leadership. At the start of the week, yields rose despite the absence of major catalysts, driven by increased BoJ rate-hike expectations, and the curve bear steepened amid a global bond selloff. Against this backdrop, the 5y JGB auction produced a solid result, suggesting a degree of firm demand for the medium-term sector even amid rising yields. Subsequently, on 19 August, JPY rates bull flattened sharply after US yields declined with the US Treasury’s announcement of an increase in UST buybacks. The JGB yield curve continued to bear-steepen in the first half of the week in line with global trends amid still-thin domestic trading. However, the belly zone ended up outperforming over the week as a whole after the US Treasury Department’s announcement of an increase in its buybacks beyond the 10y sector appeared to arrest the market’s momentum, at least temporarily. Market participants are now likely to be focusing on the potential reversal of the recent global bond yield sell-off. Our US rates strategists believe that bear-steepening trend has been driven less by concerns about fiscal deterioration risk and supply/demand pressures associated with the recent surge of AI-related corporate bond issuance than by rising energy prices as well as uncertainty pertaining to central banks’ policy-reaction functions. Our US rates strategists view the buyback announcement as a clear signal that the Treasury Department is keeping a very close eye on the super-long portion of the UST curve and, moreover, now see an increased likelihood of super-long (coupon-bearing) bond issuance being cut back to levels more commensurate with market demand. Higher real yields could start weighing down on risk-assets as well. Indeed, we took off our long 5y5y inflation swap trade yesterday, as levels are back to the top of the recent range ($220k profit 2pm 8/20/26; see US Rates Strategy - Taking profits on long US 5y5y inflation vs Europe ). Yields are also materially lagging the drop in hard data economic surprises (Figure 9). records.text: e 20 plots the 5y5y implied breakeven inflation rate against the 5y5y nominal JGB forward rate. Japan lacks a probability-distribution survey comparable to that of the New York Fed, so we use the implied breakeven rate as a proxy for the inflation risk premium . This premium—which represents the market's price for upside skew in the inflation distribution—is computed from the forward spread between inflation-linked JGBs. The 5y5y window sits beyond the direct impact of the food tax cut, which takes effect in April 2027, leaving the measure largely immune to the temporary drag on headline CPI. Furthermore, b ecause the liquidity premium in linkers tends to depress breakevens, the resulting level can be seen as a conservative lower bound. The 5y5y BEI currently stands at 1.72% and has tracked the 5y5y nominal forward rate closely. On the policy front, the BoJ revised its FY26 inflation forecast down to 2.5% at the July meeting, while simultaneously adding the exchange rate to the list of factors that could prompt a policy adjustment. A gap is emerging between measured CPI, which is slowing into the 1% range, and underlying inflation, which remains in the upper-2% range. This gap, soon to be mechanically widened by the food tax cut, creates a risk that soft headline prints could be used to justify delaying policy normalization, allowing inflation expectations to drift higher. Conclusions A deep dive into Japan's current and capital account data makes the Yen's underperformance harder to explain through conventional long -term portfolio flows alone. In 2025 Japan recorded a simple global basic balance surplus of Y22tr and an estimated Y8tr a fter applying our inward portfolio hedge ratios. Against the US, the same framework produced a modest Japanese deficit of Y4.2tr, or $26bn. That bilateral deficit may have contributed to Yen weakness, but it is not large enough to settle the question by itself. In any case , the first half of 2026 has seen Japan enjoy strong across the board surpluses , mainly due to the fact that Japanese investors were net sellers of global bonds in the first six months of this year. So far this year Japan has enjoyed a simple basic balance surplus globally of Y24tr which drops to Y16tr with hedging assumptions. That is still a surplus of over $100bn. With the US its hedged surplus is Y8.2tr or over $50bn. The obvious conclusion to draw is that it is likely speculative rather than long -term capital flows that explain the persistent weakness in the JPY. Macroeconomic data over the last couple of weeks have been unilaterally on the dovish side of expectations. Non-farm payrolls have averaged around 20k jobs per month over the last three months and while unemployment has moved lower, it was mainly a function of participation rate moving lower. There are no signs of overheating in the labor markets. More importantly, 0.1% MoM increase in average hourly earnings shows that there are no risks of wage inflation that can lead to price inflation in the future. Despite a fairly low unemployment rate, limited wage inflation and low hiring rate point to labor market that is significantly different from previous years. Moving on to inflation, two consecutive months of lower-than-expected CPI inflation have led to market lowering the chances of a hike in September. Inflation across most major CPI categories has continued to decline in recent months. Increases in inflation in recent months are confined to transitory components of the CPI basket like energy prices (Figure 29).
