records.text: US Rates Weekly 21 August 2026 Citi Research 19 Turning to relative value, we see the spread trading very close to our fair value metric (Figure 33). For our fair value metric, we are considering the cost of carry to delivery combined with the CTD’s rich/cheap against our fitted Treasury curve. Recent TU rolls have also traded close to their fair value at this stage of the roll month. But once asset manager longs started to move into the back contract, the bearish pressure on the front futures contract led to the roll cheapening relative to fair value in the first week of the roll month. In the last week of the roll month, after most of the asset manager longs have rolled, we converge back to the fair value. However, due to the decreased long positioning, we do not expect the initial cheapening to be as significant compared to previous cycles. Moving on to macro, the TU CTD slope is correlated to the 1s2s SOFR curve (Figure 33). A 10bp steepening in the 1s2s SOFR curve will result in a ~0.4bp steepening in the CTD curve based on historical beta and that translates to ~0.3 tick higher TU roll. As we mentioned in the macro section, pricing of rate hikes in 2027 will continue to be slowly faded and pushed into 2027 and beyond. This should lead to a steepening of the 1s2s curve over the next couple of weeks, which should also steepen the TU CTD slope which is currently trading slightly steep based on its historical relationship to the 1s2s curve. However, the possible disappointment in LNG export volumes means that production might not necessarily hit capacity limits of egress pipelines in the out years, unlike some market participants appear to believe. A key assumption is that, based on the current capacity build-out projection of egress pipelines and the expected gas demand from data centers and LNG export terminals, assuming strong or close to full utilization, Haynesville production could hit capacity limit around the 2030 timeframe. However, our analysis shows that global LNG demand growth should remain weaker than anticipated – where East Asia and Europe do not need much more LNG, likely peaking then plateauing or falling thereafter – that US LNG exports should get curtailed in a global LNG oversupply. The Middle East turmoil can lead to incrementally more contracting of US LNG as an alternative source, but whether the LNG will indeed be “lifted” would depend on future prices. Thus, given the price-responsive nature of a number of Haynesville producer, more moderate LNG offtake demand and more moderate prices should lead to slower Haynesville production growth in the long run. U.S. Treasury intervened in the bond market this week with a surprise announcement of doubling the long-end coupon buybacks. While the announced increase is fairly small , it highlights Treasury’s more activist approach with a willingness to deploy tools more creatively and using communication tactically to keep long -end yields contained. While the initial bond rally was largely retraced with higher oil prices being a driv er, the risk of further interventions makes it more difficult to hold steepeners. Treasury’s intervention also reinforces our bias for swap spread steepeners as reductions to long -end supply are replaced by increased bills or belly issuance. On funding markets, the impact likely will be limited given the relatively small scale and because of potentially lower repo demand from leveraged accounts with the long end richening. records.text: 10 Bram Kaplan, CFA AC (1-212) 272-1215 bram.kaplan@jpmorgan.com Global Markets Strategy 24 August 2026 J P M O R G A N MRNA move appears overdone: prefer puts over outright shorts Our biotech analysts (Jessica Fye and team) maintain an Underweight on Moderna (MRNA) with a Dec’27 price target of $77 (~47% downside) following the expected positive outcome in the INT (mRNA cancer vaccine) Phase 3 trial in adjuvant melanoma. Ahead of the readout, they assigned an 85% probability of success based on a strong Phase 2 readout. While positive data were broadly anticipated by both our team and the Street, MRNA still rallied by a record ~177% on the release, likely driven more by positioning/short covering than a fundamental re-rating. While the result is an important milestone (the first cancer vaccine paired with Merck’s Keytruda), the near-term commercial impact is confined to a relatively narrow setting (adjuvant melanoma), which our analysts estimate adds only ~3% to MRNA’s valuation. For INT to become a more meaningful incremental driver, it would likely need to expand into additional indications across other cancers, a multi-year pathway as ongoing trials read out. Our analysts continue to apply risk to assumptions around how well INT’s success translates beyond melanoma. We attribute much of the move to technicals (i.e. a short-squeeze). Regulatory infrastructure creates a more durable moat than model access. Corgi spent multiple years and tens of millions of dollars establishing the licenses, capital and operating infrastructure required to participate at the insurance-carrier and reinsurance layers. The company controls underwriting, pricing, reserving, regulatory documentation and claims while frequently relying on brokers, agencies and other partners for distribution. This structure allows Corgi to redesign and automate regulated workflows without depending on a legacy carrier’s systems or priorities. Regulatory approvals, capital requirements and insurance operating expertise are substantially more difficult to reproduce than access to foundation models. AI-native companies can build durable positions by combining technology with control of regulated infrastructure. Model commoditization shifts value toward applications and workflows. records.text: Next week, economists from around the world will gather in Jackson Hole for the Federal Reserve’s annual symposium. Outside of individual rate decisions, this conference is traditionally one of the most prominent global central banking events of the year. Given the historical lull in central bank communications in August, Jackson Hole is the highest profile opportunity to hear from policymakers ahead of the resumption of rate decisions in the Fall, with markets watching closely to gain insights on policy themes for the rest of the year. As a result, Jackson Hole—and the keynote address in particular—can generate meaningful FX volatility (Exhibit 1). In this Global Markets Daily, we address some of the most common questions around the logistics of the conference, things to watch, and some specific topics of interest this year. Our estimate of the weighted median CPI inflation rose to +0.9% in July from +0.8% in June. Meanwhile, the weighted median excluding imputed rent remained flat at +1.6%. The rise in the weighted median suggests that inflation is bottoming out across a wide range of items, rather than being driven by a few outliers. Outlook and implications for monetary policy We believe further acceleration in the inflation rate is likely, considering the upward pressure from upstream prices, as represented by the Corporate Goods Price Index (CGPI), and the growing willingness of companies to raise prices, as seen in various business surveys. In fact, the three-month moving average of the seasonally adjusted core-core CPI has already accelerated to an annualized rate of +3.2%, indicating strong near-term inflation momentum. We forecast that core-core CPI inflation will accelerate to around 3% in the first quarter of 2027. Subsequently, we expect the inflation rate to decline significantly due to the consumption tax cut scheduled for April 2027. However, this outlook assumes that the tax reduction will be fully passed on to retail prices. Indonesia continues to screen rich versus peers in our model portfolio framework, trading around 15bp tighter than the fitted average rating spreads. While the recent fiscal messaging helps the near-term narrative and should reduce immediate tail risks, we do not think current spreads offer enough compensation for the elevated uncertainties surrounding the macro outlook, budget execution and policy credibil- ity. We have been UW Indonesia for some time, but still believe current levels do not reflect enough risk premia to compensate for these risks. On ratings, our base case remains that Indonesia avoids a downgrade, but this depends on the data staying on track into 4Q26. The 2027 budget proposal should help ease rating agency concerns in the near term, particularly if fiscal outturns continue to show a commit- ment to staying below the statutory deficit ceiling. We do not think a one-off breach of the 3% ceiling would necessarily trigger a downgrade, but a consistent breach over the next couple of years would be more material for the rating trajectory. grammes, likely to shrink reserves by an average of 20% and 16% respectively over the next two years. Repo operations at the BoE meanwhile have picked up sharply and continue to partly offset QT. We thus expect a more contained y/y drop this year and next, averaging just 5%. Reserves may still seem ‘abundant’, but…: When measured as a percentage of nominal GDP, the reserves picture needs some differentiation. As a first observation, G4 reserves still amount to 30% of nominal GDP. However, liquidity is already well through the pre-Covid regime of 35%, and the main reason for the still optically elevated level is BoJ liquidity, which stands at 70% of nominal GDP, compared with 9.6% at the Fed, 15.7% at the ECB, and 21% at the BoE. What’s more, we project a steady drop in the G4 level, to 25% of nominal GDP by end-2026, and to 20% by end-2027, a level not seen since early 2015. Hence, while still arguably high, this steady decline masks an important shift in global liquidity. Also noteworthy, according to our projections, ECB reserves would reach 10.1% of GDP by end 2027, marking an important shift, from ‘abundant’ to ‘ample’. Historically, speeches on the Saturday panel tend to stick close to previously published views and relate more directly to the conference theme than the Fed Chair’s keynote address. records.text: Valuation & Risks Iron Mountain (IRM, Buy, covered by George Tong): Our 12-month price target of $153 is based on 23.0x our NTM + 1YR AFFO/shr estimate of $3.22. Our target multiple is in-line with the median multiple of 23.3x for self-storage and industrial REIT peers reflecting attractive organic growth trends as the company’s growth portfolio continues to expand, mitigated by IRM’s transformation from a legacy records management company into a data and technology company that comes with execution risk and medium-term financial uncertainty. Risks to the downside for IRM shares include competing technologies in records management, acquisition integration risk, financial leverage and FX risk. Moody’s (MCO, Buy, covered by George Tong): Our 12-month price target of $593 is based on 29.0x our NTM + 1YR EPS estimate of $20.43. Long and superlong term premia Long and superlong sectors Yield movements in the long and superlong JGB sectors continue to be driven primarily by term premia and our model suggests upward pressure on term premia over the next 12 months, with an increase in the long-term sector and a more modest rise in the superlong sector. However, a reduced risk of the BoJ falling behind the curve due to an accelerated pace of rate hikes (ie, lower upside inflation risk), as well as potential changes to pension asset allocations and an expansion of retail JGB issuance, could more than offset these factors. Taking these factors into account, we expect the long-term sector to remain broadly stable, while the superlong sector retains some scope for further compression. The sharp rise in term premia over the recent period has been driven largely by an increase in inflation risk premia, a measure of uncertainty surrounding future inflation ( Figure 9 and Figure 10). As discussed below, inflation risk premia can be viewed as reflecting upside risks to inflation relative to the 2% inflation target due to BoJ behind-the-curve concerns or fiscal worries. For Japan, the local trough came in late June, just before fiscal concerns intensified around the government's annual policy blueprint. Our 5s10s term premium measure, an average of the ACM and KW models, has risen since then—a move that ranks in the 75th percentile historically, going back to 2000. This turn occurred at almost the same time as in the US, where the trough in term premia coincided with Chair Warsh's June press conference. This rise in term premium is consistent with our longstanding outlook. With the BoJ tapering its bond purchases, the supply that must be absorbed by price - sensitive private investors continues to grow. Fiscal expansion —including the consumption tax cut on food (representing roughly JPY 5.8tn/yr in foregone revenue)—adds further pressure. Meanwhile, upside inflation risk remains elevated. The fact that August's super-long bond sell-off (which saw the 30-year yield approach 4.1%, the high for this move) was driven by term premium repricing rather than by transactional flows supports this view. records.text: 2 Insights Information Classification: General The most important question, however, is not whether Warsh signals a hike or hold in September. What markets want instead is greater clarity on the Fed's reaction function. How is the Committee assessing inflation? What metrics carry the most weight? How does Warsh view the current inflation backdrop, and what level of overshoot is he willing to tole rate? How does he view the juxtaposition of Treasury’s goal of lower borrowing costs versus the Fed’s goal of price stability? The answers to those questions matter more than any explicit signal on September. When asked about his plans, Warsh suggested he may choose to "frame the big questions". Whether that proves sufficient will ultimately be decided by the bond market. The bond market reaction to Chairman Warsh's July press conference highlighted the risks of communicating with too broad of strokes and not enough detail. A bear-steepening move was characterized by lower front -end yields and higher long -end yields. The rise in long -end yields was driven by breakevens , while the decline in front -end yields reflected lower real rates, highlighting uncertainty about the Fed's willingness to raise rates to contain inflation (Figure 4). Since the meeting, market pricing suggests inflation expectations have continued to edge higher. From 2028 onward, the deficit could turn out significantly higher than our current projection of 4%, unless the federal government succeeds in closing the substantial fiscal gap in its medium-term financial plan ("finanzpolitischer Handlungsbedarf"), which totals EUR 109 bn (cumulative amount for the period 2028-30). Should these consolidation steps fail to materialize, the federal deficit would, on a purely mechanical basis, drift toward 5% of GDP by 2030. Moreover, according to the newly released 2027 Financial Report , the actual consolidation pressure appears to be significantly greater than the above fiscal adjustment needs communicated so far. This is because, in addition to these consolidation needs, the government has assumed flat-rate spending cuts for the years 2028 to 2030, factoring them in as so-called global spending cuts ('globale Minderausgaben'). These total EUR 74 bn over this three-year period, meaning the government effectively needs to achieve a total consolidation volume of more than EUR 180 bn between 2028 and 2030 to comply with the requirements of the debt brake. In its latest Monthly Report, the Bundesbank also pointed to these very high global saving targets, which – according to the Financial Report – average nearly EUR 25 bn per fiscal year between 2028 and 2030. 2 Ultimately, any deficit-reducing under-spending could be at least to a smaller degree offset by higher federal loans to the Federal Employment Agency. records.text: of yield and equity growth, creating a sharp net outflow that explains Yen weakness. It is a neat and logical argument given the generally low yields available in Japan. Unfortunately, for the majority of this decade, it simply isn’t true. Figure 2 below shows Japan’s annual net portfolio investment flows. For four of the last six years it has actually enjoyed a net portfolio investment surplus, with 2025 seeing a positive inflow of Y16tr (just over $100bn). While Japanese investors do continue to accumulate overseas assets – portfolio outflows totalled just over Y15tr in 2025 - this was more than offset by Y31tr of net inflows . Thus far in 2026 the trend has accelerated with Japan enjoying a net portfolio inflow of Y19tr. If this trend persists in H2 it would deliver Japan’s largest ever annual net portfolio inflow. Figure 2 Surpluses, not deficits Source: State Street Markets, Japan Ministry of Finance This buying of Japanese assets has been, a little surprisingly perhaps, made up primarily of buying of long-term Japanese debt securities which saw Y21tr of inflows in 2025 as international investors reacted to rising JGB yields. This was the largest net overseas investor buying of Japanese long - term debt since the data began in 1996. Indeed, it was close to double the previous highest year. So far in 2026, we have seen Y13.5tr of overseas buying of Japanese long-term debt which again, if replicated in H2, would far surpass the previous record (Figure 3). 0 5 10 15 20 25 3

records.text: Financial L.P., J.P. Morgan The dovish Riksbank reinforces our bearish SEK bias and sees us engage in krona shorts this week. Riksbank left rates unchanged as expected and the statement to us appeared to push back on market pricing for tightening with language such as “the picture is not clear-cut… companies pricing plans have been subdued”. Core guidance read that “the prob- ability of a rate increase later this year remains” which implies that the prior rate path holds as opposed to some mar- ginal increase in confidence for tighter policy given that infla- tion and growth have come in above forecasts, which the statement itself did acknowledge. Coming in to the meeting with markets having assigned around 50% of a September hike and ~39bps for the year we would expect this to moder- ate and hold SEK back, going forward. After closing our short SEK positions in July we have refrained from engaging in longs as domestic data have improved, due to several fac- tors including carry, energy risk and Riksbank. The bar for domestic growth to support the currency is higher if global yields are sticky and the market is searching for valid funding currencies. records.text: Japan Macro Watch21 August 2026 ab 2 BoJ: forecast revised to a September rate hike We revise our Bank of Japan policy rate forecast and now expect the next rate hike in September rather than October. In addition to growing expectations of an earlier hike following the recent FX intervention, media reports suggesting that the government has become more accepting of further rate increases have strengthened the case for September action. An October hike would be easier to justify from a data-dependency perspective, as key information such as the Tankan survey will be available by then. However, with markets already pricing in nearly an 80% probability of a September move, we believe the BoJ will prefer to avoid a dovish surprise that could trigger renewed yen weakness. In our view, policymakers are increasingly concerned about the risk of falling behind the curve on the currency front. That said, October remains a close alternative and the decision is still finely balanced. In addition to incoming inflation and FX data, speeches by Deputy Governor Himino on 27 August and by board member Masu, who is generally viewed as one of the more centrist policymakers, will be important signals. We also revise our expected pace of tightening. Previously, we had assumed one hike every six months, reaching policy rates of 1.75% by end-2027 and 2.0% by end-2028. However, the BoJ's latest Summary of Opinions placed greater emphasis on the possibility of accelerating the pace of rate increases.

Harvey’s Vaults product can similarly analyze up to 10,000 documents and extract structured answers across workflows such as side-letter review. Agentic applications can encode specialized professional methods in repeatable software while allowing experts to inspect and refine the results. Open-source models improve application-layer economics. The narrowing performance gap between open-source and frontier models allows applications to route simpler tasks toward lower-cost models while reserving frontier intelligence for complex work. Harvey evaluates models across roughly 1,200 legal tasks and approximately 60 private evaluation sets to determine which models perform best for specific workflows. The company can also post-train smaller models using proprietary legal evaluations and task environments without absorbing the substantially higher cost of pretraining a foundation model. A multi-model architecture can optimize accuracy, latency and expense as model capabilities evolve. records.text: size of 10-to-30y buybacks (from $2 to $4bn per operation, with 7 operations through the rest of the quarter) suggested a level of discomfort with the level of long-end yields that brought sharp but short-lived relief to the recent selloff. While the removal of duration supply implies a shift in the long-end supply-demand balance, we think the drivers of higher long-end yields have been macro-related rather than a function of UST supply indigestion. Cyclical resilience, the year-to-date reassessment in the Fed policy path, AI capex and related longer-term growth optimism, ongoing fiscal pressures, and global spillovers have contributed to a higher fair value for long-end yields. Meanwhile, policy uncertainty, ongoing energy risks, and the broader issuance trajectory have likely contributed to higher term premium and led to weak appetite to add duration risk through the selloff (Exhibit 1). Despite the recent moves, however, long end USTs are not materially misaligned with macro fundamentals. In broad strokes, reducing the amount of long-end supply does not address the main factors that have contributed to recent long-end cheapening and is thus unlikely to sustainably dampen risk premia unless reinforced by a shift elsewhere. Within Florida, local governments have a wide array of security types outstanding. Accord- ing to Moody’s, the measure has the most throughput for bonds backed by a non-ad valorem pledge, which is subordinate to essential operating expenses of the government. Essential operating expenses are typically considered net of operating property taxes and thus, by reducing ad valorem taxes, the pledge would actually hamper coverage on non- ad valorem bonds. Additionally, while the measure would not directly impede the GO security (cities and counties would still be required by law to levy property taxes at whatever rate is necessary to cover debt service), by narrowing the tax base, this levy (Florida GO bonds are payable from a property tax levy dedicated to debt service) could require a higher millage and this burden would effectively be reallocated to the properties that do not benefit from the new exemption. The measure would not have a direct impact on municipal utility revenue bonds or on special tax bonds, beyond the extent that they weaken the credit quality of the issuing cities and counties generally, per Moody’s. Traditional clinical trials can take years while medical models may improve every few months, creating a mismatch between technical progress and evidence generation. Adaptive trials can reuse evidence when a new model agrees with a validated predecessor and focus incremental enrollment on cases where their recommendations differ. Greater agreement between versions can reduce trial size, cost and duration without eliminating prospective validation. Evaluations must also reflect full clinical workflows because isolated images and captions may not measure performance on complete imaging volumes and diagnostic reports. records.text: Exhibit 15 ). Over the past 10 years, the average 1Q gap between company guidance and consensus has been -6.7ppt. In other words, consensus estimates have historically anticipated subsequent upward revisions to typically conservative company guidance. In the current 1Q results, however, the gap between company guidance and consensus is only -1.8ppt. Given the high 1Q progress against company guidance not only in manufacturing, where the earnings impact of AI demand is substantial, but also in non- manufacturing, we believe there is a strong likelihood of upward revisions to company guidance. In our view, consensus estimates have yet to fully incorporate either the recent rapid pace of earnings growth or the scope for guidance hikes.

records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 23 Aug 2026 19:21:10 ET │ 10 pages Japan Developed Markets July nationwide CPI: Set to rise above 2% again CITI'S TAKE The July nationwide core CPI (excluding fresh food) rose 1.8% YoY, in line with the market consensus. While this marks the seventh consecutive month below 2% since January of this year, it represents an acceleration of 0.2ppt from the 1.6% recorded in June. Looking at the breakdown, food excluding fresh food continues to be the largest contributor, and the positive contribution from services (excluding policy-related factors) is also growing steadily. Going forward, as the impact of higher oil prices feeds through to CPI with a lag, the contribution from energy—which has been held down by policy-related factors—is expected to gradually expand its positive contribution heading into early next year. We continue to expect core CPI to rise above 2% again from the summer onward, temporarily exceeding 3% heading into early next year. Contrary to the Eurozone, the increase was driven by improvements in services while manufacturing fell. Specifically, the Services PMI was up 0.7 points to 52.8 with solid details: new business (+0.5 points to 51.3) and business expectations (+1.9 to 67.0) increased, and employment also rose (+1 point to 48.5). The Manufacturing PMI was down 0.4 points to 51.5, due to "geopolitical uncertainties and elevated cost pressures" according to the press release. Output (-1.7 to 51.2), new orders (-1.3 to 51.0) and new export orders (-1.2 to 50.2) all declined, but employment rose (+1.8 to 51.9). Also in contrast to the Eurozone, composite input and output prices rose this month in the UK. This report has been prepared by UBS AG London Branch. Start with corporates. Issuance is booming on the back of a surge in technology spending and normalizing M&A volumes (see last week's Start). Our credit strategy team continues to forecast record issuance this year. Yet, we think this debt can still be absorbed with only modest spread widening. The starting point for balance sheets is good: US corporate debt/GDP that is unchanged over the last decade and lower since COVID. Coupled with low hyperscaler leverage and high AI ROIC that can justify ‘paying up’, don't expect yields to stop this historic financing wave. The household sector has even more debt, yet looks even better. US household debt/GDP (~67%) is lower than it was in 2000 (~70%) and 6pp better than 2019 (74%). And if anything, that may overstate things; much of that debt is in mortgages struck at historically low rates, while the asset side of household balance sheets has improved substantially. This strong aggregate does hide dispersion between the top and the bottom. But for overall spending, the aggregate matters, helping to explain why consumer spending has held up so well despite higher rates and energy prices. The Big 6 US banks are not members of a CDX index, but we include them here because they have been a significant contributor to the overall increase in Americas CDS volumes. Big 6 CDS volumes have increased 76% y/y, driven by a sharp increase in CVA activity and meaningful protection selling by structured credit desks as CLNs have grown in popularity. Within Europe, SenFin constituents were the clear standout, with aggregate single-name CDS volumes rising 58% y/y. The increase was notably broad based, with all 30 constituents recording higher trading activity than a year ago. Growth was evenly distributed across banks and incos (proportion adjusted), with ALVGR (+158%), CMZB (+125%), and STANLN (116%) posting the largest percentage gains. While increased scrutiny of insurers' private credit exposures may have provided some support at the margin, we believe the rise in trading activity was driven primarily by the same structural factors as in the US market: elevated CVA demand and increased protection selling by structured credit desks as CLNs have gained traction. Main constituent volumes also increased, albeit by a more modest 18% y/y, and driven entirely by financials. Excluding the sector, Main constituents volumes were down 8% y/y, with telecoms, energy, and consumer goods recording the largest declines in activity. The banal fact is that the dollar had been slipping even before this week owing to the de-pric- ing of Fed hiking expectations on soft NFP/CPI releases, and has now unwound the entirety of its post-June optimism. That US equities did not react more positively to lower UST yields following the buyback announcement was somewhat surpris- ing, but ex-US asset markets took the news positively, which buttressed the middle-of-the-smile global cyclical environ- ment that has been supportive of FX carry and a handbrake on the dollar in recent weeks. That said, we live in narrative driven markets, and are respectful of their capacity to drive meaningful FX moves over short horizons, and con- cede that the soft dollar patch could extend over coming weeks if (a) Chair Warsh remains non-committal on policy at next week’s Jackson Hole symposium; (b) core PCE next week undershoots JPMe 0.3%+ projection and August NFP (due in early Septmber) disappoints again; and (c) more poli- cy surprises arrive, particularly on the Yen (Secretary Bessent this week alluded to having ‘asymmetric information’ on the US - Japan co-ordination). We are also mindful that that time is not the dollar’s friend in coming weeks; the bur- den of proof has shifted to the dataflow to justify the hawkish Fed outlook that we hung our constructive USD hat on, and the passage of time without data validation is likely to weigh both on Fed pricing on the OIS curve and the dollar via an unwind of existing USD longs.

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 11 3Q GDP tracking at 2.2% Weak retail sales data a week ago cut our estimate of 3Q real GDP growth to 2.2% from 2.7%. A decline in goods spending in July along with downward revision to earlier months lowered our 3Q consumption tracking to 1.8% from 2.4%. Since then, weaker July housing starts cut our estimate of residential investment, but with little effect on overall GDP. The Atlanta Fed estimate is much stronger than ours. The difference primarily is in inventory investment: they have a sharp rebound contributing 1.7 pct pt to 3Q real GDP growth; we have no boost. Indeed, low real inventory/sales ratios suggest the possibility of faster restocking. When that restocking happens, and whether it comes through imports or domestic production will be important for GDP. Workflows involving irreversible financial, clinical or safety outcomes require more rigorous evaluation and control systems. Near-term value creation should concentrate in narrow processes where risk can be measured and accountability can be assigned explicitly. A trust infrastructure layer could unlock enterprise AI adoption. Enterprise agents need certification, independent evaluation, monitoring, incident reporting and insurance frameworks comparable to those used in aviation and other safety-critical industries. Human review alone may be insufficient because attention can deteriorate when systems are consistently correct and reviewers may defer excessively to AI recommendations. A credible framework must define which decisions agents can make, when humans intervene and which party accepts liability for each failure. This creates opportunities in pre-deployment testing, agent-specific insurance, reliability benchmarking, incident reporting and standardized certification. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 Oil Tracker: Elevated Prices, Falling Inventories We continue to track the evolution of petroleum-product inventories, production, trade, and prices. The latest data suggest that crude oil inventories in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) fell further, whereas total US crude oil and petroleum-product inventories edged higher. US domestic crude oil production remained broadly unchanged, while net imports of crude oil and petroleum products maintained their upward trend. Meanwhile, oil prices moved higher. As of August 14, US stocks of crude oil and petroleum products, which represent the EIA's estimate of how many barrels of crude oil and petroleum products are physically sitting in US storage at period-end, remained broadly unchanged from a week earlier. The stocks of crude oil in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) continued to fall to around 293 million barrels, the lowest level since April 1984. The Energy Department said the SPR's minimum inventory is determined by "cavern mechanics," which, when applied across the full system, translates to a conservative operational minimum of about 70 million barrels. If the SPR continues to decline at roughly its recent pace of 30 million barrels every four weeks, inventories would approach the operational minimum by the end of February 2027. Page 25 The cost of Japan's FX intervention Steven Zeng, CFA | Strategist | +1-212-250-9373 Note: This note was originally published on 19 August 2026 Japan has spent roughly $169bn on FX intervention this year: $73bn between April and May, and an estimated $96bn in July. Based on the June Treasury TIC data released this week, we estimate that the first round of intervention consumed more than half of Ja pan’s T-bill holdings, which fell from $153bn at the end of April to $70bn at the end of June. Although there was no FX intervention in June, we assume the decline in T-bills was due to Japan rebuilding its dollar deposits at the Fed’s foreign repo pool, which were drawn down in late April before rebounding in June. The July intervention is not yet covered by the TIC data. In the July TIC report, due mid-next month, we would expect to see a further decline in Japan’s T -bill holdings. While there have been suggestions that Japan could use the Fed’s FIMA repo facility to finance its interventions, relying on dollar deposits and proceeds from maturing T -bills makes more sense economically. Both dollars invested at the Fed’s foreign repo p ool and short -dated bills earn a lower yield than the cost of borrowing from FIMA. That said, once Japan exhausts its remaining T-bill holdings (plus other maturing coupon securities), use of FIMA repo could become more likely should additional FX intervention be needed. Fig

But that negative domestic story appears to be waning; data for 2Q has been impressive after the 4Q/1Q26 malaise, while our economists forecast a better out- look for 2027 as well (today’s retail sales for June beat expec- tations). records.text: has already been moving toward shrinking its balance sheet and the Committee gave some attention to the balance sheet in the July minutes, so that could be a likely topic for him to expound upon. However, we see some chance that Warsh further promotes his limited communication strategy, although recent market interventions by the Treasury Secretary could complicate his message. Warsh got a good family fight The July FOMC meeting minutes showed growing concern that policy may not be suffi- ciently restrictive to guide inflation back to target, and the discussion likely reflected not only the three hawkish dissents but also support for higher rates among a larger subset of participants, including non-voters. Notably, “many” expressed concern that, after some six years of above target inflation, expectations could become unmoored if inflation remained elevated. Despite the louder voices among those with hawkish proclivities, we suspect the data-de- pendent centrists on the Committee are still comfortable remaining in a holding pattern for now. The minutes also revealed that “most participants anticipated that inflation would step down over the rest of the year.” This conviction among a majority on the Committee (“most” is greater than half, whereas “many” typically is less) that current inflation is likely to prove temporary has gotten some support from recent data releases. In which case, the relationship of stocks to bonds can be different from prior periods. The bad news is what's playing out right now harks back to 2021-2023 when markets were concerned about stagflation. As we've pointed out over the past few years, the 'classic' negative correlation between stock and bond returns is underpinned by the 'traditional' relationship of growth and inflation travelling in the same direction: stocks offset losses in bonds as growth rises alongside inflation, and vice versa. The moves across DMs were led by domestic and global drivers, with significant repricing of monetary policy expectations partly behind the move higher in yields across the curve. The twist steepening of the US Treasury curve following the Fed’s press conference in July was also partly attributed to Chair Warsh potentially moving the goalposts in terms of price stability. While inflation worries and central bank credibility are often mentioned as catalysts behind the steepening move, our analysis here showed that the excessive steepness of the US Treasury curve vs. other DM curves and short-end USD rates could not be explained by higher long-term inflation breakevens, validating our point that Fed independence concerns were not in the price. The moves this week continue to validate this argument. Moreover, we note that fiscal concerns remain a critical driver across DM, particularly in Japan. However, DM long-end swap spreads have remained relatively stable over the recent steepening move, suggesting that the fears of lax fiscal policy as the catalyst for the steepening were overstated. records.text: M Idea 10 The effective tariff rate, tariff receipts, and refunds Tariffs averaged 6.8% over April-June, and we expect that it will rise to near 10% USTR's final forced-labor Section 301 action was broadly in line with our expectations. Effective July 24, the agency imposed additional tariffs on imports from 60 economies, setting a 10% duty on economies that have adopted, partially adopted, or committed to adopt a forced-labor import prohibition and a 12.5% duty on most others. The final action also preserves several key carve-outs, including goods already subject to Section 232 tariffs, USMCA-compliant imports, and a range of general and country-specific product exemptions. Overall, both the tariff structure and the principal exemptions closely resemble the proposal, reinforcing our expectation that Section 301 would serve as the broad country-level tariff floor. We continue to expect that the statutory effective tariff rate will converge toward ~10% by year-end. In the May 2026 data, the effective tariff rate is estimated at ~6.9%, and over the past three months of trade data (March, April and May), the tariff rate averaged 6.8%. The analysis covers federal budget developments up to July, including the core budget, the Federal Armed Forces Fund (SV BW), and the Infrastructure & Climate Protection Fund (SV IK). n The expansion of the deficit gained traction in July, confirming Germany’s visible fiscal policy shift. The total federal deficit widened to EUR 159 bn on a 12-month moving-sum basis, equivalent to 3.5% of 2026F GDP and approaching the full-year target of 4%. Year-to-date (YTD), the deficit reached about EUR 90 bn, roughly EUR 50 bn above July 2025. n Defense and investment spending continue to trend higher, but disbursements have been sluggish relative to the ambitious spending targets. While YTD spending levels are well above last year’s figures, as of July less than half of the full-year spending targets have been reached. n Defense spending continues to rise, but still falls short of the pace required to meet the full-year target. At EUR 48 bn, YTD total defense spending was c. EUR 11 bn or approx. 30% higher than one year ago (targeted 2026 increase: c. EUR 32 bn or +37%). For the US, the local trough came around Chair Warsh's June press conference, and the increase in our 5s10s term premium measure since then is in the 85th percentile of two-month moves back to 2000. This rise in TP is in line with our longstanding outlook. Even with increases over recent years, US term premia remain at moderate levels by long-run standards and, in our view, should move up given increasing bond supply to be absorbed by price-sensitive investors and elevated upside inflation risk. For context on the latter, the chart below plots the expected skew of 5y5y inflation against 5y5y nominal UST. The skew measure comes from the NY Fed's Survey of Market Expectations , computed as the average probability placed on 5y5y CPI realizing above 3% less the probability of it realizing below 1 .5%. On a seasonally adjusted MoM basis, the headline, core, and core-core indices increased by 0.4%, 0.3%, and 0.3%, respectively, confirming that inflationary pressures are persisting. A closer look: Price increases seen in energy, durable goods, and services The primary driver of this month's inflation acceleration was higher energy prices, led by increases in electricity and gas charges. In addition, durable goods prices contributed to the rise in inflation, reflecting a pass-through from increasing upstream goods prices. The broadening of price pressures was evident in both goods and services. The index for goods excluding fresh food and energy accelerated to +2.7% YoY from +2.5% in June. In this context, we view the most recent actions by the Treasury to buy more of its debt as simply the latest effort to do just that. It's well known that the Treasury has been funding more of the deficit at the front end of the curve since 2020. They are effectively using the excess reserves in the banking system first created by direct injections of liquidity by the Fed during COVID via QE and post the regional bank crisis in addition to the de-regulation of the banking system last year. At this stage, bank reserves are ample rather than abundant, which leads to periodic rises in stress in the funding, Treasury and currency markets. The Fed, Treasury and other central banks and governments will intervene as necessary to maintain stability in financial conditions. Recently, we witnessed two such interventions by Treasury—first with the JPY/USD market and then with the back-end of the Treasury market directly via buybacks. In our view, both were attempts to stabilize financial conditions so that markets could continue to operate and maybe even entice some buying of Treasuries under the assumption the Treasury will do whatever it takes. We don't think this is QE or Yield Curve Control as that would require a much larger amount of buybacks given the absolute size of this market and the significant supply coming. The main outlier has been the relentless cheapening of OATs in relative terms vs other EGBs. As today’s chart shows, for the first time this year, the YTD cumulative residual of 10y OAT/Bund has exceeded that of BTP/Bund. These residuals capture the relative performance of each country spread when adjusted for its beta to the average EGB spread (estimated over 2025). OATs had a negative residual, i.e. sign of outperformance, up until early June. This was mostly a carry-over of their outperformance early this year on the back of the 2026 budget approval. This negative residual was gradually being eroded since the beginning of the Iran war. Since early June, this residual turned positive, i.e. a sign of relative underperformance, and the pace of cheapening accelerated further in August. On the contrary, the cheapening move seen in BTPs in July was partially corrected in August. Since these residuals by construction have to sum up to zero, OATs’ recent cheapening has to lead to other EGBs’ richening. records.text: European Economic Perspectives21 August 2026 ab 3 Tracking stimulus − from budget outlays to production To recap, we track how the stimulus moves through the economy by looking at numerous indicators across different stages of transmission in a heatmap format. First, we expect business confidence in the affected business sectors to pick up in anticipation of increased public demand. Second, higher expenditures should become visible in the monthly budget data and in the quarterly reported disbursements from the special fund infrastructure as the government starts disbursing funds. Third, orders and − with some lag − production data should pick up. Fourth, as capacity utilisation increases, firms may start to expand capacity, which should become visible in employment growth. We track the data for the two sectors that should be most affected: defence-related (including weapons, ammunition, explosives, and other transport equipment, which includes military vehicles) and construction (especially civil engineering). One example is the evolution of the debt-service ratio (DSR) of the private non-financial sector. According to BIS data, the US private non-financial sector DSR peaked in 2007Q4 at the start of the subprime crisis (Exhibit 8). Significant Fed rate cuts and various government debt restructuring programs helped reduce the DSR by more than 4 percentage points over the ensuing seven years. In contrast, China’s private non-financial sector DSR initially peaked in 2020Q3, when the “three red lines” policy aimed at deleveraging the property market was first introduced. But later, between 2022Q1 and 2025Q4, China’s DSR increased by almost 2 percentage points. In other words, against the backdrop of three years of Covid lockdowns and a severe housing downturn, China’s private sector had to allocate a rising share of income to debt servicing over the past five years. These elevated financial burdens squeezed purchasing power, weighed on sentiment, and left the domestic economy prone to notable weakening whenever growth headwinds emerged. Another fundamental reason lies in the government’s strategy of focusing almost exclusively on tech innovation and high-tech manufacturing. As the Pareto-optimal curve of intelligence ebbs and flows, we are increasingly confident that independent software vendors like Microsoft, Cloudflare, Databricks and Vercel will be able to capture value by giving enterprises tools to orchestrate models while keeping their own content proprietary. Rise of world models suggests that the next AI platform shift may look bigger than LLMs. A growing number of researchers are shifting focus beyond LLMs over the last 18 months, arguing that next-token prediction alone is unlikely to capture how the real world behaves. Instead, the next generation of AI will need to model environments, causality, physics, and real-world interactions. The competitive moat could also look different from the LLM era. Rather than training on largely shared internet-scale datasets, many world model applications depend on highly specialized data tied to physical systems, industries, and operating environments. That creates a fundamental debate around whether value accrues to broad foundational models or vertically specialized systems built on proprietary datasets. The economic opportunity could ultimately exceed that of language models. Physical, industrial, scientific, and robotic systems represent a much larger addressable problem set than text generation alone, with many workloads requiring substantially greater compute intensity. Fed credibility concerns are a key part of the price action in US yields, with 2y yields falling since the July FOMC, and 30y yields rising – a K shaped bond market (see Figure 2). Such markets are rare, with only six such instances since the GFC. The most comparable episode is Q3 2023, where 30y yields rose by nearly 100bp in Q3 20 23. It’s worth digging into the potential motivations behind this announcement, as outside of the financial crisis, the only other off-cycle announcement we can recall was when the Mnuchin Treasury announced the reintroduction of the 20-year bond for delivery later that year (see Welcome to the Roaring 20s, 1/17/20). This expansion reflects real money accounts being on the sidelines, more than fiscal fears, in our view. Their reluctance to add duration has been due to the uncertainty around the Iran conflict, persistent inflation, the unknown reaction function for Chair Warsh, and the strong growth expectations on the back of the AI buildout . Only the inflation side of the equation, which is a small driver, would be somewhat mitigated by a September rate hike. However, a rate hike would likely diminish real money demand for duration further, as it increases upside tail risks at the front end. Finally, a rate hike would run counter to Bessent’s goal for a weaker USDJPY . A weaker Y en could encourage outright UST sales by MoF due to further currency defense (for our base case see US Rates Weekly - Could reserve managers go on a T reasury strike?). Putting this together, we do not expect much from Chair Warsh’s Jackson Hole speech next week. He is likely to emphasize that multiple inflation measures are normalizing . Where could our view be wrong? Historically, the Fed, and not T reasury nor long- end supply, dominates the curve. records.text: rce: MIC, UBSe Fiscal implications of an r > g Long-term Japanese government bond yields continued to rise this week, with the 10- year yield reaching 2.945% on 18 August, its highest level in roughly three decades. The move was driven largely by global factors. Although yields stabilized later in the week following intervention efforts by the US Treasury, markets are likely to remain focused on the possibility of yields moving above the 3% threshold. A sustained breach of 3% would be significant. The government's assumed long-term interest rate for FY2026 is 3.0%, meaning higher borrowing costs could begin to exceed official projections. At the same time, nominal GDP growth reached 3.2%y/y in Q2, narrowing the gap between nominal growth and nominal interest rates. The government assumes nominal growth of around 3% in their medium term projections. When nominal interest rates exceed nominal growth (r > g), the government debt-to- GDP ratio no longer stabilizes automatically, implying a violation of the Domar condition and increasing fiscal vulnerability. Equation of debt outstanding B: Debt outstanding, Y: Nominal GDP , r: interest rate, g: nominal growth, and PB: primary balance UBS expects core CPI to accelerate from 1.8% to 3.1% by year-end. Long-term yields have risen sharply and are approaching 3%. The 3% threshold is significant as the gap with nominal GDP growth continues to narrow. Nominal interest rates exceeding nominal growth would undermine fiscal sustainability.

records.text: Japan Viewpoint | 24 August 2026 7 High hurdles to a shift in fiscal policy On the fiscal side, the Takaichi administration has consistently criticized previous policy as excessively austere and has argued that large-scale investment aimed at strengthening Japan's productive capacity will ultimately contribute to yen stability. As such, the probability of a significant retreat from its expansionary fiscal stance in order to counter yen weakness appears low. Moreover, the cabinet has already approved several flagship initiatives, including the Basic Policy on Economic and Fiscal Management and Reform 2026 for the FY2027 budget, the Japan Growth Strategy incorporating ¥370tn of strategic investment, and a reduction in the consumption tax rate on food products from April 2027. Reversing these policies at this stage would likely require substantial political capital. In practice, fiscal policy implementation could once again prove more restrained than the government's expansionary rhetoric, as has often been the case in the past. However, with a wide range of fiscal measures currently under consideration, it will be difficult for markets to gain confidence in the near term that actual fiscal outcomes will be more restrained than initially expected. The near-term focus will be the FY2027 budget requests due to be released over the coming one to two weeks. records.text: 6 Japan Viewpoint | 24 August 2026 Repricing of BoJ rate hikes first, followed by forceful intervention if needed The US and Japanese finance ministries may be pursuing a strategy that balances two objectives. On the one hand, they are unwilling to tolerate yen weakness beyond USD/JPY 160, limiting damage to the credibility of the currency authorities. On the other hand, they may also be reluctant to engineer a break below 155 through intervention, given the risk that sudden yen strength could undermine the BoJ's rate hike cycle. Provided the US economy remains resilient, USD/JPY could remain in a 155-160 range through the September BoJ policy meeting or until the BoJ delivers a renewed hawkish signal. This appears to be a strategy that prioritizes durable yen stabilization over short- term exchange rate gains, even at the cost of larger intervention volumes or some erosion of policy credibility in the near term. The 2% policy rate level that markets view as necessary for yen stabilization is an intuitively appropriate level, as it implies a zero real policy rate assuming 2% inflation. Market pricing for the terminal rate likewise appears to be around 2.0-2.25% (Exhibit 9). At present, markets are pricing in the policy rate reaching 2% by early 2028 (Exhibit 8). However, that path still lies more than a year away and implies four rate hikes over five to six quarters, leaving uncertainty around the timing of rate hikes. Source: Barclays Research JPY outlook (last updated 23 June) • We expect USDJPY to remain elevated around 160 as Japan’s policy risk premium and net• capital outflows are offset by FX intervention (and fears thereof). Specifically, Takaichi administration’s “high pressure economy” policies, alongside higher oil prices, have pushed USDJPY via inflation risk premium well above our mid‑140s fair value estimate. At the same time, FX flow dynamics remain negative for JPY, as outbound investment (~JPY40trn) continues to exceed the current account surplus (~JPY20trn), reinforcing sustained net selling pressure. Household portfolio reallocation into foreign assets (including ~JPY10trn annual through NISA) and robust outbound FDI should keep capital outflows elevated. FX interventions are unlikely to shift the trend in USDJPY amid hawkish Fed pricing, while the BoJ is unlikely to accelerate its rate hiking cycle. We see room for some break above 2024- high of 162 in USDJPY due to greater headwinds for the JPY and a failure or perceived unwillingness to intervene risks an even greater upside in USDJPY. records.text: Implications for Business & Information Services and Software Business & Information Services Sector Implications Proprietary information assets become more valuable when combined with domain expertise and workflow context. AI increases the utility of differentiated data by making it easier to retrieve, connect and apply inside customer decisions. That said, durable differentiation depends on more than owning a large dataset. Leading platforms combine authoritative content with validated models, specialized taxonomies, customer context and experts who understand how the information should be used. This combination can generate more accurate and verifiable outputs in financial analysis, legal services, insurance, risk management and healthcare. Business & Information Services companies with unique, continuously refreshed data and deep industry expertise should therefore strengthen their competitive positions as foundation-model capabilities become more accessible. AI expands the sector from information delivery toward workflow execution. Business & Information Services companies have historically monetized data, analytics and professional expertise through subscriptions, reports and labor-intensive services. Agents can now structure unorganized information, perform analysis, monitor changing conditions and initiate downstream actions within a common workflow. records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures 24 August 2026 1 EU gas: Tight, risky – but not panicky With little more than two months left in this year’s European gas injection season, we thought it would be a good moment to take stock. Using the framework set out in our 16 July note Gas storage woes. Molecules, spreads and arbitrage, we look at how the EU gas market has evolved since and assess the risks ahead. In that note we highlighted that to be able to assume significant gas storage injections in northwestern Europe (the region with the largest shortfall versus target and with a significant share of commercial storage), we would need three things to happen simultaneously: molecules, spreads and arbitrage. • ‘Molecules’ references the availability of LNG cargoes in the market hence is linked to the return of Middle Eastern LNG. • ‘Spreads’ captures the fact that commercial storage operators need a winter price that is above the summer one to incentivize filling storage. • ‘Arbitrage’ argues that European prices need to incentivize suppliers to supply Europe over Asia. We indicated at the time that none of these criteria was met and therefore projected further upside to TTF. This materialized with TTF pricing about EUR10/MWh above the 16 July price. Asia’s LNG premium has come down: June-to-date has seen a trend of a narrowing JKM premium over the European LNG benchmark. This summer JKM priced on average about USD2.3/MMBtu over DES NW

For the opposite direction, US data indicate that Japan represents around 8% to 10% of US foreign portfolio holdings. Allowing for stronger marginal US participation in Japanese equities in recent years, we use 20% as the base- case US share of foreign portfolio inflows into Japan. Combining these assumptions with previous data we find a Japanese bilateral basic balance with the US of -Y3.8tr. However, if we apply to 60% hedge ratio to fixed income inflows and 5% to equities this falls further to a deficit of Y4.2tr or $26bn. Adding speculative Yen selling into this now starts to likely explain why the Yen has proven so weak against the US Dollar. However, if we do the same calculation using the data from the first half of 2026 we get a very different result. In the first half of 2026 Japan has actually enjoyed a raw (unhedged) net surplus in capital flows with the US of Y8.6tr. Even if we add in our 60% FI and 5% equity hedging ratios the surplus is still Y8.2tr. On a global basis Japan’s capital flow surplus i n H1 2026 is Y24tr on an unhedged basis (compared with Y22tr for the whole of 2025) and Y16tr using our hedging assumptions (compared with Y8tr in 2025). Production in the coming months should also have upside surprises. A pipe-by-pipe analysis of egress capacity from Haynesville – one of the most active regions in midstream expansions besides the Permian – shows the capacity and limits of southbound flows in particular. Combining this production outlook, as well as the pipeline and LNG export build-out, we estimate that regional basis differentials to Henry Hub are likely to widen further until the Pelican pipeline comes online. More broadly, stronger Haynesville production expected, along with strong Permian production growth, supports our view that 2027 Henry Hub should average $2.8/MMBtu. This report examines these developments – production, pipeline infrastructure and pricing – from the commodity angle. Haynesville is one of the most crucial natural gas producing areas globally, as the closest major gas play to Henry Hub and to most US LNG export terminals. Thus, this analysis is also relevant to market participants outside of the US. Enterprise software is moving from systems of record that store information toward systems of action that execute work. Agent architectures combine model routing, tools, protocols and trust controls, allowing employees to supervise substantially more activity than they could perform directly. Adoption will remain uneven because organizations differ in their ability to instruct, supervise and integrate agents. Verification controls adoption. AI adoption is advancing fastest where outputs can be objectively validated, with coding remaining the clearest breakout category. Progress is slower in mission-critical workflows where errors carry material consequences and human review becomes the primary bottleneck. Better verification and lower oversight costs are critical to expanding AI into higher-stakes applications. Early revenue can mislead. Rapid expansion from zero to $50mn of revenue may reflect enterprise experimentation budgets instead of durable product-market fit. Customer diligence should establish a clear ROI, recurring budget source and reason to renew after the initial trial period. Retention and expansion will separate products delivering measurable value from those benefiting primarily from AI testing. While most companies have yet to report a meaningful uplift in orders or revenues, project inquiries, lending growth and infrastructure demand indicators point to gradually strengthening momentum. While some sectors are directly impacted by higher spending (defence, construction), others (real estate, banks) are expected to benefit more indirectly from higher activity induced by more spending. Corporate management teams generally expect the most significant economic and earnings impact to materialise in 2027-28, reflecting the long lead times associated with major defence and infrastructure investments. Our equity strategy team has recently upgraded defence and fiscal spending beneficiaries. See full sector details overleaf. records.text: ab 21 August 2026 Global Research European Economic Comment Eurozone PMIs: Manufacturing gaining momentum Composite PMI slightly up, but with clear improvement in manufacturing The Eurozone Composite PMI rose by a marginal 0.1 points to a 9-month high of 52.1, moderately exceeding consensus expectations (51.7). While Germany saw a modest increase in business activity and France a further decline, the rest of the Eurozone enjoyed the fastest expansion in more than 4 years, according to S&P Global. The Eurozone Services PMI was unchanged at 51.7, while the Manufacturing PMI rose by 0.9 points to a 51-month high of 52.8. The improvement in manufacturing was broad- based and visible in higher output (+0.5 to a 54-month high of 53.4); better employment, which saw a modest rise for the first time in over three years; rising orders at home and from abroad (the latter rose for the first time in 4½ years) and an improving business outlook. Aggregate employment strengthened (+0.7 to 50.7) while aggregate input and output prices both moderated a bit, but remained elevated. The one-year business outlook softened moderately. Today's data bring the average Composite PMI for July and August to 52.1, well above the Q2 average of 49.1 and suggesting a pick-up in activity in Q3, compared with Q2. However, in recent months money and credit data have contradicted these expectations, demonstrating robust performance that supports domestic economic activity. In the June print, lending flows remain robust, with broad-based strength encompassing both household and corporate lending. For the July print, base-effects should provide some support to the credit impulse this month. But our key focus will be on whether lending flows and the credit impulse continue to remain robust, signalling continued domestic resilience, or whether the uncertainty from the war in Iran and other events finally starts to pull back on some of the domestic support from the bank lending channel. In June, long- term business borrowing (5+ years) rose strongly, suggesting firms were willing to look through the uncertainty and continue to invest. JGB: This Week in Review, The Week Ahead Will the BoJ Reach for the Door to a September Policy Rate Hike? Deputy Governor Himino’s speech on 27 August will be the first public communication by a Policy Board member since the July meeting and the starting point for a sequence of communications ahead of the 17–18 September Monetary Policy Meeting, giving this opening signal particular weight. The bond market survey and press conferences by individual Board members will follow, but the market already prices a 70–80% probability of a September hike and almost a full hike cumulatively by October—effectively, the perimeter has been secured without an explicit commitment. This elevated pricing reflects the yen’s renewed weakness following coordinated intervention, reports that a hike could come “as early as September,” and calls from the US Treasury Secretary for a policy response. The market is seeking three clear messages: (1) confirmation that the September meeting is “live”; (2) an interpretation of inflation data that includes special factors; and (3) an assessment of market functioning as the 10-year JGB yield tests 3%. In our view, although Himino has previously engaged in de facto policy “groundwork,” his stated philosophy makes an explicit commitment to a specific date unlikely; our base case is that he stops at signaling a hawkish tone. Our EM Strategists remain constructive on duration in the major Asian economies, namely China, India, and Indonesia. The convergence of improving supply-demand dynamics and pull back in inflation and geopolitical risk creates a compelling case for going long duration in the region simultaneously. Across markets, supply pressures are peaking or already moderating: in China, PBoC bond purchases have become a monthly, institutionalized tool (RMB 50bn in Jul'26), absorbing incremental CGB supply and recent economic data has skewed weaker, increasing odds of more easing. RBI held rates and reduced inflation forecasts, with flows expected to generate receiving pressure in OIS and IGB buying flows for at least the next month. Room seen for end-2027 rate pricing to fall toward 6.5% terminal. With the ECB hiking only one more time, CEE rates should do well. Hungary is still in a cutting cycle. In Latam, much will depend on the Fed but post- election, sogginess in Brazil rates should pass as Copom stays in a cutting cycle. Banxico is also unlikely to hike in the near term. The bar for hikes is high, given contained core goods inflation, subpar economic growth, and a resilient MXN. We go overweight EM rates with a custom hedge that favors the high carry names, which also tend to be commodity heavy, offering some protection against higher oil

records.text: value? Record Bund yields are eye-catching but as usual we believe it is important to define drivers and which parts of the curve offer the best value. We believe that the area around 2y3y offers the best value in the medium term, as it also benefits from some recent cheapening. In line with previous pieces from May and July we think that money market expectations had been by far the most important driver of the overall euro rates market. What has changed in the past few weeks is the analysis of term premium. In the past we flagged a downward impact on yields coming from international term premium, possibly linked to reduced anxiety about policies such as "Liberation day" and re- balancing from equities to fixed income. A recent update instead (Exhibit 5 ) shows that since a trough on July 23, the contribution coming from the US curve became positive, in our view mostly in reaction to the July FOMC delivery. The full impact of the US Treasury announcement, trying to quell an increase in term premia, will become clearer in coming days. Our colleagues have already expressed their views, holding steepeners. Dynamics at the short end of the curve are remarkable: consensus expectations captured by the ECB and SMA show median views of a peak in the ECB depo rate at 2.50% with cuts closer to the neutral in subsequent months, whereas the market prices only a handful of bps of easing in 2H27 ( Exhibit 6 ).

Chairman Warsh effectively endorsed higher long-end interest rates at recent FOMC meetings as a mechanism for tightening financial conditions and restoring price stability. Although Secretary Bessent rejected the idea that larger buybacks signal easier financial conditions or complicate the Fed's actions, Treasury's action suggests greater concern about the consequences of the same increase in long- term yields. This creates a potential conundrum. If the Treasury has become more sensitive to increases in long-term borrowing costs and higher term premiums are viewed by the Fed as needing to reduce inflation, then expanding buybacks may increase the probability that the Fed needs to raise short-term interest rates to achieve price stability. That said, market participants could just as easily infer a lower tolerance for additional policy-rate increases from the Fed or for balance-sheet reforms that place further upward pressure on term premiums. That inference is plausible, in our view, but extends beyond what can be learned directly from the buyback decision. We simply say the announcement raises questions about what will be contained in any new Treasury-Fed Accord. Our examples have been American but these trends are global. Europe has seen higher government debt/GDP balanced by (even more) corporate and household deleveraging. In Japan, public borrowing is up while private-sector leverage is stable. To a great degree, this reflects a policy choice. Countries get to decide how to balance taxes and spending. And recently, a conscious effort has been made to shift resources from the public to private sector. The US, France, Japan, Sweden, Switzerland, Italy and the UK have all lowered tax rates in the last decade. Worsening public relative to private balance sheets is hardly a shocking result. But how long can this persist? If corporates and households are less responsive to these rate levels, do we need look elsewhere for a different type of ‘break’? Recent days have seen rising yields coincide with interventions in US long-end rates and Japanese currency markets. Yet neither 10yr US inflation expectations (~2.3%), curve steepness (average), or rate vol (low) suggest undue stress or a lack of 'credibility'. We think the impact of these interventions will be short-lived (i.e., the US 7s30s should resume steepening), although a more active US Treasury should weigh on the USD. records.text: China’s July activity data showed renewed growth weakness, and we estimate n that official real GDP is running at around 4% yoy in early Q3. The combination of lower volumes and lower prices indicates that the weakness is demand-driven. July’s growth deceleration is more concerning than April’s because it came from n a lower starting point and impacted areas that had previously looked resilient. Q2 real GDP growth was only 4.3% yoy, below the government’s full-year target of 4.5–5%. By our estimates, growth of services retail sales slowed to 3.2% yoy in July after running above 5% earlier this year, raising questions about household consumption momentum. Looking back over the past few years, policy support has been too small relative n to the shock, leaving the private sector under sustained financial pressure. Policymakers’ near-exclusive focus on technology innovation and high-tech manufacturing does not easily lend itself to a more virtuous cycle of stronger employment, income and consumption, as manufacturing accounts for only around 20% of employment in China. These factors help explain why growth tends to soften notably whenever headwinds emerge. After the July Politburo meeting turned more dovish, the government announced n various easing measures, including faster government bond issuance and starting the new policy-based financing instrument to invest in the “Six Networks” and major projects in the 15th Five-Year Plan, support for large sectors with long value chains

Excluding the rebound periods following the GFC and Covid, these were the highest revenue and profit growth rates in the past 20 years. Manufacturing was the driver of record earnings. Sales at manufacturers increased 14.6%, while recurring profit surged 91.0%, highlighting the outsized growth on the profit side. Though growth in non-manufacturing was lower than in manufacturing, with sales up 11.5% and recurring profit up 12.0%, we view the results as resilient. Financials continued to show strong earnings momentum, with revenues up 20.5% and recurring profit up 54.0%. Positive contributions to recurring profit growth were concentrated in four industries; earnings growth in oil & coal products was driven mainly by inventory valuation gains: The +51.4% increase in recurring profit was driven by electrical appliances (+11.5ppt), transportation equipment (+7.5ppt), banks (+6.5ppt), and oil & coal products (+4.6ppt; Exhibit 2 ). To be sure, this has played out so far: as the issue rises in salience with voters, third parties report an estimated ~$156 billion worth of projects were cancelled or delayed in 2025, and $130 billion already in 1Q26. For crude oil in particular, where July import values surged by 87.8% y/y, import unit prices have remained elevated for both Middle Eastern and US crude, reflecting JPY depreciation and higher premiums. International benchmark crude prices reversed at the start of July and are currently in an upward trend. With the overlapping impact of JPY depreciation, import-led inflationary pressure is likely to persist. As a result, the wave of cost pass-through originating from crude oil prices is expected to continue spreading to downstream products, including final consumer goods. Accordingly, we expect core-core inflation to recover to 2% and rise temporarily to around 2.4% before declining again and stabilizing at around 2% from summer 2027 onward (Figure 5, Figure 6). In contrast to the core budget, the combined monthly deficit of the two off-budgetary funds (SV BW, SV IK) declined slightly in July, falling to just above EUR 5 bn from nearly EUR 7 bn in June. Manifesting in the latest year-to-date (YTD) numbers, the fiscal regime shift shows a cumulative total deficit since the start of 2026 that hit about EUR 90 bn in July – roughly EUR 50 bn higher than in July 2025 (see Figure 3). Not surprisingly, the year- on-year increase was largely driven by higher defense and investment spending, which accounted for more than EUR 40 bn of the total rise. Despite this sharp increase, the government has reached only about half of its full-year deficit target of roughly EUR 182 bn during the first seven months of the year. While around half of the deficit target has already been met in the core budget and the SV IK, budget execution for the SV BW is still lagging significantly behind its spending target, with a current execution rate of just under 40% (see Figure 14 in the appendix). Assuming an even distribution throughout the year, nearly 60% of the deficit targets should have been reached by July. Europe: good earnings, but oil worries just won’t go away. Earnings season was good enough in Europe too, considering the energy supply shock due to the conflict in the Middle East. As our equity strategists report, European earnings came roughly in line with historical average. While decent, it was still well below the US (and well below the US historical average). The theme of broadening keeps coming back, but we fail to see structural flows into cyclicality without a definite resolution to the US-Iran conflict. PMIs in Europe have mostly priced out all the energy worries. The comeback in sentiment has been so strong that our favorite signals for long European equities have triggered (ZEW / IFO above 3m moving average). Unfortunately, the conflict is still ongoing and Brent crude keeps on creeping higher and NatGas is back at the yearly highs (not to mention crack spreads). As we are seeing this week, with equities close to the ATH and oil rallying again the risk reward to be long decreases significantly. Hence, we think a more structural European long requires confidence in a resolution to the US-Iran conflict, as we have pointed out before. We remain neutral. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures Private sector QT also in the mix: The BoJ’s steady progress on QT has led to a decline in deposits (relative to nominal GDP) at private banks (see top chart opposite). While such a relationship is natural, we still see it as notable that strong loan growth of about 4% y/y, has not managed to fully offset this trend. We think this decline in deposits may actually be felt more strongly than implied by the number. There are two reasons for this. First, the time-lag in fiscal spending. When private sector investors buy JGBs, deposits fall initially but theoretically then recover when the government deploys the related spending. However, there is a good time lag for such cycle. This spending has often taken a form of a ‘fund’ or ‘reserve’ and is therefore not immediately put to work in the economy, leading to a lengthy period out of circulation. Second, we think the steepness of the curve may be important. Because the JPY yield curve is steep, holders of cash (liquidity) have a large opportunity cost relative to investing in long-term assets. This may not quite suggest a liquidity ‘shortage’, but certainly implies there would be no surplus, which would be a support for tighter USDJPY xccy basis. This implies total capacity to add approximately JPY90.6tn of interest-rate risk. This is JPY9.1tn higher than last year, reflecting both the shorter duration of 10-year JGBs as yields have risen and the increase in Tier 1 capital (+JPY4.4tn). That said, it is highly unrealistic to assume that all banks would increase interest-rate risk all the way to their IRRBB limits. In practice, banks may not even add half of this theoretical capacity. Our estimates suggest that JGBs outstanding in the market, excluding BoJ hold- ings, will increase by JPY28tn in the 6-10Y sector alone over the one-year period from June 2026 to June 2027. IRRBB is unlikely to become a constraint on banks' JGB purchases over the next year, but it may become a more important consideration over the next two to three years.
