The downside news in this component came from motor vehicles, where inflationary pressure has weakened in the past year (Figure 10). Semi-durable inflation was stronger than expected, accelerating 0.5pp to 0.2% y/y, offsetting the miss in durable inflation. The strength in semi- durables came from clothing and footwear, which the ONS cited was due to discounting being brought forward into June this year, and demand effects from good weather. We ultimately view these two factors as temporary, and do not adjust our semi-durables forecast. We assess the July print as favourable to our core goods outlook, with 3m/3m annualised momentum now running at 1.1%, and no discernable pass through from energy costs to consumer goods prices in the inflation data yet, although we do expect some pass through to come (Figure 9). Marking to market, we now expect core goods inflation to be on average 1bp lower over the next 12 months. We expect core goods inflation to reach 1.2% y/y in Dec-26, and average 1.1% y/y in 2027. 21 August 2026 4 Barclays | UK inflation forecast update

records.text: the workflow interpreted complex policy language and automatically mapped risks, occupancy types and coverage details into standardized classifications required for downstream pricing and risk models. The second workflow showcased a natural-language analytics interface that enabled users to evaluate portfolio exposures, catastrophe losses and reserve requirements without requiring programming expertise. Using an Australian wildfire scenario, the platform analyzed loss exposures across multiple return-period scenarios and identified portfolio concentrations and potential reserve impacts in real time, illustrating how AI can help insurance professionals move from data gathering to decision-making. Meeting Takeaways Connected intelligence breaks down data silos. Risk decisions increasingly require connecting credit, KYC, supply-chain, climate, cyber and insurance data rather than analyzing each domain independently. Companies must understand second- and third-order dependencies across suppliers, infrastructure, counterparties and ownership relationships. Moody’s combines proprietary data, entity linkages and specialized models around the decision a customer needs to make. A common data structure can also create consistent answers across insurers, brokers, reinsurers and other market participants. AI is shifting enterprise software from delivering isolated information toward connected and actionable intelligence. Proprietary data and domain expertise remain the primary AI moat.

ClickHouse Company Introduction ClickHouse is an open-source analytical database and real-time data platform that enables organizations to store, process and analyze large volumes of data. Originally developed for analytics workloads, the platform has expanded into machine learning and AI-related use cases that require fast access to large datasets. ClickHouse supports real-time analytics, data processing and retrieval across structured and unstructured information. The platform is used by organizations to support AI agents, retrieval systems, customer-facing applications and other latency-sensitive workloads. Meeting Takeaways Real-time analytics remains the core platform, while observability is becoming an increasingly important wedge into the enterprise. ClickHouse was built to power large-scale, low-latency analytics workloads, and management continues to view real-time analytics as the company’s foundational use case. However, some of the strongest recent commercial momentum is coming from observability-related workloads, particularly log analytics and AI application telemetry, where customers are looking to reduce spend on platforms such as Splunk and Elastic. Management emphasized that winning observability budgets is often a more effective entry point than pursuing wholesale warehouse migrations, positioning observability as an increasingly important path to enterprise expansion. records.text: as not been published for the 2025-year index, data from the previous index (2005 base year) showed that while wooden structures accounted for 38% of private rental housing, they accounted for an extraordinarily high 77% of owner-occupied housing, the basis for imputed rents. This outcome is unsurprising given that a huge proportion of owner-occupied homes in Japan are wooden, and we suspect that this pattern is largely unchanged under the new standards. That is, because imputed rents are calculated primarily by referencing wooden private rental housing, a segment characterized by lower growth, its own growth tends to lag that of private rental housing overall. Therefore, imputed rent growth is estimated to be lower than actual trends due to the high proportion of wooden structures and the lack of quality adjustments. Imputed rent in the first place is not an expense actually paid by owner-occupied households. What they pay is the housing price, and the housing investment deflator in GDP data rose a marked 4.2% YoY in 2Q 2026. Because the growth of imputed rents, which are not actually paid, is calculated low statistically, a significant gap has emerged between the published CPI inflation rate and inflation as actually perceived by households in their daily lives. Fed Watcher Fed Watcher Date 24 August 2026 A divided Fed keeps September in play Fed communications over the past week showed the Committee remains nearly evenly divided on the appropriate policy path ahead. The minutes from the July FOMC meeting showed broad support for holding rates steady, alongside a clear conditional bias from “many” officials toward further tightening if inflation fails to moderate. Indeed, while most participants expected disinflation over the remainder of the year as their baseline outlook, many officials highlighted risks of greater inflation persistence amid p rolonged supply -chain pressures stemming from a protracted Middle East conflict and emergent AI -related price pressures. Part of the reason for the stability in views between the June and July meetings was the presence of only a few additional data points, setting up the September meeting as a possibly more important date for a policy re-think. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 9 Financial Conditions: Easing Since the July FOMC Following the conflict in the Middle East and the uncertainty it brings to the next steps for monetary policy, we continue to track our FRB/US-based measure of financial conditions. As of the August 20 market close, financial conditions remained tighter than before the recent escalation in the Middle East, yet meaningfully easier than at the time before the July FOMC meeting. Since the July FOMC meeting, financial conditions have eased by 25bp, primarily driven by positive equity returns and U.S. dollar depreciation. Financial conditions eased temporarily on August 19 following the Treasury buyback announcement, but that easing has mostly reversed as of August 20. The index aims to capture how changes in asset prices weigh on future economic activity. It includes five daily variables: the 10-year Treasury yield, S&P 500 returns, the corporate BBB credit spread, the valuation of the U.S. dollar, and the price of oil. These are aggregated based on their estimated growth elasticities relative to the federal funds rate using the Federal Reserve's FRB/US model. As a result, the index can be interpreted as the equivalent change in the federal funds rate, expressed in basis points, required to generate a similar effect on economic activity. At the same time, as we have consistently noted, the impact of higher oil prices will gradually feed through to CPI with a lag, and the positive contribution from energy is expected to gradually expand heading into early next year. We estimated the effect would be close to 10bp on headline CPI, all else equal, but the realised impact was roughly 1bp. The lower figure could be due to the pass through being less than the 75% we assumed, although there is evidence to suggest there was a broad take-up in terms of passing on the VAT cuts. The temporary VAT cuts are to be reversed in September, so we adjust our forecast to remove the bounceback we had accounted for in our profile path. It's probably more fair to say that stock-bond correlations can break this time. Because what's driving the spike in equity-bond return correlations feels different. Unlike in the other episodes of correlations surge where nominal rates were driven by inflation expectations, this time it's driven by real yields – i.e., uncertainty around policy. We think it means it could take more time, and more than just inflation being unstuck (which is already happening) for stock-bond correlations to normalize. This makes bonds less effective of a ballast against market volatility in portfolios than before, at least in the medium term, arguing for a lower allocation. The bigger story may be what the surprise announcement reveals about Treasury’s reaction function and approach to debt management going forward. First, Treasury is acting on its commitment to keep long-end yields contained while also signaling that it is perhaps more attuned to market conditions than many thought. On this, the use of tactical communications is now officially part of Treasury’s toolkit. The buyback announcement also comes on the heels of Treasury’s recent suggestion that Japan should make greater use of the Fed’s FIMA repo facility to finance its FX interventions. The combination of tactical signaling and a willingness to operate outside established precedent raises the bar to market participants being short rates and could help to limit long-end yield increases in the near term. The detailed agenda will be released closer to the event (see here). Euro area | First August inflation prints and survey data: The key data focus next week will be on the first country inflation prints for August arriving on Friday. Intervention as deterrent, BoJ tightening as the main tool The US and Japanese governments appear aligned on the objective of stabilizing the yen. However, uncertainty remains over how they intend to achieve that goal. Having observed actual intervention tactics, we have revised our previous view that authorities aimed to push USD/JPY below 155 and alter short-term market positioning through intervention. Instead, the more likely policy sequence is that the Bank of Japan (BoJ) shifts further in a hawkish direction through rate hikes. If the underlying trend of yen weakness remains intact even then, authorities would use forceful intervention to stabilize the currency. Monetary tightening amid fiscal expansion To make the effects of FX intervention durable and achieve lasting yen stability, Japan ultimately needs a shift in its policy mix. A near-term change in the Takaichi administration's fiscal stance appears unlikely. For now, the most plausible policy mix remains monetary tightening amid fiscal expansion. FX: Bullish yen view unchanged, but it may take time Our year-end forecast of USD/JPY at 149 remains unchanged. records.text: M Global Idea Sunday Start | What's Next in Global Macro $40T of Debt: Brake or Break? Morgan Stanley & Co. International plc+ Andrew Sheets Strategist Andrew.Sheets@morganstanley.com +44 20 7677-2905 ©Morgan Stanley 2026 Early in the last decade it was all people could talk about. On the heels of the GFC and the response required to contain it, markets turned their attention to the threat of government debt. Research reports, TV and conferences abounded with charts of rising debt/GDP and stern warnings of the consequences. It was the issue that would shape our financial future, and what a bleak future it was: high debt, low growth, and grinding austerity as far as the eye could see. Or not. The dire predictions of that period did not materialize. Global growth was fine. Investment expanded and capital deepened, thwarting concerns of ‘secular stagnation’. DM equities and currencies were the great beneficiaries (refuting the conventional wisdom at the time). And the concern about rising debt? A distant memory. In its first 240 years the United States accumulated ~$20T of Federal debt. It has borrowed another $20T in the last ten. Comparing this debt to the size of the economy is more appropriate. Earlier fintech innovation focused on numerical databases and general ledgers, while foundation models can now process the unstructured language that defines insurance products and workflows. Corgi has automated most of the underwriting production process, although regulators may still require human review of a policy sample. In trucking insurance, this automation can reduce quote times from roughly two weeks at legacy carriers to approximately two minutes. Foundation models can therefore address language-based workflows that traditional financial software could not reliably automate. AI-native platforms can compete through a better customer experience. Corgi uses AI primarily to complete insurance workflows faster and more effectively, with cost reduction serving as a secondary benefit. Automation across underwriting, regulatory documentation and claims can compress processes that traditionally take weeks into minutes or days. During catastrophic events, AI voice agents can scale first-notice-of-loss intake dynamically when claim volumes exceed the staffing capacity of legacy carriers. Faster claims resolution can improve customer satisfaction while reducing reserve uncertainty and regulatory pressure. Corgi illustrates how AI can support growth by improving speed, reliability and responsiveness instead of competing primarily on price. We can turn to our fair value model (Figure 4) to quantify the amount of shift in expectations necessary to explain the observed steepening, as our model uses Treasury WAM as one of the drivers. Given a coefficient of ~0.1, a shortening in WAM of three months would result in TFP decreasing by ~0.2 bp/year, which is about the reduction in TFP that we observed on Wednesday. This indicates that market expectations may have shifted towards a sustained reduction in long-end issu- ance. However, our UST strategists note that they don’t think this would be a prudent action, as they continue to forecast a funding gap of more than $3.5tn in the coming fiscal years, which is likely to require more duration supply, not less. Therefore, we think the price action in swap spreads following the announcement was excessive and have thus rec- ommended exiting swap spread curve steepeners. Looking ahead, the steepening of the spread curve over the week has resulted in a sharp correction in TFP (Figure 5), and TFP now appears only one standard deviation above our estimate of fair value. Therefore, we remain neutral on the swap spread curve for now. records.text: 21 August 2026 US Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank Securities Inc. Page 12 Fed and repo outlook A string of soft economic data over the past week has reduced market pricing for Fed hikes this year to just under one hike by December. The odds of a September hike have also fallen to around 35%. The scale of the move feels slightly stretched for two reasons. First, the data details were more mixed than the headlines suggested. Payrolls were significantly weaker, but the unemployment rate also fell to its lowest level in 18 months. Retail sales were weak as well, but that followed several months of strength and may have been distorted by the timing shift associated with Prime Day. Second, there is still a meaningful amount of data before the next FOMC meeting, whose outcome will likely depend on new developments around labor market conditions, the Middle East, a nd energy prices. Our economists maintain their base case for a 25bp hike in September, though conviction is arguably lower. In terms of market pricing, Fed funds OIS for the Z6 carry period is near the top of the estimated range implied by plausible FOMC outcomes over the next three to four months. This reflects the view that the Fed is still likely to hike at least once this year, which we think is broadly justified. For the SOFR-FF basis, nearly $500bn of net bill issuance during July and August, or about $450bn after Fed purchases, has been absorbed well, with little spillover into repo. records.text: ed 8-10 year periods like we experienced during the ~40-year disinflationary boom between 1982 and 2020. Instead, we are now in a period more akin to the post WWII era during which economic cycles were driven by higher nominal GDP growth and persistent inflation well above 2%. This means higher economic volatility and a more reactive monetary policy environment as inflation ebbs and flows. Perhaps the best evidence we have that the secular trend in disinflation ended with COVID is the long-term chart of Treasury yields. As shown below, it doesn't require much technical analysis experience to see how conditions have changed in the bond market. After enjoying what was perhaps the greatest secular bull market in Treasury bonds from 1982 to 2020, the reversal is clear with very important considerations for all capital markets. This story is now appreciated but far from over, in our view. Based on the well- established 36-year (peak-to-trough) Kondratieff cycle for bonds, we believe the trend in yields remains higher in the longer term, with the occasional cyclical bull market along the way, much like we experienced between 1945 and 1982 (the prior ~36-year secular bear market for bonds).

records.text: Recent UK term premium rise not (yet) because of fiscal risks. Although front-end n UK yields have drifted higher alongside higher energy prices, this week’s labour market and inflation releases did little to change our UK macro view, namely that the BoE are unlikely to hike while labour market quantities are weak and private sector pay growth decelerates. Energy prices remain a risk for the UK front-end, but we continue to think the UK 2s10s curve will steepen further, helped by the global weakness in duration. Our estimate of the 10-year term premium has risen towards its recent highs, but we do not think this reflects UK-specific risks — as above, most major bond markets have shown relatively bearish impulses recently. Another illustration of this is our measure of UK country risk, which has trended lower since Q2, in contrast to prior periods of rising UK risk premium (Exhibit 4). While this is a source of some comfort, the Gilt market is a reminder of the limited effect of supply tweaks on the overall level of yields — since 2025, supply of long-end Gilts has shrunk to its lowest levels in decades (Exhibit 5). Although this supported long-end Gilts on asset swaps, high long-end yields suggest macro factors dominate supply dynamics. Moreover, as attention starts to turn to the Budget, UK risk premium is likely to remain sticky. That asymmetry continues to argue for a steeper GBP curve and reinforces our 2s10s steepening bias. We are Neutral on Brazil equities for 2H26 as the setup is no longer supported by the two pillars that typically drive Brazil outperformance: a strong global macro environment that lifts EM and high beta, and a compelling domestic easing story that lowers the equity discount rate, improves the credit impulse, and broadens earnings participation. That balance has shifted: global cross-currents are more mixed, and the “rates down” catalyst has materially weakened. This matters because Brazil generally needs either sustained global flow support or credible domestic easing and earnings tailwinds to offset its persistent policy and event-risk premium. Globally, the HALO framework still helps explain why Brazil can look attractive at times. As the AI and semiconductor trade cools, investors often rotate toward “hard asset, low obsolescence” cash flows, which tends to favor commodity-heavy LatAm, with higher oil reinforcing that asymmetry. This is supportive at the margin, but it does not neutralize near-term election risk. Brazil has historically underperformed into elections as uncertainty rises and then rallied after the vote as risk premia compress, but this year’s pre-election drawdown has been relatively modest (~10% so far), which may limit the upside from a post-election relief move. There is one big caveat with these numbers and those on "sensitivities" earlier. These relationships between equities, credit, FX, commodities with rates and yield curves in large part are based on what yields and the curve implies for growth and inflation – e.g., curve bull steepens going into a patch of weakening growth so rates rally but spreads widen and stocks underperform. But as we argued earlier, if yields are now reflecting growing policy uncertainty as much as growth and inflation, then how stocks and credit could fare across curve scenarios can also look very, very different. This is even before we get to how the AI capex cycle that's driving earnings and higher corporate credit issuance is relatively macro- indifferent! In short – expect some curve balls.

Page 26 Inflation skew and term premia Matthew Raskin | Strategist | +1-212-250-1741 Note: This note was originally published on 18 August 2026 Global term premia are on the rise. For the US, the local trough came around Chair Warsh's June press conference, and the increase in our 5s10s term premium measure since then is in the 85th percentile of two-month moves back to 2000. This rise in TP is in line with our longstanding outlook. Even with increases over recent years, US term premia remain at moderate levels by long-run standards and, in our view, should move up given increasing bond supply to be absorbed by price-sensitive investors and elevated upside inflation risk. For context on the latter, the chart below plots the expected skew of 5y5y inflation against 5y5y nominal UST. The skew measure comes from the NY Fed's Survey of Market Expectations , computed as the average probability placed on 5y5y CPI realizing above 3% less the probability of it realizing below 1 .5%. This sits at a record high (back to 2011) and has correlated highly with 5y5y UST. Given Warsh’s mixed signals on the 2% inflation target at the July press conference, skew and any pass-through to term premia bear close monitoring. The ONS linked June's jump partly to World Cup spending and a summer heatwave that lifted arts, entertainment and hospitality. Pub transactions hit a 2026 peak on Saturday 27 June for England-Panama at five times the year's daily average, up 389.9% on the day and 161.7% y-o-y. Trend growth in the economy may be stronger than we thought. The ONS alternative (RTI-based) measure of labour productivity has had three straight quarters of positive annual growth in output per hour, +1.6% in Q4 -25, +2.1% in Q1-26, and +0.7% in Q2 -26, well above the 2010 –2021 average of 0.5%. Additionally, ICT and machinery investment was again a key driver of Q2 -26's pickup in business investment, even after dragging on investment as recently as Q4-25. Stay bearish gamma amid steeper vol term structure The Treasury’s announced increase in its long-end buyback this week, following its rare involvement in the JPY currency intervention a few weeks prior, is evidence of Treasury Secretary Bessent’s focus to contain US long-end yields. By highlighting that the buybacks could be larger than the announced $4bn and that there are other options in its toolkit, the Treasury is signaling its willingness to enforce an implicit ceiling on long-end yields. We believe this implicit backstop support should exert downward pressure on upper-right vols and reduce the right tail of the 30y rate distribution in the near-term. Notably, the growth of 2L debt in the US HY index stands in stark contrast to the leveraged loan market, which has seen 2L debt decline meaningfully in recent years (see Leveraged Loans: Where did all the 2nd liens go?). Today, junior secured debt makes up roughly 3.2% and 1.3% of the HY Index and LLI, respectively (Figure 2). To explore this 1L/2L dynamic, we segment our analysis in an attempt to answer two distinct questions: 1. Is there a difference in where 1L debt trades depending on the amount/type of debt subordinate to it? 2. What do 1L-2L relationships look like across the HY market today? Not all capital structures with 1Ls are the same For issuers with 1L debt, the value of the 1L rank in a waterfall can vary depending on what sits beneath it, and is therefore able to absorb increases in L TV/losses. To be sure, this is not in the data yet: PMIs at 52.1, received this morning, are consistent with EA growth around a 0.3%Q pace (we see 3Q26 a touch lower at 0.25%Q because of potential paybacks from 2Q26 in some sectors – see here). But the global manufacturing cycle likely has room to improve further, and Europe finally looks like it is benefiting too. On the other side of the equation, we would stress the significant tightening of financial conditions this summer: on our estimates the ECB indicator of “macro- finance FCI” increased by around 25bp since mid-June, mostly because of the sell-off in the bond market. Surely, the recovery is solidifying, but key risks remain. With all that, what is the ECB likely to conclude in September? It will likely see upside risks to growth and to inflation since June. In our view, this backdrop cements a September hike. With no clear evidence yet of the transmission from higher energy prices to core and with some tightening of financial conditions, we don’t expect the ECB will be in a rush to hike any further. But, while our call is for a hold in December, the ECB is unlikely to close the door to another hike in December. Given how risks are skewed, we suspect the Council will not mind markets pricing a slightly higher terminal rate than 2.5%.

records.text: M Idea 2 Treasury buybacks and the limits of long-end intervention What did the Treasury announce? On August 19, Treasury Secretary Bessent announced that the Treasury would "at least" double the maximum size of its liquidity-support buybacks of longer-dated nominal Treasury securities, raising the cap from $2bn to at least $4 billion per operation in both the 10–20y and 20–30y sectors. The larger operations will begin on September 9 and remain in effect through the end of the current refunding quarter on November 4, when presumably the Treasury will provide updated guidance. Treasury attributed the change to strong participation in recent long- end operations and a desire to provide greater liquidity support in these sectors. As we discuss in more detail below, the timing of the announcement was notable. The change was made outside the normal Quarterly Refunding schedule, making the timing of the change itself an important feature of the announcement, in our view. Our take: Heightened focus on long-term yields In our view, the buyback announcement is best understood as a reaction to rising long- term Treasury yields rather than as a routine adjustment to debt-management policy. Normally, Treasury buybacks are conducted with an eye toward improving liquidity in off- the-run Treasuries and constraints on dealer balance sheets. records.text: M Idea 10 The effective tariff rate, tariff receipts, and refunds Tariffs averaged 6.8% over April-June, and we expect that it will rise to near 10% USTR's final forced-labor Section 301 action was broadly in line with our expectations. Effective July 24, the agency imposed additional tariffs on imports from 60 economies, setting a 10% duty on economies that have adopted, partially adopted, or committed to adopt a forced-labor import prohibition and a 12.5% duty on most others. The final action also preserves several key carve-outs, including goods already subject to Section 232 tariffs, USMCA-compliant imports, and a range of general and country-specific product exemptions. Overall, both the tariff structure and the principal exemptions closely resemble the proposal, reinforcing our expectation that Section 301 would serve as the broad country-level tariff floor. We continue to expect that the statutory effective tariff rate will converge toward ~10% by year-end. records.text: Japan Macro Watch21 August 2026 ab 4 However, this constraint will emerge only gradually because the relevant interest rate is the effective interest rate on outstanding debt rather than the market yield on newly issued bonds. The weighted average coupon rate on government debt remains low at 0.98%, while the average maturity of JGBs is 9.4 years. As only around 13.4% of outstanding debt is refinanced each year, it will take considerable time for higher market rates to feed through fully. Indeed, Cabinet Office projections suggest that even if long- term yields rise from 3.0% in 2027 to 3.8% in 2037, the effective interest rate would not reach 3% until around 2035. Nonetheless, the speed of the recent move remains concerning. Long-term yields have risen by roughly 1.2 percentage points over the past year. If this trend persists, the effective interest rate could approach 3% as early as 2030, forcing policymakers to place greater emphasis on achieving a primary fiscal surplus. As indicated in our research (see here), inflation is positive for most stocks—especially cyclicals—and particularly after a recessionary outcome has been priced and forecasted in earnings growth. The point of bringing this up today is to simply remind readers that what's happening more recently is part of a much bigger story that has been playing out for years, if not decades. Almost every experienced investor appreciates and understands how significant the Financial Crisis was to the structure of financial markets. Of all the events we have lived through in our 35 years as a market participant, the GFC ushered in some permanent changes, many of which are still dominating how we invest today. The foray into quantitative easing and the use of other extraordinary policy tools has contributed to some of the most powerful investment themes of the past 20 years, including the secular trend toward passive investing and the "buy the dip" mentality, much of which is due to the proverbial Fed Put. While safety and security need to be protected, these policies, especially when aggressively implemented, could have a negative impact on economic activity. For example, after the Shanxi coal mine accident in May, Chinese coal production dropped 12%, similar to the decline in January-February 2020 when the country was under a national Covid lockdown (Exhibit 11). We interpret the higher contribution now as evidence of increased fiscal spending. According to this simplistic calculation, the fiscal package has added c.40bp to GDP growth of 0.7% since then, broadly in line with our assumptions (and driven less by investment). However, this estimate should be treated with caution: First, it could overstate the effect as the increases in government spending also reflect other things apart from the fiscal package. Second, and perhaps more importantly, it is likely to understate the effect as fiscal spending, notably on investment, has triggered private investment (e.g. Rheinmetall building a new ammunition factory). National accounts spending detail is not granular enough on a quarterly level to detect these effects at the sector level. A different approach is looking at the production side of the economy, notably those components most likely impacted by fiscal spending. In industrial production, for example, defence-related sectors (explosives, weapons/ammunition, other transport) has made a positive contribution of 23bp to the overall growth in industrial production since Q2 2025 (which has fallen 0.6% over the same period, dragged lower by motor vehicles and machinery and equipment), Figure 24I n d u s t r i a l p r o d u c t i o n , c h a n g e Q 2 2 0 2 6 v s Q 2 2 0 2 5 , w e i g h t e d c o n t r i b u t i o n s ,

records.text: he key development of recent months has been the growing importance of foreign portfolio flows. Foreign investors have been significant sellers of Taiwanese equities in 2026, and dividend-related outflows have also weighed heavily on the currency. These cyclical flow pressures have likely played a larger role in recent TWD weakness than further reductions in life-insurer hedging activity. As dividend outflows fade and assuming that foreign equity selling moderates, the market's attention is likely to shift back toward Taiwan's underlying balance-of-payments strength. We believe the recent depreciation in TWD increasingly looks stretched relative to the strength of Taiwan's underlying balance-of-payments position. While lower hedge ratios help explain why TWD has not appreciated in line with the surge in Taiwan's current account surplus, we no longer view them as a compelling reason to expect sustained further TWD weakness. The bulk of the adjustment in life-insurer hedging behavior now appears to be largely complete, while FX reserve capacity continues to expand and Taiwan's external surplus remains exceptionally large. 21 August 2026 43 Barclays | US Credit Alpha: Spreads not yielding to rates

records.text: US Rates Weekly 21 August 2026 Citi Research 14 Looking at the swaption payer skews on 30y tails, it seems that the sentiments for long-end rates are mixed and nuanced with dependency on the outlook horizon. In the gamma space, 1m30y payer skew is consistent with the US board put skew mentioned earlier in that it is still elevated after only a slight pullback on the increased buyback announcement (Figure 25). But in contrast, 3m30y payer skew has been drifting lower and did not bounce higher, like 1m30y skew earlier this month. And when compared against our realized skews fair value model, the 3m30y implied risk reversal skew currently looks relatively low (Figure 26). As a reminder, we calculate realized skews as the model value of OTM options from the empirical SABR model calibrated to the recent (3m) realized dynamics of ATM volatilities and rates. We believe this shows that the market is likely not as concerned about the long-end becoming de-anchored in the near-term as the narrative would suggest. With that said, long-dated payer skew, such as 5y30y, has drifted higher since the start of the conflict to its long-run peak, and the 5y30y implied risk reversal skew looks relatively high based on our realized skew model. Anecdotally, part of the richening in bottom-right payer skew has been driven by non-rates investors’ demand for long-dated deep OTM payers as tail hedge for the long-term fiscal fears. Share buybacks remain an effective means of returning surplus capital, but one-off distributions that are not linked to a growth strategy or target balance sheet may increasingly be interpreted as a sign of limited reinvestment opportunities. Under the previous deflationary, low-growth environment, attractive investment opportunities were limited, making it rational for companies to accumulate cash and ultimately return surplus funds to shareholders. Today, however, growth and investment opportunities are expanding amid inflation, AI/DX, labor shortages, industry consolidation, and government-led strategic investment. Companies are increasingly being asked whether they can redeploy not only cash and deposits but also “dormant assets,” such as real estate and cross shareholdings, toward areas offering higher returns. We believe the companies likely to be rewarded are not those making a binary choice between growth investment and shareholder returns, but those that prioritize high-return investment opportunities and then return genuine surplus capital in a disciplined manner. Since 2023, TSE reforms have likewise focused not simply on increasing shareholder returns, but on sustainable growth and medium- to long-term corporate value creation through management that is conscious of the cost of capital and share prices. Financial Innovation and Deposit Competition Digital banks, money market funds, stablecoins, and other liquid alternatives make bank deposits more contestable. Greater competition may raise deposit betas, causing policy- rate changes to pass more rapidly into bank funding costs and potentially strengthening the bank lending channel of monetary policy. The same mechanism can increase fragility. Lower switching costs allow depositors to pursue higher yields in normal times but also facilitate faster withdrawals during stress. Policy implication: Greater competition can strengthen monetary transmission while making bank funding less stable. Regulation and liquidity requirements need to account for both effects. Stablecoins Stablecoins resemble private money as well as having characteristics of a new asset class. Issuers create par-redeemable liabilities backed largely by Treasury bills, deposits, repo, and other liquid assets. The relevant risks resemble those associated with money market funds and narrow banks. Policy implication: Regulation should follow economic function rather than technology. records.text: Global Asset Allocation 21 August 2026 Citi Research 7 Rates – Neutral duration, now long EM local against Japan We are staying neutral duration. In the bigger picture the story for duration has not changed. First, uncertainty with respect to Iran has risen again, and rates are the main asset class that very closely trade with Iran risk and oil. At this stage the news flow is not overly comforting, with Iran seemingly playing hard ball, making it hard for President Trump to find an off-ramp. However, when developments looked bleak in the past, it often followed by surprising developments, improving oil market sentiment, at least for a few weeks at a time. Two sided risks for oil make a strong duration position hard to implement. Second, and somewhat related, Chair Warsh is still somewhat of an enigma for the market. While the news flow has turned more dovish for the Fed, the reaction function of chair Warsh and the extent of his control over the committee are untested and uncertain. US not the preferred underweight anymore. When we initiated the US underweight at the end of June, it was a very natural choice, given that oil was under downside pressure, while the AI boom kept going, creating inflation pressures much less tied to oil than was the case in other regions. We stay MW BRL after closing our OW earlier this year. BRL has been more resilient to the electoral noise this year compared to prior political cycles, likely on the back of a strong appetite for carry. But despite high rates, a crowded BRL position and the lack of risk premia still leave the currency in a fragile position ahead of the election. The two election scenarios (continuity vs. transition) seem to offer broadly symmetric payoffs from here towards 5.50 in the bearish case and 4.90 in the bullish case. We also stay MW Brazilian local rates and bonds. So far this year, Brazilian rates have been driven more by global factors than domestic politics/macro, but election sensitivity is likely to rise in the weeks leading up to the first round. Election risk looks fairly priced, yet outcomes can still trigger large moves: bearish implies bear steepening and about +90bp higher GBI-EM Brazil yields; bullish implies bull flattening and roughly a 160bp rally led by the back end. With political risk rising, rates lack a clear anchor (similar to Colombia pre- election), so stay neutral at current levels. Notably though, this dovish shift is not being led by Warsh ; as interpretation of Fed speak has drifted more dovish, coverage of Warsh has maintained a steady hawkish tone (Figure 6). Figure 6 A chair on his own Source: State Street Markets, MKT MediaStats This is important for two reasons. First, Jackson Hole provides the Chair with an opportunity to articulate their own views rather than the Committee's collective stance, a key distinction from post -FOMC speeches. Given current perceptions of Warsh's tone, the bar for him to be viewed as materially more hawkish is relatively high. Second, when a large gap emerges between perceptions of the Chair and the broader Fed, history suggests the rest of the Committee often shifts in a more hawkish direction to align with the Chair. Figure 7 shows the monthly change in aggregate Fed tone during periods of extreme hawkish divergence. The relationship is mild but the rest of the Fed tends to get more hawkish to narrow the gap with the Chair. While history may not repeat itself, the current divergence, which ranks in the top 1% since 2015, appears difficult to sustain. Investors are not looking for a definitive signal on September policy so much as clarity on the Fed's reaction function at a time when inflation remains problematic, the Treasury is actively supporting the long -end through buybacks and uncertainty around the interaction of fiscal and monetary policy is growing. Against that backdrop, markets enter the Symposium with policy expectations unsettled, the USD under pressure and long-end yields elevated. The current practice of spreading regional meeting dates more evenly through the calendar and announcing them earlier was itself advocated by Himino; the Saitama event is simply a product of that arrangement. The move to higher yields briefly paused on Wednesday amid Treasury’s buy- back announcement. records.text: 21 August 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 31 A summer of relentless OATs' cheapening Ioannis Sokos | Strategist | +44-20-754-75680 Note: This note was originally published on 17 August 2026 Besides the well documented correlation to oil prices and geopolitics in general, EGBs have exhibited some significant idiosyncratic moves over the summer months. The main outlier has been the relentless cheapening of OATs in relative terms vs other EGBs. As today’s chart shows, for the first time this year, the YTD cumulative residual of 10y OAT/Bund has exceeded that of BTP/Bund. These residuals capture the relative performance of each country spread when adjusted for its beta to the average EGB spread (estimated over 2025). OATs had a negative residual, i.e. sign of outperformance, up until early June. This was mostly a carry-over of their outperformance early this year on the back of the 2026 budget approval. This negative residual was gradually being eroded since the beginning of the Iran war. Since early June, this residual turned positive, i.e. a sign of relative underperformance, and the pace of cheapening accelerated further in August. On the contrary, the cheapening move seen in BTPs in July was partially corrected in August. Since these residuals by construction have to sum up to zero, OATs’ recent cheapening has to lead to other EGBs’ richening. Morgan Treasury futures September - December rollover outlook sum- mary As we approach the period where the majority of Treasury futures positions will need to be rolled forward from September to December expiries, we discuss our outlook for the various Treasury futures calendar spreads. A detailed discussion may be found in our recently pub- lished U.S. Bond Futures Rollover Outlook September 2026 / December 2026 (8/12/2026), and we summarize key details here. First, we note that although repo rates have been trading in a 16bp range, indicating greater volatility compared to the last roll, we expect financing rates to be mostly stable over the course of the roll and thus not be a driver of calendar spreads. Over the past few months, aggregate open interest in the Treasury futures complex has con- tinued to increase and is now at new highs. This means that technical imbalances could once again play a factor during this roll cycle. Our metric to gauge positioning imbalances is net asset manager longs (as they prefer to avoid delivery and roll their positions early). Asset managers are net long across all contracts ( Figure 15). records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 15 Preliminary estimate of the benchmark revision to payrolls. The BLS will release its preliminary estimate of the benchmark revision to payrolls. The estimate is based on administrative data from the unemployment insurance system that provide a direct count of payrolls and a benchmark for the level of payrolls as of March 2026. This is just a preliminary estimate. The full and final revision will be pulled into the monthly payroll estimates next February. We expect little revision, for several reasons. First, through December 2025, the 12-month changes for QCEW and for payroll survey estimates of private payrolls are very similar; the slowing between March 2025 and December 2025, too, are very similar. Second, the BLS last year adopted new methods for estimating the effects of business 'births' and deaths', which should have (marginally) improved the accuracy of the initial, pre- benchmark estimates. That said, this estimate of the benchmark revision will incorporate QCEW data for 1Q that are not yet published; and the 1Q data could make a difference. Payrolls are currently shown as accelerating sharply.

In addition, crude oil import prices have remained elevated for both Middle Eastern and US crude, reflecting JPY depreciation and higher premiums ( Figure 14). International benchmark crude prices reversed at the start of July and are currently in an upward trend. With the overlapping impact of JPY depreciation, elevated levels are likely to persist. On the export side, autos, electronic components such as semiconductors, and semiconductor-manufacturing equipment contributed to growth. Autos boosted y/y export growth due to increased shipments to the EU and the rebound from a sharp decline in export prices to the US a year earlier amid the impact of tariffs. records.text: Takeaways from UC Berkeley and UCSF AI Lab Biography Adam Yala is an Assistant Professor of Computational Precision Health, Statistics and Electrical Engineering & Computer Science at UC Berkeley and UCSF. His breast cancer prediction tool, Mirai, has been deployed across 66 hospitals in 30 countries and now supports prospective clinical trials. His work has been featured in major outlets. He earned his BS, MEng, and PhD in Computer Science from MIT, where he was affiliated with the Jameel Clinic and Computer Science & Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL). Research Adam Yala’s research focuses on developing machine learning methods to personalize healthcare and bring them into clinical practice, with an emphasis on predicting cancer risk and designing individualized screening strategies. His work aims to deliver the right medical interventions, such as screenings or treatments, tailored to each patient’s unique risks and preferences. His research centers on three major themes, including modeling comprehensive patient records using multi-modal data to better understand outcomes, optimizing clinical decisions through AI-driven predictors and translating these tools into real-world healthcare settings. Meeting Takeaways Medical guidelines could become continuously improving algorithms. While hedge flows are smaller, they still provide further incremental support to TWD. Indeed, while forward points were positive for a prolonged period following the regulatory changes noted above, they have turned negative more recently, largely as a result of such hedging activity. Lower hedge ratios primarily represent a reduction in structural USD-selling flows rather than outright spot USD demand. While this has reduced the amount of Taiwan's current-account surplus that is recycled back into TWD, there is still ongoing recycling. Expansion of FX volatility reserves is also one reason we are less concerned about the risk of forced changes in overseas asset allocation. Taiwan life insurers continue to hold substantial foreign-currency exposure, but the combination of lower hedge ratios, larger reserve buffers, and revised accounting treatment has materially improved their flexibility in managing currency risk. While this reduces structural USD-selling flows, it also lowers the likelihood of abrupt hedging demand or forced asset sales in response to FX volatility. More broadly, Taiwan life insurers remain among the largest holders of foreign assets globally. records.text: relevant to market participants outside of the US. US natural gas prices will increasingly exert their influence on global prices through higher US LNG exports and the expected emerging global LNG oversupply. US natural gas, Asian JKM and European TTF prices will become more correlated. Haynesville production has set new highs, based on analyzing pipeline scrape data not just from flow points inside producing counties, but outside to capture missing production. The EIA has revised its Haynesville production estimate to the upside multiple times. Haynesville production should take another leg higher, possibly 1 to 2-bcf/d sequentially over the coming couple of quarters, partly based on the sharp rig count increase early this year. We also study pipeline networks in the three egress regions out of Haynesville and how future infrastructure developments affect this major shale gas play. These egress regions include: the Southeast and impacts of Transco’s Southeast Supply Enhancement Project (SSEP), Southeast Texas and impacts of Permian gas from West Texas reaching East Texas, and Southern Louisiana and developments of new pipelines. Negative means stocks up/ USD down or stocks down/ USD up. Vice versa for positive. What can break/brake this climb in stocks-bonds, stocks-USD correlations? Only when markets gain clarity on policy and institutional credibility, in our view. We don't even need to look at EM space, we saw examples of this in DM too. For example – in the US, S&P 500-USD correlations remained high during the debt ceiling crisis through 2015. The UK saw elevated FTSE 100-GBP correlations from 2020 through 2022. In Europe, EURO STOXX 50-EUR correlations were climbing and persistently high during the European sovereign crisis. Stocks-FX correlations eventually fell – in the US, after the debt ceiling was suspended, and for the UK, after the resolution of the 2022 mini-budget upheaval. For Europe, stocks-EUR correlations dropped rapidly to extremely negative territory after then-President of the ECB Mario Draghi's "bumblebee" speech. In all three instances, stocks-FX/bond correlations normalized when markets gained clarity on policy. records.text: Foreign Flows in U.S. Fixed Income 24 August 2026 Citi Research 7 swings in Canadian holdings have become common over the last year and are most likely due to some custodial shifts. Foreign investment data from Government of Canada showed that Canadians were net sellers of US Treasuries in June. So, this is likely some other country’s buying, with Canada as a custodial center. We would not attach much significance to a single data point from Canada, unless we see a string of monthly sales or purchases. The large increase in Canda holdings was offset by sales from the Cayman Islands and the UK. The Cayman Islands had a decrease of $32.1bn in long-term holdings (z-score of - 3.03). We think this was private investors rotating into some T-bills, as Cayman T-bill holdings increased around $15bn in June. It could also be hedge funds domiciled in Cayman Islands moving out of cash-futures basis trades as basis opportunities decreased significantly in recent months. The United Kingdom decreased their long-term holdings by $9.2bn in June (z-score of -0.81). In the first five months of the year, private investors in the UK bought around $80bn of USTs, so it would make sense that investors exited some of their positions that they entered when volatility picked up in June. We also saw holdings in Germany, Spain, and Belgium increase by $19.5bn collectively. This will chiefly be driven by aggressive QT programmes at the European Central Bank and at the Bank of Japan, in contrast with a stabilising Federal Reserve, while a revived UK repo market slows down the Bank of England QT process. This is the backdrop against which we will assess here the outlook for xccy basis. Our global liquidity forecasts suggest a steady decline in G4 central bank reserves at a year-on-year pace of about 10% through to end-2027 – only a modest retreat from the 11% contraction seen in 2025. This would leave G4 reserves at USD8.67trn at end-2026, and at USD7.8trn at end-2027, versus USD9.65trn at end-2025. At USD7.4trn at the end of 2028, G4 central bank reserves would still remain above pre-Covid levels. ECB, BoJ lead the drop: With the Fed’s balance sheet on a stabilising path, this decline would primarily be driven by the ECB and BoJ QT programmes, likely to shrink reserves by an average of 20% and 16% respectively over the next two years. Follow-through from the Treasury announcement. We are inclined to fade some of the recent strength in US inflation rates on the back of this week’s rally. Long- end TIPS were excluded from Wednesday’s Treasury announcement, which increased buyback operations for longer-dated nominal Treasuries from a current maximum of $2bn per operation to “at least” $4bn. While the estimated size remains small, the announcement deviated from the TBAC’s prior stylized analysis of when to change buyback sizes by sector and came two weeks after the August refunding, pointing to an attempt to stem the rise in long end bond yields. While our prior analysis of the UK market indicated a short half-life for flattening in the nominal curve, we observe a much more persistent impact on the UK inflation curve. Catalyst.Metric: Fuel prices, Brent crude, headline inflation

records.text: el prices are driven by two key components. The first is the pass-through of crude prices, which takes place within a few weeks and can differ if Brent prices increase or decline. The second is tax policies, which can be structurally different across countries and can be adjusted in response to oil price shocks. The latest news does not point to significant tax changes in the short term. Many temporary tax cuts aimed at shielding consumers from higher energy prices have now ended. The exception is Spain, where fuel price increases beyond a cer- tain threshold automatically trigger policy responses. France remains the country where the policy response has been the most muted, due to its fiscal consolidation objective. With no significant tax changes in sight overall for the region, the key driver for fuel prices in the near term will be Brent. In our forecast (Table 1), we take into account available weekly fuel prices through mid-August and assume that the price of Brent will average $85 a barrel in September before declining gradually to $75 at year-end and $70 at the end of 2027. We also assume a modest pass-through to core inflation by year-end (0.2%-pt, partly offset by fading wage pressures). Based on these assumptions, headline inflation increases by 0.5%-pt by September to 3.4%oya and then stay there for the rest of the year. We then expect a gradual decline during the course of 2027, as the impact of energy prices fades, together with a decline in core inflation. This

CROSS-ASSET THEMES | US Public Policy Outlook ▪ Midterm elections are unlikely to shift the macro outlook. Major 2025 policy changes occurred via executive authority, and that trend should continue – especially if Democrats gain at least one chamber. Bank regulation proceeds unchanged; AI remains a bipartisan strategic priority. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 Policy implication: Stablecoin reserve requirements are potentially macroeconomic policy. Whether issuers hold bank deposits, Treasury securities, or central bank reserves determines how adoption affects bank credit, safe-asset prices, and monetary transmission. Central Bank Digital Currency CBDC can compete with commercial bank deposits and potentially raise bank funding costs. But disintermediation is not mechanical. As Niepelt (2026) emphasizes, if the central bank recycles funds displaced from deposits back into banks, aggregate bank funding need not decline. The macroeconomic effects therefore depend critically on CBDC remuneration, quantity limits, and central bank balance-sheet policy. A more important concern may arise during stress. A readily accessible risk-free digital asset could accelerate withdrawals from banks. Bidder, Jackson, and Rottner (2025) call this "fast disintermediation." Policy implication: CBDC design must consider not only steady-state bank disintermediation but its effect on the speed and severity of runs. Settlement Speed and Financial Stability Faster settlement reduces counterparty exposure but increases immediate liquidity needs because institutions have less opportunity to net offsetting payments. Faster is therefore not necessarily safer. The optimal settlement speed reflects a trade-off between counterparty risk and liquidity conservation. records.text: US Rates Weekly 21 August 2026 Citi Research 11 –In Figure 19, we estimate the share of T-bill as % of outstanding under the risk scenario that Treasury does not increase coupon auction sizes for the remainder of the administration. The pronounced increase in T-bill share would occur in 2028, and in this scenario, we estimate that T-bill share could be closer to 29% of outstanding by the end of 2028. What to expect next year? nThe debt ceiling next year will keep liquidity elevated. As we have recently discussed, the current debt ceiling sits at $41.1tn, while the debt outstanding subject to this limit is ~$39.9tn. This means that Treasury can issue an additional $1.24tn of debt before they need to implement extraordinary measures and/or draw down the TGA. Since we expect a divided government after the November 2026 elections, we’ll likely see extraordinary measures used along with a drawdown of the TGA next year before the debt ceiling is suspended or raised (see FX Basis Quarterly - Could next week’s FOMC jeopardize the basis?). We think Treasury will deploy extraordinary measures and begin drawing down the TGA balance as soon as May 2027. The move lower in TGA will increase reserves in the system, particularly towards the second half of the year (see Figure 20). At the same time, Treasury bill supply will have to be reduced while the TGA is drawn down. records.text: M Idea 14 August. We expect nominal personal income rose 0.2% m/m. Labor compensation is just slightly stronger than the headline, right on the border of a 0.2% and 0.3%. We expect farm proprietors' income is a slight drag again as Supplemental Disaster Relief Program payments slow. Asset income is also soft after unusually strong dividend payments in June. Real disposable personal income is flat on the month and the saving rate stalls at 2.7%. Durables orders probably continue to expand at a decent pace, but with less of a push from rising prices. GDP. We are tracking 2Q real GDP growth at a 1.4% q/q annual rate, little changed from the advance release's 1.5%. Consumer spending probably is little revised at 3.1-3.2%, but its composition shifts—with a bit more spending on services and a bit less on goods. GLOBAL LIQUIDITY Steady decline: Our global liquidity forecasts suggest a steady decline in G4 central banks reserves, at a year-on-year pace approximating 10%, not too different from 2025’s 11.5% contraction. G4 central banks reserves would reach USD8.56trn at end-2026, USD7.76trn at end-2027, down from USD9.5trn at the end of 2025. By 2028, reserves would still remain larger than pre-Covid. ECB and BoJ lead the drop in global liquidity: With the Fed’s balance sheet on a stabilizing path, the decline would be primarily driven by the ECB and BoJ QT programmes, likely to shrink the amount of reserves by an average 20% and 16% on average, respectively, over the next 2 years. Repo operations at the BoE meanwhile have picked up sharply and thus continue to partly offset QT, leading to a more contained drop averaging just 3.5%. Reserves in excess of 20% of nominal GDP: Relative to GDP, the picture needs to be differentiated. One the one hand G4 reserves would still be in excess of 20% of nominal GDP by 2028, suggesting very accommodative liquidity conditions, well into the ‘abundant’ characterization. On the other hand, the decline is steady, from current 35%, and the main reason for such high levels, optically, is BoJ liquidity, which currently stands at 70% of nominal GDP, compared with 9.6% at the Fed, 15.7% at the ECB, and 21% at the BoE. records.text: i 31 is the only viable candidate; from February onward, the carry tailwind flips to favor BEI (break- even inflation) tighteners in JGBi 29 and 30. This temporal structure breaks into three distinct phases. During Phase 1, which runs through mid-November, a small hump of +3.0 to +3.7bp builds into October 24th, before fully unwinding by November 24th, leaving cumulative carry at +0.5bp for 29 and 30, and +2.0bp for 31. This occurs because the reference index briefly picks up the summer CPI overshoot before the assumed autumn pullback takes it back out. Consequently, chasing this hump has little merit; there is no urgency to enter, and the post-roll-off levels offer a better entry point. Phase 2, from December 24th to February 24th, represents the main event. This two-month window delivers +14.0bp for JGBi 29, +12.4bp for 30, and +12.2bp for 31—representing 96% of the peak cumulative carry for 29 and 30, and over 80% for 31—with a front-loaded profile of +8.0 to +9.0bp from December 24th to January 24th alone. Through the three-month indexation lag, the reference index absorbs the step-up in the September-to-November CPI level, including the October price revisions, plus part of December's data. Critically, by a mid-December entry, the October and November CPI prints are already published; the only unknown is the December CPI, which affects only a portion of the February indexation. These included a writedown of the remaining investment in toob (c.1% of NAV) and the disposal of PPP assets ahead of carrying value. Management reiterated guidance from the recent trading update that the June 2026 NAV per share is expected to be broadly unchanged or slightly higher versus December 2025 but that still implies a relatively muted H1 return of c.3%. • toob writedown (0.9% NAV impact): INPP will effectively exit its equity investment in fibre broadband operator toob, transferring its stake to lenders for a nominal amount. Management believe that conditions in the UK altnet market no longer justify additional capital support. The write-down relates to a £24.1m investment (0.9% of December 2025 NAV), leaving INPP with a smaller £2.6m debt-like exposure and a retained right to participate in any future value realised from a sale of the business. Elsewhere, Community Fibre continues to perform in line with expectations. • PPP disposals: INPP has agreed to sell its stakes in nine UK PPP school projects, covering 15 schools across four London boroughs, for more than £58m. records.text: M Idea 6 Payments Systems Are Not Just Plumbing Payments systems are financial plumbing, but they also generate information relevant to credit allocation. Banks traditionally bundle deposits, payments, transaction data, and lending. As fintech firms capture payment flows, they can therefore shift valuable information away from banks. Parlour, Rajan, and Zhu (2022) show that fintech competition in payments can lower costs while weakening the informational complementarities between payments and bank lending. Similarly, He, Huang, and Zhou (2023) show that greater consumer control over financial data through open banking need not unambiguously improve welfare, because disclosure itself conveys information. Policy implication: Payments policy is therefore partly information policy. Interoperability, data portability, and privacy can promote competition, but they can also reshape information production and credit allocation. The relevant policy trade-off extends beyond payment costs to the consequences of unbundling payments from banking. Competition Between "Money" Digital innovation expands the set of assets that can serve as money, including bank deposits, stablecoins, tokenized deposits, and potentially CBDC. Lines can become blurred. Adoption depends on acceptance, interoperability, and switching costs. In the short sector, the DMO expects to reopen the new 3-year gilt maturing on May 22, 2030, 4F 32 and 4E 33. In the medium sector, it anticipates reopening 4S 36, 4F 37 and 5Q 41, while the choice of gilt for the single long conventional auction remains open. In addition, the DMO plans an index-linked syndication in November 2026 and is seeking views on whether to issue a new or existing index-linked gilt. The reopening of the EUR benchmark CB did not happen via the usual issuers - no German and no French bank has issued any new EUR benchmark CB yet. While the announced increase is fairly small, with a doubling in size amounting to just $16bn per quarter, or $64bn per year if made permanent, the news was delivered outside the normal Quarterly Refunding process, on what was likely to be a quiet morning session ahead of a key FOMC minutes release. The timing appears to have been carefully calibrated to maximize the immediate market impact. Two weeks ago, we highlighted the possibility that Treasury could increase buyback sizes at the August QRA, as it had been one year since the last adjustment and Treasury indicates that it regularly reviews the program. Those increases did not materialize, nor did Treasury provide any indication that buyback changes were under consideration. As a result, this week’s announcement was almost certainly not on anyone’s radar. As Treasury is also committed to keeping coupon issuance sizes unchanged for the next several quarters, the increase in long-end buybacks will effectively be funded with T-bills. The analysis below examines market performance both ahead of and following the initial rate hike. Specifically, we compare returns during the quarter and month preceding the first hike with performance over the subsequent month and quarter, allowing us to assess how different segments of the equity market have historically responded as monetary tightening begins. Our key observation is that the onset of a Fed hiking cycle has historically marked a clear inflection point for equity leadership: while large caps and economically sensitive sectors such as Energy and Industrials often perform well in anticipation of the first hike, equity markets tend to struggle once tightening begins, with small caps experiencing the sharpest underperformance. The precise target level of the coordinated US-Japan intervention remains speculative. Officially, the G7 and G20 consensus is that FX intervention should be used to address excessive volatility rather than target specific exchange rate levels. However, the definition of excessive volatility is inherently ambiguous, and exchange rate levels themselves can influence market volatility. In particular, the yen has continued to weaken regardless of market volatility and despite improving fundamentals, including a better balance of payments backdrop and ongoing BoJ rate hikes. The pass- through of higher costs has also continued in repairs and maintenance. In YoY terms, the increased contribution of energy to Japan-style core inflation was also notable, reflecting higher electricity and piped-gas charges as well as base effects from the previous year. Among private-sector general services, prices for meals outside the home also continued to rise strongly, increasing 0.4% MoM and 4.2% YoY. records.text: Takeaways from Moody’s Company Introduction Moody’s (MCO) is a global provider of credit ratings, research and risk analysis. It operates through two primary segments: Moody’s Investors Service, which issues credit ratings for debt instruments and entities, and Moody’s Analytics, which offers data, software, and advisory services for financial risk and economic analysis. The company’s products are used by financial institutions, corporations, governments, and regulators to assess creditworthiness and manage risk. Moody’s supports decision-making in areas such as investment analysis, regulatory compliance, and economic forecasting. Its services are grounded in quantitative models, proprietary data, and expert research. Product Demo Moody’s product demo walked through AI-powered insurance workflows built on its Intelligent Risk Platform, combining proprietary data, catastrophe models and domain expertise to improve underwriting and portfolio management decisions. The first workflow transformed unstructured insurance submissions, including PDFs, spreadsheets and policy documents, into standardized data for underwriting, reducing a process that can take hours or days manually down to seconds while maintaining source-level traceability and high accuracy. Beyond extracting information, the workflow interpreted complex policy language and automatically mapped risks, occupancy types and coverage details into standardized classifications required for downstream pricing and risk models

Rising long-end yields are raising some concern among poli- cymakers given the pass-through into borrowing costs. Our interest rate strategists see this as the key concern (and not broader market liquidity conditions) that motivated the US Treasury’s surprise announcement to increase the size of buy- back operations for longer-dated nominal Treasuries this week. They view these efforts to manage rates lower as likely to be ineffective, however, if they don’t address the underly- ing sources of pressure. Indeed, actions that move the Trea- sury further away from its “regular and predictable” tenet are likely to drive term premium higher over time, pushing yields higher and the US dollar lower. The implications of rising yields for the Fed and other central banks are not straightforward. As Chair Warsh emphasized in the July FOMC press conference, rising long-term yields reflect a tightening in monetary conditions that limit the need for higher rates. While rising term premia are a drag on their own, expectations for higher short-rates will eventually have to be met. We do not expect any mention of the recent Treasury actions. Looking earlier and more BoJ tightening The BoJ’s preference for a gradual normalization no longer looks tenable. Following last week’s FX intervention, persis- tent yen weakness, and rising inflation expectations have increased pressure for an earlier policy move, leading us to bring forward our next hike from October to September. Fis- cal policy is complicating matters as the government’s planned consumption tax cut will support already-strong domestic demand while mechanically lowering inflation, intensifying pressure on the BoJ to normalize more quickly than its preferred gradual pace. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 Oil Tracker: Elevated Prices, Falling Inventories We continue to track the evolution of petroleum-product inventories, production, trade, and prices. The latest data suggest that crude oil inventories in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) fell further, whereas total US crude oil and petroleum-product inventories edged higher. US domestic crude oil production remained broadly unchanged, while net imports of crude oil and petroleum products maintained their upward trend. Meanwhile, oil prices moved higher. As of August 14, US stocks of crude oil and petroleum products, which represent the EIA's estimate of how many barrels of crude oil and petroleum products are physically sitting in US storage at period-end, remained broadly unchanged from a week earlier. The stocks of crude oil in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) continued to fall to around 293 million barrels, the lowest level since April 1984. The Energy Department said the SPR's minimum inventory is determined by "cavern mechanics," which, when applied across the full system, translates to a conservative operational minimum of about 70 million barrels. If the SPR continues to decline at roughly its recent pace of 30 million barrels every four weeks, inventories would approach the operational minimum by the end of February 2027. The “anti-involution” campaign that started last July led to sharply higher prices in a few sectors, such as steel and polysilicon, for several months. However, without solid demand to support higher prices, and with concerns over labor market stability preventing significant supply cuts, prices eventually fell back to levels similar to, or even below, those seen before the campaign. Why We Are More Concerned About July Data Weakness Over the past year, we have observed a consistent pattern of IP and the NBS manufacturing PMI strengthening into quarter-end months, such as March, June, and September, before falling sequentially in subsequent months, such as April, July, and October (Exhibit 5). In our view, this pattern may reflect manufacturing output being frontloaded into quarter-end months to support stronger readings of production-based official GDP measures. Back in April, we were not too concerned about the sequential decline in growth momentum. However, we think the July weakness points to increased downside risks for three reasons. First, the April growth deceleration came after 5.0% yoy real GDP growth in Q1, which was at the upper end of this year’s 4.5-5% growth target range. records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures The Fed believes that an ‘ample reserves’ or ‘demand-driven floor’ framework is defined by the constellation of money markets trading at the midpoint of the fed funds target range – or more specifically, by TGCR (triparty repo) settling at, or slightly below, IORB (see US rates: Take profit on long May SOFR/FF basis trade, dated 16 December 2025). The idea is that this keeps banks adequately active in both money markets and reserves, gives other liquidity providers a level playing field, and maintains policy rate credibility. The Fed reached ‘ample’ in Q4 2025. once reserves (and RRP balances) as a percentage of bank assets fell below 13%. This prompted the end of QT and the start of reserve management purchases (RMP). The objective of RMPs is to maintain steady-state liquidity levels by offsetting the effects of trend growth in non-reserve liabilities and to accommodate an assumed increase in bank liquidity needs as the economy grows (see US rates: Fed to buy SO-MAny T-bills, dated 3 October 2025). The timing and size of future RMPs seems to be at the New York Fed's discretion, suggesting a more dynamic and active approach to keep USD funding rates close to IORB (see US rates: How do you like them ample reserves, dated 18 May). records.text: gorithms. Many clinical guidelines still rely on a few variables such as age and family history despite their limited ability to identify which patients will develop disease. AI can extract additional signals from mammograms, CT scans, MRIs and longitudinal records containing billions of tokens of patient context. Imaging models have already outperformed traditional risk calculators in forecasting breast and lung cancer. Better predictions could personalize screening, identify patients requiring additional testing and reduce late diagnoses and unnecessary procedures. Healthcare’s standard of care could therefore improve at the pace of model development instead of depending on guidelines updated every several years. Medical AI is shifting toward broad foundation models. Earlier imaging models addressed one modality, disease or task, while emerging models can span imaging formats, anatomical regions and time periods. Pillar-0, an open-source model trained on roughly 200,000 exams, evaluated approximately 350 conditions and performed about ten points better on average than five competing models. Broad pre-training also reduces the data needed to model pediatric diseases, brain cancers and other rare conditions. Pillar-1 extends this approach across mammography, CT and MRI, using tens of millions of exams to generate full radiology reports and disease-specific forecasts. In the meantime, Japan-US coordinated intervention and comments from US Treasury Secretary Bessent expressing expectations for an early rate hike have also helped advance market pricing of a September hike. Taking these factors together, we bring forward our forecast for the next rate hike from October to September. However, we still see both September and October as viable options, with the difference between the two remaining limited. In light of the series of hawkish events, we also change our post-September rate-hike path and now forecast hikes in January and July 2027, with a terminal rate of 1.75% (previously, we expected hikes in October and April, with a terminal rate of 1.5%). records.text: US Rates Weekly 21 August 2026 Citi Research 23 USTs: Demand slowed in June Data on foreign holdings of USTs (TIC) showed that demand for long-term USTs decreased in June after increases in March, April, and May. Overall, foreign holdings of long-term USTs decreased by $28bn on a value-adjusted basis (Figure 44). This was the largest MoM decrease this year and was mainly driven by foreign official investors, whose long-term UST holdings decreased by about $28.3bn (z-score of -0.84). In the first half of the year, foreign official investors purchased around $3bn of USTs. This is significantly better than the first half of 2025, which saw around a $90bn decrease in foreign official long-term holdings. Foreign private investors for June were almost flat with only a $0.4bn increase in long-term holdings (z-score of -0.43). This is the sixth straight month of net UST purchases by foreign private investors. Overall, in the first half of the year, foreign investors purchased $240bn of long-term USTs, which was mainly driven by private investor purchases. That is significantly higher than the $139bn purchases in the first half of last year. After selling $43.5bn of T-bills in May, foreign investors reduced their T-bill holdings by another $29bn in June (z-score of -1.16). Foreign private investors have increased their T-bill holdings by $6.57bn in June. Foreign official investors, though, have decreased their T-bill holdings by $35.6bn in June. We do not think BoJ QT is used as a tool in any such negotiation. But we understand why the market is inclined to arrive at this interpretation as the BoJ’s JGB purchases have influenced JGB supply–demand and yield levels more than they have impacted liquidity. T-bill supply reduction supports 3m xccy basis tightening: Even though tight xccy basis is a disincentive to supply USD via asset-swapped JGB T-bills, 3m xccy basis managed to trade between −15bp and −20bp in 2026. We think that such stability owes much to the reduction of JGB 3m T-bill supply. Weekly supply has fallen from JPY4.7trn in Q1 to JPY3.8trn in July, mainly due to FX intervention and a budget ‘surplus’ (JPY2.6trn) for 2026 when the book was closed. Therefore, even though the spread of JGB T-bills swapped into USD is less than 10bp over SOFR (see lower chart opposite), the xccy basis market can afford to be stable.
