Buybacks are normally conducted in a way that does not alter the outstanding maturity of Treasury debt (e.g. purchases of off-the-run securities are offset by issuance of on-the-run issuance of similar duration). Announcements of changes to the buyback schedule are normally made during the Quarterly Refunding process, part of the Treasury's historical preference for "regular and predictable" issuance patterns. Rising long-term yields likely prompted the expansion in buybacks We see the decision to expand long-end buybacks outside the normal Quarterly Refunding as unusual in this regard, and see the announcement as carrying more informational content than the size of the purchases alone would suggest. Put simply, we interpret the move as evidence that Treasury had become uncomfortable with the speed and character of the rise in long-term interest rates. Ultimately, the Treasury's ability to influence long- term rates is limited, but alterations to buybacks can provide an effective circuit breaker against a disorderly rise in yields, akin to central bank intervention in currency markets. It may be the case that some steepening of the yield curve is acceptable, or even useful if it tightens financial conditions during a period of above-target inflation, but the timing and content of the announcement suggests that we reached a point beyond which further increases in long-term interest rates was becoming counterproductive. Weights are determined by the R-squared values from a single-factor regression between the metric (relative to its 100-day moving min max) and the CSI 300 (relative to 100MA) performance. This weighting method gives greater emphasis to indicators that have historically demonstrated stronger correlations with market movements, ensuring that the overall index reflects sentiment components most relevant to A-share performance. Step 3: Constructing the MSASI (Weighted) Using the weighted sentiment indicator derived in Step 2, we construct the MSASI (Weighted) as the composite measure of overall market sentiment. This index is then re-scaled to a 0-100 range, based on its distance from historical high and low values since January 2024. This scaling allows the indicator to reflect relative sentiment strength over time – where higher readings indicate stronger investor enthusiasm, and lower readings reflect weaker sentiment or risk aversion. Step 4: Constructing the MSASI (Weighted 1MMA) To highlight underlying trends and reduce short-term volatility, we apply a one-month moving average to the MSASI (Weighted). The resulting MSASI (Weighted 1MMA) smooths out high-frequency fluctuations, providing a clearer picture of medium-term sentiment dynamics and improving interpretability for tactical or strategic analysis.

To be sure, Barclays economists do not anticipate any Fed rate hikes through 1H27, arguing that recent CPI, PPI, and import price data, and their pass-through to core PCE inflation, should be sufficiently benign to keep most FOMC members on hold pending further evidence. Nevertheless, market pricing has increasingly shifted toward the possibility of a rate hike by the first FOMC meeting of 2027 (Figure 1), even as both near- and medium-term inflation expectations (Figure 2) have moderated. Against this backdrop, we revisit the historical experience of Fed tightening cycles and examine how different segments of the equity market have performed around the onset of monetary tightening. USD funding associated with the US-Japan investment initia- tive has remained extremely limited so far. Moreover, as financing is likely to continue to rely in part on lending from US banks, we believe the burden on USD funding markets will remain modest for the time being. Meanwhile, Yankee bond issuance by Japanese non-financial corporates continues to remain elevated (see Figure 16Y a n k e e B o n d I s s u a n c e e x c l u d i n g b a n k s ). Because the proceeds raised in foreign currencies are typi- cally converted back into JPY , these flows have continued to exert narrowing pressure on the USD/JPY basis. The key theme for the market remains the balance between USD fund- ing demand associated with the US-Japan investment initiative and JPY conversion demand generated by Yankee bond issuance. That said, while a sharp increase in USD funding demand related to the investment initiative appears unlikely at this stage, wider US credit spreads and seasonal factors could lead to some moderation in Yankee bond issuance toward 4Q. As a result, the key theme into year-end is likely to be a slowdown in JPY conversion demand resulting from weaker Yankee bond issuance, rather than a sharp increase in USD funding demand. records.text: From Weak to Weaker A Weak Batch of Data China’s July activity data weakened from June and disappointed already-low market expectations. Industrial production (IP) was relatively resilient, rising 4.5% yoy, supported by robust export growth. By contrast, retail sales grew only 0.6% yoy, and fixed asset investment (FAI) contracted 6.7% yoy in the first seven months of this year, implying double-digit year-over-year declines in July. With the construction sector still contracting and high-frequency data not pointing to a noticeable pickup, the July official IP and services output index suggest that China’s official real GDP growth is running at a pace of around 4% yoy in the first half of Q3.1 Following the weaker-than-expected macro data and the PBOC’s mid-month overnight reverse repo operations to inject liquidity, our conversations with traders and investors suggest that market expectations of monetary policy easing increased somewhat. The yield on 10-year Chinese Government Bonds (CGB) also fell below 1.70%. Compared with end-February, just before the start of the Iran War, 10-year CGB yields have declined by more than 10bp, suggesting the market’s view that this year’s energy-driven inflation is likely temporary, growth headwinds remain strong, and policy easing is warranted. In sharp contrast, yields on 10-year government bonds in other countries have climbed substantially since late February (Exhibit 2). In the three months to June, the unemployment rate sits at 4.9%. LFS data even pointed to some growth in employment (roughly 190k jobs). And while vacancies have slipped, they haven’t fallen too far behind from the start of the year. Survey data have also seemingly plateaued with some indications of a (marginal) pick up in hiring plans (see the manufacturing PMI, DMP survey, etc.). The resulting combination of proprietary data, recruitment infrastructure and behavioral modeling may prove more defensible than the underlying open-weight models. Simulation can make market research more frequent and accessible. Traditional surveys, focus groups and consulting engagements can be slow, expensive and difficult to repeat, limiting how frequently organizations test new ideas. Simulation platforms allow users to evaluate pricing strategies, product concepts, customer segments and marketing initiatives through iterative counterfactual analysis. Users can filter populations, ask follow-up questions and generate updated reports without commissioning a new study for every scenario. Early customers are also using Simile to conduct research that previously would not have justified the time or budget required by traditional methods. Simulation could therefore expand research demand while materially reducing the incremental time and cost of testing additional scenarios. Trust and uncertainty remain critical adoption barriers. Enterprise users need to understand not only what a simulation concludes but also how much confidence to place in the answer. For Japan, the local trough came in late June, just before fiscal concerns intensified around the government's annual policy blueprint. Our 5s10s term premium measure, an average of the ACM and KW models, has risen since then—a move that ranks in the 75th percentile historically, going back to 2000. This turn occurred at almost the same time as in the US, where the trough in term premia coincided with Chair Warsh's June press conference. This rise in term premium is consistent with our longstanding outlook. With the BoJ tapering its bond purchases, the supply that must be absorbed by price - sensitive private investors continues to grow. Fiscal expansion —including the consumption tax cut on food (representing roughly JPY 5.8tn/yr in foregone revenue)—adds further pressure. Meanwhile, upside inflation risk remains elevated. The fact that August's super-long bond sell-off (which saw the 30-year yield approach 4.1%, the high for this move) was driven by term premium repricing rather than by transactional flows supports this view. Boonnuch). From the sovereign perspective, the budget is a near-term positive given the key drivers of Indonesia’s underperformance have been negative investor sentiment around policy uncertainty, fiscal credibility and external buffers. The recent BI leadership transition has added to these con- cerns, given the already elevated focus on central bank independence, but Senior Deputy Governor Destry Damayanti serving as acting governor and her reported nomination as a governor candidate should help signal policy continuity in the near term. Destry is a well-es- tablished central banker and the market should take some comfort from continuity at BI (Indonesia: Rupiah defense meets leadership transition, C. Boonnuch). However, the fiscal targets remain ambitious and we believe the market will need to see evidence of implementation before fully pricing in the improvement. records.text: 2 Japan Viewpoint | 24 August 2026 Defense lines, intentions, target levels, and strategy Intervention involving four key actors The latest FX intervention involves four key actors: Japan’s Ministry of Finance (MoF), the US Treasury, the Takaichi administration, and the Bank of Japan (BoJ). However, differences in mandates and institutional objectives suggest they are unlikely to be acting with complete unity. Uncertainty surrounding each institution's priorities, as well as the balance of influence among them, makes intervention strategy and tactics difficult to interpret. Nevertheless, intervention actions to date and remarks by senior officials provide several clues. Japan's defense line and the authorities' intentions First, the Japanese government's apparent defense zone for the yen lies in the USD/JPY 160-165 range. Both the April-May intervention campaign and the intervention conducted in July-August were launched after USD/JPY had moved into the 160s and 162s, respectively (Exhibit 1). Specific levels such as 160 or 165 may not carry particular economic significance. However, round numbers such as 5-yen and 10-yen intervals are important psychological milestones, while the cycle high near 164 represents the weakest yen level since 1986. However, when banks shift from BoJ current account balances into JGBs, they face two key constraints: the leverage ratio and IRRBB (Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book). With regard to the leverage ratio, BoJ current account balances are excluded from total expo- sure, whereas JGBs are included, meaning that such a shift would weigh on leverage ratios. In addition, moving from zero-interest-rate-risk BoJ current account balances into JGBs with interest-rate risk would worsen IRRBB. Token demand from world models creates an S curve that will layer on top of our enterprise forecast for compute to support 24x more tokens in the next 5 years. This likely drives tighter supply/demand dynamics for longer, benefiting Microsoft, Oracle and CoreWeave. Durable differentiation will come from ownership of workflow context, not just data. The vertical vs. horizontal debate increasingly misses the real source of differentiation. Simple AI wrappers appear most vulnerable as model capabilities improve, while horizontal platforms benefit from scale but remain exposed to feature competition. The strongest positions may belong to workflow-native software companies that combine domain expertise, embedded processes, and proprietary context. In an AI world, owning the workflow may matter more than owning the application. The same principle applies to data. Access to customer data is often mistaken for a moat, but many forms of enterprise data access are effectively commoditized. Any vendor integrated into the same systems can often see the same underlying information. The more durable advantage comes from being embedded in the workflow that continuously creates, structures, and enriches that data over time. As software creation becomes cheaper and faster, unique workflow context may become one of the few remaining forms of defensible differentiation.

It is no longer driven by a net trade surplus, but rather income from Japan’s huge overseas asset holdings. In 2025 Japan actually ran a small deficit on its trade in goods but the income earned from overseas investments still produced its largest ever current account surplus. Japan’s Net International Investment Position (NIIP) is a surplus of over Y560tr (a little over $3.5tr) or, around 90% of Japan ese nominal GDP. Numbers thus far in 2026 would seem to bear this out with a net current account surplus so far this year of Y17tr which if repeated in H2 would be another record surplus. March alone set a new monthly high of Y4.8tr. The takeaway is that the current account surplus is likely to remain structurally supported. Its large net international investment position provides a substantial income stream, and continued surpluses add to the overseas asset base. Why then, is the Yen so weak? The further decline in LFPR in July reflected those younger than and older than prime age. We do not think the younger group is disengaging from the labor market; and we don’t think the older group is disengaging any faster than the normal retirement pace. Both the front and back contracts currently share the same CTD bond, the 1E39 gilt. The implied repo rate is higher when delivery occurs on the first delivery date, implying that shorts are likely to deliver at the start of the delivery period, on Tues day, 1 September. Our models suggest that the fair value of the switch option is negligible for the U6 contract, while we estimate the fair value at 0.56p for the Z6 contract. In our view, higher rates are more a function of strong nominal growth as opposed to structural concerns around the debt and deficit. We think the coming 1-2 weeks of very light supply and strong month- end demand at these higher yields levels will reset dealer inventories lower prior to Labor Day but will be watching closely the extent to which this plays out. Over the past 4 years, about 70% of the total September supply has come in the first two weeks post Labor Day. However, last year September supply set a new record of $214bn, but given a later than typical Labor Day holiday this year and a very heavy wave of supply in August, it is a little less likely that September supply will hit new record highs. records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 21 Aug 2026 10:44:52 ET │ 9 pages US Economics Stronger services PMI out of line with hard data CITI'S TAKE The preliminary release of August PMI data showed a strong increase in services PMI to 56.8 but a slight pullback in manufacturing to 53.2. Softer manufacturing may be partly a consequence of usual summer production holidays and could bounce back. Still, we are cautious to take many signals from stronger services PMI as survey data are a bit out of line with recently softer hard activity data to start Q3. The employment component has increased substantially in recent months but has not tracked well with hard employment data (and at points has even been inversely correlated). Price indices, both input and output prices and in services and manufacturing, fell in August. We do not take signals from survey data literally for our inflation forecasts, but this at least suggests price pressures are not continuing to build even after months of higher energy costs. records.text: rate hikes in September 2026, January 2027 and July 2027, with the terminal rate reaching 1.75%. Previously, we had expected hikes in October 2026 and April 2027, with a terminal rate of 1.50% (details in Our call for next rate hike frontloaded to September with latest BoJ summary, 10 August). This upward revision to the BoJ's hiking path, accompanied by a higher terminal rate, exerts a broadly parallel upward shift on the policy-rate component of JGB yields (risk-neutral yields; Figure 6). For example, it implies roughly 17bp of upward pressure in the 2y sector and around 23bp in the 10y sector (one year from now, the impact on shorter maturities would also approach 25bp). The revised terminal-rate assumption is also broadly consistent with the distribution of 2y- forward short-term interest rates implied by the swaption market ( Figure 7). At the same time, however, the width of that distribution, reflecting the possibility of an even higher terminal rate, has expanded further relative to previous estimates. One reason market participants have broadly revised up their BoJ hiking expectations may be the growing pressure on the BoJ to tighten policy. This began with the historic coordinated JPY- buying intervention by the Japanese and US authorities at the end of July and was reinforced by comments from US Treasury Secretary Bessent, who stated that he believed Governor Ueda would “take the necessary actions” (TBS, 5 August). records.text: Japan Macro Watch21 August 2026 ab 6 GDP update: maintaining a constructive outlook Although this week's GDP release came in below expectations, it does not materially alter our outlook. We have revised our FY2026 and FY2027 real GDP growth forecasts down by 0.1ppt each, to 0.9% and 1.1%, respectively. Even after these adjustments, our forecasts remain above consensus by 0.3ppt and 0.2ppt. While consensus expectations imply near-zero growth in Q3, we continue to project solid expansion following Q2's 1.1% annualized growth rate, with Q3 growth reaching 0.9% annualized. July trade data showed that real exports remain stronger than imports, and we continue to expect domestic demand to hold up well. Incoming indicators suggest that consumer spending has recovered meaningfully from the weather-related weakness seen in June. Credit card spending data point to a strong rebound in July, while robust real disposable income growth should continue to support household consumption. Corporate demand also remains healthy. This week's machinery orders data suggest that domestic demand is still firm. Although business investment has been weak over the past two quarters, we expect capital expenditure to return to growth in the coming quarters. Our outlook for food inflation remains the same as our last update, with, in our view, the July print validating this outlook. We continue to see the balance of risks as to the downside in the near-term, but to the upside in 2027. As the energy shock and climate induced disruption of food production begins to feed into consumer prices, we expect FAT inflation to accelerate over 3% y/y next year. These impulses will develop alongside weak base effects from this year, which could add further pressure to the annual inflation rate. We forecast FAT inflation to be on average 19bp lower over the next 12 months. Medium-term outlook In our view, recent data have continued to show the labour market as loose, which we believe is weighing on inflationary pressure in the UK economy. Non-energy inflation reached 2.4% y/y in July, down 2pp in the last 12 months, and is now at the lowest level since July 2021 (Figure 14). Our expectation at the beginning of the conflict (see here) for weak domestic dynamics to weigh on inflation is currently being validated by the incoming data, and as such, we maintain our current expectation for limited indirect and second-round effects. The key risk to this outlook remains a strong reacceleration in energy prices due to developments in the Middle East. records.text: M Idea 2 Lower participation rates could lessen labor slack But we expect prime-age participation to rebound In the year through May, the labor force participation rate (LFPR) moved sideways, after correcting for the BLS annual population adjustments. However, in the two months since then, it fell a cumulative 0.4 pct pt, raising concerns that labor supply is tightening. Most of the decline was in June and reflected prime-age workers, with only a very limited rebound in July. We expect further rebound. The further decline in LFPR in July reflected those younger than and older than prime age. We do not think the younger group is disengaging from the labor market; and we don’t think the older group is disengaging any faster than the normal retirement pace. Finally, there’s a potential impact from the revocation of Temporary Protected Status for unauthorized Haitian immigrants, but we think the effects on labor supply are likely to be small and slow. records.text: 21 August 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 29 The cost of Japan's FX intervention Steven Zeng, CFA | Strategist | +1-212-250-9373 Note: This note was originally published on 19 August 2026 Japan has spent roughly $169bn on FX intervention this year: $73bn between April and May, and an estimated $96bn in July. Based on the June Treasury TIC data released this week, we estimate that the first round of intervention consumed more than half of Ja pan’s T-bill holdings, which fell from $153bn at the end of April to $70bn at the end of June. Although there was no FX intervention in June, we assume the decline in T-bills was due to Japan rebuilding its dollar deposits at the Fed’s foreign repo pool, which were drawn down in late April before rebounding in June. The July intervention is not yet covered by the TIC data. In the July TIC report, due mid-next month, we would expect to see a further decline in Japan’s T -bill holdings. While there have been suggestions that Japan could use the Fed’s FIMA repo facility to finance its interventions, relying on dollar deposits and proceeds from maturing T -bills makes more sense economically. Both dollars invested at the Fed’s foreign repo p ool and short -dated bills earn a lower yield than the cost of borrowing from FIMA. That said, once Japan exhausts its remaining T-bill holdings (plus other maturing coupon securities), use of FIMA repo could become more likely should additional FX intervention be needed. This divergence is consistent with the US remaining the primary source of macro volatility this year, while Europe has been comparatively uneventful. The US market is also more directly exposed to AI-driven themes, with the addition of several hyperscaler names to CDX.IG this year likely providing a further boost to trading activity. iTraxx SenFin recorded the weakest growth among the major CDS indices, with volumes rising just 4% y/y. This is perhaps unsurprising given the absence of European political volatility, which has historically acted as a catalyst for activity in the index. Furthermore, European financials have exhibited a relatively muted response to this year's geopolitical developments compared with other sectors, likely lessening the need to express views on the sector at a macro level. That said, with French elections scheduled for April 2027, political risk could move back into focus over 2H, potentially providing a tailwind for a pickup in SenFin volumes. Election risk pricing has shown a tendency to soften into the event, although the somewhat subdued pricing in the current cycle has perhaps more to do with the broader risk- supportive backdrop rather than pricing in an anticipated con- solidation ahead of October. As per the results, in 2018 the market appears to have overestimated the event-driven rally (options pricing implied an ~8% total, while BRL moved only 3.7% across the first and second rounds), while in 2022 options implied a ~6.8% move across both rounds, which roughly matched the realized BRL move. Our expected risk/reward appears broadly symmetric from current levels. From the current spot, the volatility pricing would imply USD/BRL moving towards the 5.50 area if the election outcome is perceived as unfavorable for fiscal consolidation. This scenario would equate to roughly a 12% BRL depreciation from levels seen in May, versus the 16% moves observed over the same May–October window in 2018 and 2022. A smaller move would be reasonable to expect if the external backdrop remains supportive for EM assets, while positive carry may at some moment allow us to re-enter BRL longs once the negative outcome is priced-in. records.text: /08/2026 GLOBAL LIQUIDITY Private sector QT also in progress: The BoJ’s steady QT has also led to decline in deposit relative to nominal GDP at the private banks (Figure x). While such relationship is natural, it is still interesting that the strong loan growth, about 4% yoy, has not managed to offset sufficiently. We think that the sense of despot reduction may be actually felt stronger than the optical decline in deposit/nominal GDP or BoJ’s current account. We think there are two reasons for this. One is the time lag in fiscal spending. When private sector buys JGBs, the deposit falls first, but it is recovered when government makes fiscal spending. But the fiscal spending has often taken a form of “fund” or “reserve” or did not actually get delivered due to shortage of resources. Therefore, there is often good period when the “money” is not locked. Another reason is the steepness of the curve. Because JPY curve is steep, holders of cash (liquidity) has a large opportunity cost relative to investing in long term assets. The sense does not go as far as “shortage”, but certainly not surplus, which is a factor for tighter USDJPY xccy basis. QT goes on regardless of rate hike: As the market recognizes the government’s preference against rate hike, we often hear an interpretation such as if the BoJ wants to hike, it has to slow down QT more than more than it decided for post Q2 2027. records.text: records. Specialized vendors can now work with health systems and make clinical data available to well-funded developers. Data pricing has also become more rational as providers recognize that inaccessible archives have limited standalone value and the marginal value of additional samples declines. Capital, data access and the ability to combine clinical expertise with compute should therefore become increasingly important competitive advantages. Personalized care requires AI to optimize actions, not only predict outcomes. Identifying elevated cancer risk creates limited value unless the healthcare system can determine whether a patient should receive an MRI, return in six months or follow another pathway. This can be framed as a control problem where clinical context represents the state, the intervention represents the action and the reward balances outcomes against cost and procedural harm. Historical patient trajectories and clinical knowledge can support simulations of alternative screening or treatment schedules. The resulting policy can also incorporate individual preferences and different tolerances for testing. AI could therefore replace fixed population schedules with dynamic pathways that personalize both disease risk and intervention trade-offs. Clinical evaluation must improve as quickly as medical models. records.text: US High Yield Reading between the liens With second-lien bonds creeping back into HY, we study 1L/2L relationships across the index. We find that 1Ls trade very differently across various forms of capital structures. We also find wide dispersion in 1L/2L relationships based on issuer quality and the loss-absorbing cushion beneath lenders. For our latest US High Yield company rating changes, click here. For our sector ratings, click here. • Second-lien bonds are making a comeback in US HY . Capital structures with 1L and 2L debt have grown increasingly common since 2023, and junior secured bonds now represent roughly 3.2% of the HY index compared with 1.3% of the leveraged loan index. • Not all forms of junior cushion beneath 1Ls are valued equally. 1Ls with unsecured debt beneath them have generally traded tighter than comparable 1Ls in 1L-only structures, while 1Ls with 2L debt beneath them now trade wider, even after controlling for ratings. We believe this is driven in part by the rationales for second-lien issuance. • The 2L-1L spread basis has widened dramatically. The median basis has increased from 91bp in January 2025 to 396bp today, while the unsecured-secured basis has remained broadly range-bound; investors now receive roughly 5x more spread pickup for moving from 1L to 2L than from secured to unsecured. • But security selection remains critical, as this cohort is of lower credit quality. The cohort of issuers with 2Ls outstanding is small and highly dispersed. 31%

records.text: ppliances, electronic equipment and machinery all fit this description, the first three appear unlikely to see major new policies stimulating production, as property destocking is still ongoing and auto and home appliance sales were already frontloaded by the government-subsidized consumer goods trade-in program. This leaves electronic equipment and machinery, including semiconductors, as the likely sectors to receive additional policy support to expand production. Housing: On August 18, the State Council announced changes to the Housing n Provident Fund (HPF) rules to expand its use. The HPF is a mandatory, government-backed savings scheme in which employers and employees both contribute to individual accounts for housing-related consumption, such as buying, renting, or renovating a home. Currently, interest rates on HPF loans are 50bp lower than mortgage rates for first-time homebuyers. However, we think the impact of the latest announcement will only have a marginal impact on the property market, as many cities have already relaxed local HPF rules, benefiting low-end properties. Agentic adoption should advance fastest where outputs are verifiable and responsibility for errors is clear. Open models should gain token volume across routine tasks, and frontier models should retain value where reliability justifies higher costs, supporting continued token and compute growth. Morgan Securities plc Europe Economic Research Euro area fuel prices: Looking under every rock 21 August 2026 J P M O R G A N The pass-through at first sight appears low. This is because many components of fuel prices are sticky, including excise duties and transport costs. EC weekly fuel prices are available excluding excise duties and taxes. Using these data show that the pass-through is larger. In this case, a 10% increase in Brent prices lifts consumer fuel prices ex. taxes and duties by 7.4%. Most of this pass-through is also seen within two weeks and continues to build over time. In the long-run, which would take more than a year, we estimate that the pass- through excluding taxes and excise duties is full. Up like a rocket, down like a feather An important question is whether fuel prices respond similar- ly to crude price increases and crude price declines. Our anal- ysis suggests that this is the case (Figure 4). The gap is larger in the very short term. The pass-through of a 10% Brent price increase within two weeks (including taxes) is 3.4%, versus 1.2% for a 10% Brent price decline. This gap reduces as time passes: the pass-through of Brent price declines catches up with the pass-through of Brent price increases. The gap after a month is economically low, representing a few basis points for headline inflation (with sizeable model error bands on top). 0 1 2 3 4 00 05 10 15 20 25 30 35 4

records.text: Outlook for the economy and prices (last updated 21 August) Real GDP growth came to +1.1% q/q saar in the initial estimate for Q2 (Q1: +1.9%), a third consecutive quarter in positive territory, but sharply undershot both Bloomberg consensus (+2.0%) and our estimate (+2.1%). Looking ahead, we expect large wage hikes to support private consumption, although growth in consumption is likely to remain moderate for the time being, as inflation rises further from autumn and the boost from durable-goods demand, including autos, runs its course. Capex is expected to remain firm, supported by demand for labor-saving investment to address labor shortages and high corporate profits. In terms of overseas demand, the temporary increase in R&D services that lifted exports in Q2 is likely to drop out, while crude oil import volumes recover, reducing the contribution to growth in Q3. From H2 FY26, fiscal policy under the Takaichi administration also appears likely to contribute modestly to growth. In the July nationwide CPI, there were signs that the impact of higher crude oil prices was beginning to feed through to some food products, resin products, engine oil and other items. Looking ahead, we expect such upward pressure from crude oil, as well as JPY depreciation, to continue materializing gradually. Aggregate hedge ratios have fallen to 42.9% as of June 2026,3 well below the approximately 60% level reported by the FSC at end-2025 and materially below the 65-70% that prevailed historically. The decline reflects the transition to the new IFRS 17 and TW- ICS framework, which allows insurers to smooth FX-related earnings volatility and rely more heavily on FX volatility reserves. An equally important development has been the continued expansion of FX volatility reserves. Under the FSC's revised framework, the maximum industry reserve capacity increased from TWD300bn to TWD960bn,4 while insurers were granted greater flexibility to reclassify existing reserves into FX reserves. The framework also allows a higher offset ratio against FX gains and losses, reducing insurers' dependence on traditional hedging instruments. Together, these changes have materially increased the sector's ability to absorb FX volatility without relying solely on NDFs and FX swaps. In practice, rising reserve capacity helps explain why hedge ratios have continued to fall even as foreign asset allocations remain elevated. Under the previous framework, insurers relied heavily on hedging instruments to manage earnings volatility. Our base case since October 2025 has been that steady-state RMPs of T-bills would average USD25bn/month to maintain reserve levels between 11–13% of bank assets, which we have defined as ‘ample’ relative liquidity levels (see top chart opposite). Outside of typical deficit-related seasonality, this should keep USD funding rates stable for the foreseeable future. We believe the objective of Fed chair Kevin Warsh’s new ‘task force’ on the balance sheet is to reduce its size through a moderation in the supply of reserves by as much as USD700bn (3pp of relative liquidity). However, this would need to be accompanied by a similar decline in reserve demand achieved through supervisory and regulatory (S&R) reform – and by a clear and coordinated messaging effort (see Fed: The balance sheet under Warsh, dated 22 May). When all is said and done, we think the USD funding environment is likely to remain stable in the long-run, and we see no signs of funding risk on the horizon (see lower chart opposite). AI is compressing complex risk workflows from days to seconds. Insurance submissions arrive through inconsistent spreadsheets, PDFs and free-form documents that must be converted into structured data before pricing and portfolio analysis can begin. Complicated submissions may require days of manual work, while Moody’s demonstrated AI reducing the process to seconds. The system must interpret nonstandard policy terms, classify exposures and encode information into insurance-specific taxonomies rather than simply extract text. Errors can affect pricing, loss estimates and portfolio concentration, making domain expertise and validation essential. High-value enterprise AI adoption is increasingly centered on automating complex workflows rather than conversational assistance. Vertical AI benefits from specialized context and validated domain models. Moody’s insurance platform represents information through risk-native concepts such as policies, portfolios, contracts and exposures instead of generic data fields. Agents can combine this context with established catastrophe, pricing and simulation models to analyze portfolios and loss scenarios.
